docs.title: TRFlearn
docs.text:
Temporal Response Function estimation in PyTorch — regularized lagged linear models between continuous stimuli and neural responses (MEG/EEG), on CPU or GPU, with named features, per-feature time windows, segment-aware cross-validation, MNE-native I/O and cohort-level statistics.

Get started API reference Tutorials

pip install -e .  ·  CPU / CUDA  ·  MNE Raw  ·  grand average + TFCE

docs.title: Why TRFlearn
docs.text:
• PyTorch core

    Regularized normal equations (XᵀX + λ·M)·TRF = Xᵀy solved on CPU or GPU. Ridge, temporal Laplacian, or an unregularized cross-correlation baseline.

  • Named features & interactions

    Select features by name, add interactions (outer products), give each its own delay window, and expand amplitudes with spline bases — all in one spec.

  • Three CV paradigms

    pooled k-fold, Crosse–Lalor averaged leave-one-out, or a simple train_test split — one factory, TRFModel(cv=...), same call surface.

  • MNE-native

    Feed mne.Raw targets, keep the montage, and export kernels as Evoked for the full MNE plotting toolbox.

  • Cohort analysis

    TRFGroup fits one spec across subjects, then grand-averages and runs threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) over delay × sub-feature × channel.

  • Plotting built in

    On-demand figures at the model, subject and cohort level: butterfly + mean/std, TFCE shading, and mne.Evoked passthroughs — see Plotting.

docs.title: 60-second example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from trflearn import TRFData, TRFModel

# Toy data: 2 minutes at 128 Hz, one stimulus feature, 8 EEG channels whose
# response is the stimulus filtered by a known kernel, plus noise.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
envelope = rng.standard_normal((128 * 120, 1))
true_trf = np.sin(np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 40))
response = np.convolve(envelope[:, 0], true_trf)[: len(envelope), None]
eeg = response + 5 * rng.standard_normal((len(envelope), 8))

data = TRFData(features={"envelope": envelope}, y=eeg, sample_rate=128)
data.create_partitions()   # 5 contiguous folds
model = TRFModel(
    TRFDataset=data, features=["envelope"], default_window=(-0.1, 0.5)
)
best_regularization, (trfs, r2) = model.gridsearchCV(validation_plot=False)
model.plot_average("envelope")

The Quickstart walks through the same steps and what each one returns.

docs.title: Development environment
docs.text:
The reference setup is a conda environment named trflearn-dev on Python 3.10, with the pinned versions in requirements.txt and the package installed in editable mode with every extra (MNE, the test suite, the docs toolchain and the tutorials' dependencies):

git clone https://github.com/NeuroLIAA/TRFlearn
cd TRFlearn

conda create -y -n trflearn-dev python=3.10
conda env config vars set PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1 -n trflearn-dev   # isolate from user-site
conda activate trflearn-dev

# Only with an NVIDIA GPU: the CUDA build first (see below)
pip install torch==2.11.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e ".[dev]"

Without a GPU, skip the CUDA line: requirements.txt then installs the CPU build on Windows and macOS. On Linux it would pull the CUDA build from PyPI; use --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu in that line instead to avoid the download. Installation explains how to tell which CUDA version your driver supports. Check the environment with the test suite:

pytest -q -n auto --dist loadscope

Develop on 3.10: it is the minimum requires-python allows and the oldest job in the CI matrix, and a bug that only appears on the oldest interpreter is invisible from a newer one — while the matrix covers the newer end for you. requirements.txt records the versions 3.10 resolves to; bump them together when a dependency changes.

docs.title: The benchmark's environments
docs.text: benchmark/ compares TRFlearn with other TRF packages, and some of them cannot share an environment with it: naplib and eelbrain live in a second conda environment, trflearn-benchmark, and Unfold.jl and the MATLAB mTRF-Toolbox run in Julia and Octave. None of it is needed to develop or test TRFlearn; benchmark/README.md lists each runtime and what runs in it.

docs.title: Linting
docs.text:
ruff check .          # what CI runs on every push and pull request
ruff check --fix .    # applies the safe fixes (import order, `typing` names)

ruff.toml holds the rules. In trflearn/ they enforce 79-column lines, type hints on every signature, NumPy docstrings and PEP 8 names (linear-algebra names such as X and XTY excepted); tests/ and the root scripts get the line length, import order and bug checks without the rest. The version is pinned in the lint extra, because a new ruff release can add checks.

There is deliberately no ruff format: it would rewrite nearly every file and splits expressions differently from the style used here. So what the linter cannot see is left to review: a bracket that breaks across lines closes on a line of its own, and comments explain the why, not the what.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text: pytest -q

docs.title: In parallel
docs.text:
The suite is dominated by model fits, so it parallelises well:

pytest -q -n auto --dist loadscope

--dist loadscope is not optional. The expensive fixtures are module-scoped: they fit a model once and hand every test in the file a copy.deepcopy. The default --dist load scatters individual tests across workers, which splits each file and makes every worker refit — parallel, and slower than running serially.

-n auto takes one worker per core. Each worker runs PyTorch and numpy's BLAS, which would each open one thread per core, so on a many-core machine the workers would fight for the same cores. tests/conftest.py gives every worker physical cores // workers threads instead; an OMP_NUM_THREADS you set takes precedence, as on CI, which sets it to 1.

Coverage is unaffected — pytest-cov combines the workers' data and coverage-summary.json comes out identical to a serial run.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
pytest --cov

Branch coverage and the measured package come from pyproject.toml, so no flags are needed. A complete, passing run rewrites coverage-summary.json at the repo root; the next docs build turns it into the Test coverage page, which records both when the suite last ran and when trflearn/ last changed, and warns on the page itself when the second is newer than the first.

Runs that should not publish a number are skipped and say so: a -k or -m filter, an explicit test file, --last-failed, or any failure. Set TRFLEARN_COVERAGE_DOCS=0 to opt out entirely. Commit coverage-summary.json when the figure changes meaningfully — CI builds the docs without running the suite, so that file is the only thing the site has to go on.

docs.title: Building the docs locally
docs.text:
mkdocs serve            # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict   # production build into ./site (fails on broken refs)

The API pages are generated from the source docstrings by mkdocstrings, and the "Examples using ..." blocks under each object are generated by docs_backrefs.py from the notebooks themselves.

Everything docs_hooks.py writes into docs/ at build time is git-ignored: the Tutorials and Examples sections are copies of the executed notebooks in tutorials/ and examples/ (each folder's README.md becomes the section index), and Test coverage is rendered from coverage-summary.json by coverage_report.py.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
Pushing to main triggers the docs GitHub Actions workflow, which builds the site and publishes it to the gh-pages branch. Enable it once under Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → gh-pages. To publish manually:

mkdocs gh-deploy --force

docs.title: Group analysis — TRFGroup
docs.text:
TRFGroup declares a model spec once, without data, then fits it per subject in a loop, keeping only the minimal per-subject results (kernels, held-out metric, selected λ, an optional bootstrap distribution) and discarding each full model — so a large cohort stays memory-light.

import numpy as np
from trflearn import TRFData, TRFGroup

group = TRFGroup(
    features=["envelope", "spectrogram"],
    default_window=(-0.2, 0.6),        # same knobs as TRFModel
    cv="pooled",
    solver="ridge-laplacian",
    regularization_grid=np.logspace(-3, 6, 20),
    regularization_strategy="mean-curve",       # one λ for every subject
)


def load(subject_id):
    features, eeg = cohort[subject_id]
    data = TRFData(features=features, y=eeg, sample_rate=128)
    data.create_partitions()           # 5 folds, stratified by segment
    return data


for subject_id in cohort:              # 1. each subject's validation curve
    group.search_subject(load(subject_id), subject_id)
group.share_regularization()                    # 2. the best λ of the mean curve
for subject_id in cohort:              # 3. every subject at that λ
    group.fit_subject(load(subject_id), subject_id)

group.summary()                        # cohort size + descriptive stats
ga = group.grand_average()             # {spec: {"mean","std","sem","n"}}

The kernels it averages, tests and draws are in original units, the recording's unit per unit of each feature. Why both choices matter when subjects are compared is in One λ for every subject and Kernel units.

docs.title: Cluster permutation tests
docs.text:
group.permutation_test(spec) tests that a feature's kernel departs from zero across the cohort while controlling the family-wise error over the whole grid. It wraps mne.stats.spatio_temporal_cluster_1samp_test and builds the full adjacency (delay — and, for a multi-column feature, sub-feature — lattices × channel adjacency) from the montage kept in TRFData.info, so the cohort's targets must be MNE Raw.

threshold picks the flavour:

from trflearn.statistics import t_threshold

# Threshold-free cluster enhancement (the default): a per-point p-value, no
# cluster-forming threshold to guess.
t_obs, pvals = group.permutation_test("envelope")
t_obs, pvals = group.tfce("envelope")               # the same thing, named

# Cluster mass at a fixed cluster-forming t: one p-value per cluster, shared by
# every point in it.
thr = t_threshold(0.01, df=len(group) - 1)
t_obs, pvals = group.permutation_test("envelope", threshold=thr)

Cluster inference does not localize

Under cluster mass the p-value belongs to the cluster, not to a delay or a channel. The honest statement is "this cluster is significant"; reading a latency off its edges is not supported by the test. TFCE gives a genuine per-point p-value instead.

t_obs, pvals = group.tfce("envelope")      # (n_delays, n_channels)
t_obs, pvals = group.tfce("spectrogram")   # (n_delays, n_subfeatures, n_channels) — kept

A scalar feature returns maps of shape (n_delays, n_channels); a multi-column feature keeps its sub-features natively — nothing is averaged away. Results are cached in group.stats_[spec].

docs.title: Comparing two cohorts
docs.text:
The permutation tests above ask whether a kernel differs. A different question is which model spec describes the cohort better — envelope alone against envelope + onsets — and no held-out metric answers it, because adding a feature block almost never makes the fit worse. compare_to ranks the two by AIC and BIC, which price the complexity:

lean = TRFGroup(["envelope"], (-0.1, 0.4), criteria=True)
rich = TRFGroup(["envelope", "onsets"], (-0.1, 0.4), criteria=True)
for sid, data in subjects.items():        # the same subjects into both
    lean.fit_subject(data, sid)
    rich.fit_subject(data, sid)

table = lean.compare_to(rich)           # a CohortComparison
print(table.summary())                  # both criteria, one row each

table.best["bic"]                       # 'self' or 'other'
table.n_favouring_self["bic"]           # how many subjects prefer `lean`
table.wilcoxon["bic"]                   # (statistic, p) across subjects
table.delta_bic_per_channel             # (n_channels,) — for a topomap

criteria=True is not optional and has to be decided before fitting: the cohort keeps arrays and discards each subject's model, so the criteria cannot be recovered afterwards without refitting. With diagnostics=True also on, both reports come out of one pass over each subject's design instead of two.

The sign is the opposite of the contrasts above

The difference is self - other and lower is better for both criteria, so a positive delta favours other. In permutation_test_contrast, a positive t_obs favours self. The two methods sit next to each other and disagree because the underlying quantities do.

docs.title: Two aggregations, both reported
docs.text:
Each subject contributes one number — their criterion summed over channels — and what to do with that (n_subjects,) vector is a modelling choice, so both answers are given rather than one chosen quietly:

reading keys what it assumes random effects .median, .n_favouring_self, .wilcoxon each subject is one observation; an unusual subject shows up in the vector instead of dragging the answer fixed effects .total the cohort as one large model with per-subject parameters; dominated by whoever contributed the most data

When the two disagree, that is the finding. It is the signature of an atypical subject, and reporting only the one that agrees with you is what this return value is shaped to prevent.

The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is the honest statistic here, and for a specific reason: the per-subject criteria are overconfident, because both assume independent samples and EEG residuals are autocorrelated — but that inflation is within a subject. Whether N independent subjects fell on the same side does not inherit it. Signed-rank rather than a t-test because one badly conditioned design produces an outlier of arbitrary size, which a rank test ignores. Below six subjects the test cannot reach p < 0.05 at any effect size, so it returns nan with a warning instead of a number nobody should quote.

compare_to refuses a comparison it cannot interpret: cohorts with different subjects, a cohort fitted without criteria=True, or any subject whose two fits do not describe the same response (different row count, channel count, or raw y'y). A criterion is an absolute number attached to one dataset, and nothing in the arithmetic notices when the dataset changed.

docs.title: Plotting a cohort
docs.text:
The group uses the shared plotting API:

group.plot_features()                             # one summary column per feature
group.plot_average("envelope", show_stats=True)   # green/red significance shading
group.plot_joint("envelope")                      # grand-average Evoked passthrough
group.plot_metric_topomap()                       # grand-average metric
group("s01").plot_average("envelope")             # a single subject's view

docs.title: Reading a subject's numbers
docs.text:
group(subject_id) gives the plots; group.results(subject_id) gives the numbers that were stored when that subject was fitted:

res = group.results("s01")
res["regularization"]                       # the λ actually fitted (searched or fixed)
res["metric"]                      # held-out metric, (n_channels,)
res["scored_on"]                   # {"score_on", "fraction"}, None if every sample
res["coef_"]["envelope"]   # fold-averaged kernel, in kernel_units,
                           # (n_channels, n_subfeatures, n_delays)
res["scales"]                      # {"target", "features"}: what the
                                   # standardization divided by
res["delays"]["envelope"]          # its lags, in samples
res["bootstrap"]                   # {"n_samples", "distribution", "random_state"} or None
res["condition_number"], res["effective_rank"]   # None unless diagnostics=True
res["vif"]["envelope"]             # that block's generalized VIF, 1.0 = nothing
                                   # shared with the other blocks
res["n_aliased"]                   # design columns that are exact combinations
                                   # of the others; 0 for a healthy design
res["aic"], res["bic"]             # channel-wise, None unless criteria=True
res["edf"]                         # effective degrees of freedom of the fit
res["n"], res["target_ss"]         # which data those criteria describe

group.subjects                     # the same view for the whole cohort
"s01" in group, len(group)         # membership / cohort size

The four diagnostics follow the cohort's diagnostics=True, off by default because it costs a full extra pass over each subject's design, and they are None otherwise.

Read vif and n_aliased together. The GVIF is computed on a full-rank subset of the columns, so that one aliased column cannot zero a determinant and take the whole report with it — which means an exact dependency is reported by n_aliased, not by a large GVIF. Two duplicated blocks read 1.0 each once the duplicate columns have been set aside: n_aliased is the one that catches them.

Read one subject at a time they cannot say much — the question a cohort asks is whether this subject's design is the odd one out, so group.summary()["diagnostics"] carries the spread of each block's GVIF across subjects and names the subjects whose design has aliased columns:

design = group.summary()["diagnostics"]
design["gvif"]["envelope"]["max"]  # the worst subject for that block
design["aliased_subjects"]         # {subject_id: n_aliased}, empty if none

The per-column arrays (vif_columns_, vif_aliased_) stay on the model: they are one entry per design column, which does not belong in a per-subject record. Refit the odd subject on its own to inspect them.

Both are read-only mappings: assigning into them raises TypeError, so a stray line in a notebook cannot corrupt the cohort behind grand_average() or permutation_test(). The arrays inside are the stored ones rather than copies, so .copy() before modifying one in place. The kernels are the exception in original units, which are computed on each call.

docs.title: Choosing how subjects are fitted
docs.text:
The fitting strategy is part of the spec, declared once on the group. cv picks the paradigm ("pooled", "averaged", "train_test"), fit_method picks whether λ is searched or fixed, and the remaining parameters of the underlying TRFModel fit are accepted as keywords:

group = TRFGroup(
    features=["envelope"],
    default_window=(-0.2, 0.6),
    cv="train_test", train_size=0.8,      # backend-specific knobs included
    regularization_grid=np.logspace(-3, 6, 20),
    metric_limit_percentage=0.05,         # prefer the smoothest λ within 5%
    bootstrap=True,
)

# ... or skip the search entirely:
group = TRFGroup(features=["envelope"], default_window=(-0.2, 0.6),
                 fit_method="fit", regularization=1e3)

Every one of those is a default that fit_subject can override per subject, and it also takes any other keyword the chosen paradigm's fit / gridsearchCV accepts — keywords belonging to fit are routed into the refit stage automatically:

group.fit_subject(data, "s07", metric="mse", per_fold_metric=True)
group.fit_subject(data, "s08", fit_method="fit", regularization=50.0)

A keyword the selected cv does not support raises TypeError listing the ones it does (e.g. inner_train_cutoff exists only for cv="pooled"). A subject fitted with fit_method="fit" ignores the group's search-only defaults (inner_train_cutoff, metric_aggregation_function, metric_limit_percentage), so a group set up for the search can still fit one subject at a known λ. Pass fit keywords such as bootstrap directly; fit_subject does not take run_fit_kwargs.

score_on restricts the samples every subject's metric is computed on (see Scoring on a subset of samples). On the group it must be one of the declarative forms — "informative", a list of features or a {feature: (tmin, tmax)} window — since those mean the same thing for every recording; a boolean array or a callable belongs to one subject's fit_subject. The cohort's figures label the metric with it, and each record keeps scored_on:

group = TRFGroup(features=["onsets"], default_window=(-0.2, 0.6),
                 regularization_grid=np.logspace(-3, 6, 20),
                 score_on={"onsets": (0.0, 0.5)})
group.fit_subject(data, "s09", score_on=artifact_free)   # a mask of its own

docs.title: One λ for every subject
docs.text:
A subject's best λ grows with its noise, and a larger λ shrinks the kernel more. Fitted each at its own λ, a noisier subject comes out smaller for the same response, so a comparison between subjects or groups partly measures their noise. One λ for a whole group has the derivation and the simulations. regularization_strategy decides:

regularization_strategy What fit_subject does "mean-curve" fits at shared_regularization_, the best λ of the subjects' mean validation curve "median" fits at the geometric median of the λs the subjects chose on their own "leave-one-out" fits at the λ where the other subjects' average kernel best predicts each subject (below) "subject" searches and fits each subject at its own λ, in one loop unset (None) as "subject", and warns once when the subjects' λs differ

The two shared strategies need every subject's curve before any final fit, and the cohort keeps no data, so they take two passes over the subjects: search_subject runs a subject's search and keeps its curve (n_values floats), share_regularization() picks the λ, and fit_subject fits each subject at it. Called before share_regularization(), fit_subject raises with that loop in the message. A banded search shares the whole λ vector, scale and ratio, and metric_limit_percentage applies to the mean curve as it would to one subject's. Following the two passes without naming a strategy shares by "mean-curve".

search_subject takes the same overrides as fit_subject that configure the search (inner_train_cutoff, score_on, validation_plot, ...), but not regularization_grid or metric: averaged curves have to share one grid and one metric. A cohort fitted at one fixed λ (fit_method="fit") already shares it and needs neither.

regularization_search_ shows what the choice was made from: the λ values searched, each subject's curve, the λ each subject's own search chose, the strategy, and the curve the shared λ was selected on.

search = group.regularization_search_
search["curves"]["s01"]        # (n_values,), one subject's validation curve
search["chosen"]["s01"]        # the λ that subject would have taken alone
search["cohort_curve"]         # the mean curve, or the leave-one-out one

docs.title: One pass
docs.text:
The two passes load every subject twice. keep_kernels_by_regularization=True makes it one: search_subject also fits the subject at every λ of the grid and keeps those kernels, and share_regularization() fills every subject's record at the shared λ. The compute is the same; the records are the ones fit_subject would store.

group = TRFGroup(
    features=["envelope"], default_window=(-0.2, 0.6),
    regularization_grid=np.logspace(-3, 6, 20),
    regularization_strategy="mean-curve",
    keep_kernels_by_regularization=True,
    n_subjects=len(cohort),
)
for subject_id in cohort:
    group.search_subject(load(subject_id), subject_id)
group.share_regularization()           # every subject is now fitted

The cost is memory, n_values × n_channels × n_columns numbers per subject, where n_columns counts every feature's sub-features times its lags. Nothing is written to disk. The size is exact before the first fit: it is printed at INFO, and past half of the memory available search_subject raises MemoryError before fitting, projected over n_subjects when it is given and over the subjects searched so far when it is not.

Spec (float32, 20 λ) Per subject 30 subjects 30, leave-one-out 64 channels, 2 features × 65 lags 0.6 MB 19 MB 22 MB 64 channels, 52 features × 77 lags 20 MB 590 MB 2.4 GB

kernels_by_regularization(subject_id) returns them, in the cohort's kernel_units: entry i of each kernel is what fit_subject would store at the i-th λ, and the metric at every λ comes with them. A saved cohort does not carry them.

With bootstrap, diagnostics or criteria, a record needs the subject's data, so share_regularization() only chooses the λ and the loop of fit_subject stays.

docs.title: Leave-one-subject-out
docs.text:
regularization_strategy="leave-one-out" chooses the λ at which the average kernel of the other subjects best predicts each subject: at every λ, each subject's recording is predicted from the others' mean kernel and scored with the cohort's metric, and the curve averages that over channels and subjects. It is the question the grand average is for — how well a kernel estimated without a subject describes them. In the inner benchmark it came closest to the best λ in hindsight for a strong predictor in heavy noise, where the mean curve over-regularizes.

It needs every subject's kernels at every λ, so it keeps them on its own, in the same single pass. It also keeps the sums of each subject's design, X'X and X'y, to score a subject after their data is gone: n_columns² more numbers per subject, whatever the channels and the grid, which is what makes wide designs expensive (the last column above). The kernels are averaged in the cohort's kernel_units, over common_channels.

docs.title: Kernel units
docs.text:
Standardize divides each subject's recording by its own standard deviation, which contains its noise, so in standardized units a noisier subject's kernel is smaller even at one λ. kernel_units="original", the default, undoes it: every kernel the cohort hands out — results, subjects, grand_average, the cluster tests, the contrasts and the figures — is multiplied by \(\sigma_y / \sigma_x\) from that subject's training data. That is the same fitted model written in the recording's units per unit of each feature, so λ keeps its meaning. kernel_units="standardized" gives the coefficients as fitted, which the figures label \(\sigma_y/\sigma_x\).

The setting can change after fitting: group.kernel_units = "standardized". The grand average follows, and cluster tests run in the other units are cleared, with a warning, since they no longer describe what the figures show. A paired contrast refuses two cohorts in different units. A cohort saved before the scales were recorded can only be read in standardized units; asking it for original ones raises and says so.

See the API and the pure helpers in trflearn.statistics (grand_average, descriptive_summary, cluster_1samp, t_threshold).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Not public yet

TRFlearn has not been released, and the repository below is private — the clone shown here will not work without access to it. This documentation site is published so the work can be read and cited in the meantime.

Installing takes four steps: a fresh environment, PyTorch built for your hardware, TRFlearn itself, and a check that the GPU (if any) is visible.

docs.title: 1. Create an environment
docs.text:
Install into a dedicated environment, not your system Python. TRFlearn supports Python 3.10 or newer and is tested on 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13; if you have no reason to pick, use 3.12.

condavenv (Linux / macOS)venv (Windows) 
conda create -n trflearn python=3.12
conda activate trflearn

python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate

docs.title: 2. Install PyTorch
docs.text:
TRFlearn runs on the CPU or on an NVIDIA GPU through CUDA. Which PyTorch build you need depends on both, so check for a GPU first:

nvidia-smi

If the command is not found, or lists no GPU, you have no usable NVIDIA GPU: install the CPU build. If it prints a table, the header shows CUDA Version: X.Y — the newest CUDA your driver supports. Pick a PyTorch build for that version or older from pytorch.org; the commands below use CUDA 12.8, which needs a driver reporting 12.8 or above.

WindowsLinuxmacOS 
# NVIDIA GPU
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

# No GPU
pip install torch

A plain pip install torch on Windows is always the CPU build, GPU or not.

# NVIDIA GPU
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

# No GPU (skips the multi-GB CUDA libraries)
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

pip install torch

Macs have no CUDA, and TRFlearn does not use Apple's GPU backend (MPS): it runs on the CPU.

Install PyTorch before TRFlearn. The other way round, pip satisfies TRFlearn's torch requirement with the default wheel, which on Windows is the CPU build.

docs.title: 3. Install TRFlearn
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/NeuroLIAA/TRFlearn
cd TRFlearn
pip install -e .

Once TRFlearn is on PyPI this step becomes pip install trflearn; the environment and the PyTorch step stay the same.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
The core install fits, scores and plots TRFs on NumPy arrays. Everything else is an extra, named in brackets on the same pip install; several go together, as in ".[mne,simulation]".

Extra Adds Install it when mne MNE-Python your targets are mne.Raw recordings, or you want to_evoked, the topomap and Evoked figures, or the TFCE cohort test simulation pandas, MNE-Python you use trflearn.simulation, the synthetic recordings with known kernels tutorials the simulation extra, ipykernel you run the tutorials or examples in Jupyter or VS Code test pytest, pytest-cov, pytest-xdist, MNE, pandas you run the test suite docs MkDocs Material, mkdocstrings, mkdocs-jupyter you build this site lint ruff, at the version CI runs you run the linter dev every extra above you work on TRFlearn itself; see Contributing 
pip install -e ".[mne]"          # MNE Raw targets, Evoked export, topomaps, TFCE
pip install -e ".[simulation]"   # trflearn.simulation
pip install -e ".[tutorials]"    # what the tutorials and examples need to run

MNE is a soft dependency: everything works with plain NumPy arrays; it is only needed for mne.Raw targets, to_evoked, the topomap/Evoked plots and the TFCE cohort test.

GPU support is not an extra. It comes from the PyTorch build of step 2: with a CUDA build installed, TRFData(..., use_gpu=True) is all it takes. To move an existing environment to the GPU, reinstall PyTorch with the CUDA command and leave TRFlearn as it is.

docs.title: 4. Verify
docs.text:
import torch
import trflearn

print(trflearn.__version__)
print(torch.cuda.is_available())   # True if TRFlearn can use your GPU

If you have an NVIDIA GPU and this prints False, the CPU build of PyTorch was installed: uninstall it (pip uninstall torch) and repeat step 2 with the CUDA command.

docs.title: Running the tutorials
docs.text:
The Tutorials and Examples are notebooks in the repository. The tutorials build their data with trflearn.simulation, so the tutorials extra is all they need; the examples run on real recordings, fetched separately as each one explains.

pip install -e ".[tutorials]"

That adds MNE, pandas and ipykernel, which lets VS Code or Jupyter run the notebooks with this environment's Python. To list the environment by name in Jupyter:

python -m ipykernel install --user --name trflearn

Contributing

Working on TRFlearn itself needs the test suite and docs toolchain too, and a pinned Python 3.10 environment; see Contributing.

docs.text: The license for TRFlearn is being finalised with the authors and will be published here once settled. Until then, please contact the NeuroLIAA maintainers before redistributing.

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
Figures are on-demand methods, not side-effects. A shared base class (TRFPlots) gives models, cohorts and single subjects one plotting API, so the same call works on all three:

model.plot_joint("envelope")           # a fitted model
group.plot_average("envelope")         # the cohort grand-average
group("s01").plot_image("envelope")    # one subject, via group(subject_id)

Every method returns the figure (or a list of them) and closes it in pyplot, so it stays usable afterwards; save_path= writes it (creating parent directories) and show=True displays it.

docs.title: The whole surface at a glance
docs.text:
Method Takes Model Cohort Subject Montage Notes plot spec ✓ ✓ ✓ optional butterfly via mne.Evoked.plot plot_joint spec ✓ ✓ ✓ required butterfly + topomaps at the peaks plot_image spec ✓ ✓ ✓ optional channels × time heatmap plot_psd spec ✓ ✓ ✓ optional spectrum of the kernel plot_psd_topomap spec ✓ ✓ ✓ required spectrum as topomaps plot_average spec ✓ ✓ ✓ optional butterfly + channel mean/std, drawn by the package plot_contrast spec_a, spec_b ✓ ✓ ✓ optional¹ the difference of two features plot_features specs=None ✓ ✓ ✓ required one summary column per feature plot_feature spec ✓ ✓ ✓ required that column, alone plot_metric_topomap — ✓ ✓ ✓ required held-out score per channel plot_source_butterfly spec ✓ ✓ ✓ centroids source-space butterfly, coloured by position to_stc spec, labels, src ✓ ✓ ✓ centroids a SourceEstimate for 3D rendering plot_bootstrap — ✗ ✓ ✗ no per-subject metric distributions validation_plot — ✓ ✗ ✗ no the gridsearchCV figure

¹ plot_contrast(..., kind="joint") does require one.

spec is a feature name ("envelope"), or a tuple for an interaction (("envelope", "onsets")) — written exactly as in features.

Two settings, not methods, read by every figure of that object:

model.plot_baseline = (None, 0)        # display-only baseline, MNE convention
model.plot_baseline = {"saccade": (None, 0)}     # or per feature
group.plot_sphere = 0.095              # fixed head size for every topomap

plot_baseline corrects a copy on the way to the plot — coef_ is never touched. plot_sphere pins the head geometry so sensors do not shift between subjects when MNE refits it per recording.

docs.title: mne.Evoked passthroughs
docs.text:
plot, plot_joint, plot_image, plot_psd, plot_psd_topomap build the kernel's Evoked for a feature and delegate to the identically-named mne.Evoked method (extra **kwargs forwarded), so the full MNE toolbox is available.

What they need depends on whether they draw a head:

  • plot, plot_image and plot_psd need no montage, nor any channel info. On a model fitted on plain arrays the channels are drawn as Target 0, Target 1, and so on; with a montage, the butterfly and the spectrum colour each trace by its sensor's position.
  • plot_joint and plot_psd_topomap draw topomaps, so they need sensor positions (MNE Raw targets, or set_montage). Without them they raise before MNE does, saying what is missing: the channel info, its positions, or sensors at all, since source regions do not lie on a head.

Common controls

  • The y-axis / colorbar is shown in coefficient units — σ_EEG/σ_x under standardization, an appropriate label otherwise — never µV. The modality name comes from the channel types in the info (EEG, MEG, sEEG, ...); target when there is no info, the types are mixed, or they are misc (source-space parcels).
  • The MNE N_ave tag is stripped: a TRF kernel is a regression coefficient, not an average of trials.
  • x_units="ms"|"s" sets the time axis.
  • title overrides the default ("<subject>-<stimulus>" in a subject view, else the stimulus).
  • subfeature chooses what a multi-column feature (d>1) contributes, since an Evoked holds one value per channel and delay:
  • "mean" (default) averages the sub-features — the same reduction plot_average shows on its top panel;
  • an int picks that column;
  • None returns one figure per sub-feature (and save_path is suffixed _sub0, _sub1, …).

It is ignored for a scalar feature.

plot and plot_joint additionally take grid, mean, std, sem (default grid=mean=std=True) to overlay a black channel-mean line with a shaded band on top of MNE's per-channel traces. plot_joint also shades the cohort's cluster result and forwards ts_args / topomap_args to MNE.

model.plot("envelope", mean=True, std=True, x_units="ms")
model.plot_joint("spectrogram")                  # the sub-feature average
model.plot_joint("spectrogram", subfeature=2)    # just band 2
model.plot_image("spectrogram", subfeature=None) # one figure per band

docs.title: plot_average
docs.text:
A montage-free butterfly + channel mean/std figure, drawn by the package itself, so it works on every owner, source space included.

  • A scalar feature (d==1) is one axis: thin per-channel traces, the bold channel-mean, and a ±channel-std band.
  • A multi-column feature (d>1) is two axes sharing the time axis: the butterfly of the sub-feature-averaged kernel on top, and a sub-features × time heatmap below (sub_labels names the rows).

style="mne" (the default) draws the top axis with mne.Evoked.plot when a montage is available and falls back to the native drawing when it is not; style="native" opts out. What is plotted does not change, only the rendering.

channel_reduce picks how the bottom panel collapses its channel axis — not its sub-features, which are the rows, and not the top panel:

  • "mean" (default): the signed average, so polarity is preserved. Drawn on a diverging scale centred at zero.
  • "gfp": the RMS. Reach for it when the response is dipolar — positive over some sensors, negative over others — where the signed mean cancels a real effect toward zero. It is non-negative, so it is drawn on a sequential scale anchored at zero, and it discards the sign.

At the cohort level, once a cluster test has run, significant delays are shaded green (positive) / red (negative) and the heatmap dims its non-significant cells. alpha_level sets the cutoff and min_sig_channels how many channels must reach it for a delay to count (an int counts channels, a float in (0, 1) is a fraction of them), each sign on its own: a delay where enough channels are significant both ways -- a dipolar topography, such as an auditory response reversing under a mastoid reference -- is shaded green over red, half the height each. show_stats=False opts out.

model.plot_average("envelope")
group.plot_average("envelope", show_stats=True, min_sig_channels=0.25)
group.plot_average("spectrogram", channel_reduce="gfp",
                   sub_labels=["0.5–2", "2–4", "4–8", "8–16", "16–32"])

docs.title: plot_contrast
docs.text:
The difference between two features of one model, spec_a - spec_b. This is the picture behind permutation_test_contrast_features / tfce_contrast_features: those return a p-value for the difference, and this draws the difference itself.

Both kernels are partial coefficients from the same design and solve, so they share an regularization, a normalization, the folds and the sample count, and each is estimated controlling for the other — which is what subtracting two separately fitted models would not give you. The canonical use is a pair of condition-coded versions of one regressor (attended vs unattended, target vs distractor) entered as two features.

  • kind="average" (default) gives the plot_average figure, montage-free.
  • kind="joint" gives the plot_joint figure — butterfly plus topographies at the peaks — of the sub-feature-averaged difference. Needs a montage.

Shading comes from the stored result for that ordered pair; testing (a, b) and plotting (b, a) warns rather than reusing the result with a flipped sign, which would only be exact for a two-sided test.

The two features must share a delay window and a sub-feature count (checked). Whether their difference means anything is yours to judge: two condition-coded envelopes are weights against the same kind of regressor, an envelope minus a spectrogram is not.

group.tfce_contrast_features("attended", "unattended")
group.plot_contrast("attended", "unattended", kind="joint")
model.plot_contrast("attended", "unattended")     # one participant, unshaded

docs.title: plot_features / plot_feature
docs.text:
The summary figure: one column per feature, three stacked rows sharing a delay axis.

  1. the butterfly of the kernel (averaged over sub-features), with significant delay intervals shaded;
  2. for a scalar feature the channels × time image with the non-significant region greyed out; for a multi-column one a sub-features × time heatmap of the channel-collapsed coefficient (channel_reduce, as in plot_average). A black curve on a twin axis traces how many channels are significant at each delay;
  3. a topomap at the peak of the significant span (the GFP peak when nothing is significant), with the significant sensors marked.

specs=None plots every feature; pass a list to choose. ylims, vlim_topo, topo_times and sub_labels accept either one value for all columns or a {spec: value} dict.

Needs a montage, for the topomap of row 3. Significance is read from the cohort's stored cluster test, so the same call renders unshaded for a lone TRFModel or a single subject.

group.plot_features()                               # every feature, side by side
group.plot_features(["envelope"], min_sig_channels=0.25)
group.plot_feature("spectrogram", sub_labels=["0.5–2", "2–4", "4–8", "8–16", "16–32"])
model.plot_feature("envelope")                      # one participant, no shading
group("s01").plot_features()

docs.title: plot_metric_topomap
docs.text:
The per-channel held-out metric as an mne topomap; the metric name (e.g. Pearson) labels the colorbar and the title. Needs a montage.

model.plot_metric_topomap()
group("s01").plot_metric_topomap()     # title prefixed with the subject id

docs.title: plot_source_butterfly / to_stc
docs.text:
Source space. Neither takes a sensor montage: both need region centroids, set with TRFData.set_source_positions.

plot_source_butterfly is the source-space counterpart of the spatially coloured butterfly MNE draws for sensors. MNE's version interpolates onto a head surface, which parcel centroids do not lie on, so this one keeps the part that carries the meaning — where a trace comes from, readable off its colour (red = right, green = anterior, blue = left) — and drops the topography. A panel on the right places each region as a dot in a top-down head outline, so a colour in the butterfly can be traced back to a place. gfp=True shades the global field power under the traces, show_stats shades significant delay intervals exactly as plot_average does, and a multi-column feature is averaged over its sub-features.

to_stc draws nothing. It paints one feature's kernel back onto a cortical surface and returns an mne.SourceEstimate, whose own .plot() does the 3D rendering. It needs the parcellation the channels are named after (labels) and the source space defining the vertices (src); subfeature picks the column, since an Evoked — and so an stc — holds one value per vertex and delay. To go straight from an Evoked you already have, use evoked_to_stc instead.

group.plot_source_butterfly("envelope")
stc = model.to_stc("envelope", labels=labels, src=src)
stc.plot(subjects_dir=subjects_dir, hemi="both")

docs.title: plot_bootstrap
docs.text:
Cohort only. Compares the per-subject bootstrap metric distributions side by side, as violins (kind="violin") or boxes, with the confidence interval ci marked — the figure that shows whether one participant carries the cohort's effect.

Requires the subjects to have been fitted with bootstrap=True. subject_ids selects a subset, sort=True orders them by score, and channel_reduce ("mean", "median", "max" or a channel index — a different vocabulary from plot_average's) collapses each subject's channels to one number.

group.plot_bootstrap()
group.plot_bootstrap(kind="box", ci=95, sort=True)

docs.title: validation_plot
docs.text:
Model only. Renders the gridsearchCV figure: the aggregated metric against the regularization grid with the selected value marked, plus one panel per feature stacking the channel-averaged TRFs over that grid. After a banded search the top panel carries one curve per band ratio over a shared λ axis, with the winning ratio drawn heavier and the selected per-band λ values in the title.

gridsearchCV records its data on every run regardless of its own validation_plot flag, so the figure can be re-rendered any time.

model.gridsearchCV(regularization_grid=np.logspace(-2, 6, 20), validation_plot=False)
model.validation_plot(save_path="validation.png")

See the whole workflow rendered end to end in the Tutorials and Examples, and the full method signatures in the plotting API.

docs.title: The core idea
docs.text:
For every response channel, TRFlearn estimates a kernel w(feature, delay) so that

\[ \hat{y}(t, c) \;=\; \sum_{f}\sum_{\tau} X(t-\tau, f)\, \cdot\, w(f, \tau, c) \]

Each feature contributes a lagged sub-design over its own delay window; the blocks are concatenated into a design matrix X, and a regularized least-squares system is solved:

\[ (X^\top X + \lambda M)\, \mathrm{TRF} = X^\top y \]

where M is the penalty (identity for ridge, a temporal Laplacian for ridge-laplacian) and λ the regularization strength.

docs.title: End to end
docs.text:
Everything below runs as-is: it simulates a stimulus and an EEG recording whose true TRF is known, then recovers it. Swap the simulated arrays for your own and the rest stays the same.

import numpy as np
from trflearn import TRFData, TRFModel

# ---- Simulated data: 3 minutes at 128 Hz, 16 EEG channels ----------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
sample_rate, n_samples, n_channels = 128, 128 * 180, 16

# A speech-like envelope: smoothed, rectified noise, shape (n_samples, 1).
smoothing = np.hanning(25) / np.hanning(25).sum()
rectified = np.abs(rng.standard_normal(n_samples))
envelope = np.convolve(rectified, smoothing, "same")[:, None]

# The ground truth: a positive peak at 100 ms and a negative one at 200 ms,
# with a different gain on every channel.
t = np.arange(int(0.4 * sample_rate)) / sample_rate
peak = np.exp(-((t - 0.1) / 0.03) ** 2)
trough = np.exp(-((t - 0.2) / 0.04) ** 2)
true_trf = peak - 0.6 * trough
gains = rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5, n_channels)

# EEG = the envelope filtered by the TRF on every channel, plus noise.
response = np.convolve(envelope[:, 0], true_trf)[:n_samples]
noise = rng.standard_normal((n_samples, n_channels))
eeg = response[:, None] * gains + 2 * response.std() * noise

# ---- 1) The data container ------------------------------------------------
# Holds every candidate feature and the response. It is lazy: nothing heavy is
# built until a model asks for it.
data = TRFData(features={"envelope": envelope}, y=eeg, sample_rate=sample_rate)
data.create_partitions()   # 5 contiguous folds

# ---- 2) The model ---------------------------------------------------------
# Picks the features to use and the delays to estimate, in seconds.
model = TRFModel(
    TRFDataset=data,
    features=["envelope"],
    default_window=(-0.1, 0.4),
    solver="ridge",
)

# ---- 3) Choose the regularization by cross-validation, then fit -----------
# Searches np.logspace(-3, 3, 13) and chooses on R².
best_regularization, (trfs, r2) = model.gridsearchCV(validation_plot=False)

# ---- 4) Look at the result ------------------------------------------------
fig = model.plot_average("envelope")

The recovered kernel has the peak at 100 ms and the trough at 200 ms that were put into the simulation; each thin line is one channel and the band is the spread across them.

docs.title: What came out
docs.text:
• best_regularization — the regularization strength that scored best on held-out data inside each training fold. model.validation_plot() shows the whole curve.
  • trfs — a dict with one kernel per feature, shaped (n_folds, n_channels, n_subfeatures, n_delays): here (5, 16, 1, 65), since -0.1 s to 0.4 s at 128 Hz is 65 delays.
  • r2 — the R² of the predicted against the recorded EEG on the held-out folds, one value per channel. λ was chosen on it too; pass metric="Pearson" when prediction accuracy is the result (see Recommendations).
  • model.coef_ — the kernels averaged over folds, (n_channels, n_subfeatures, n_delays) per feature. It is what model.predict() applies, either to the data's own stimulus or to a new one, model.predict({"envelope": new_envelope}).

docs.title: Beyond this example
docs.text:
The same four steps cover the rest of the library; only the arguments grow.

  • Several features and their interactions — pass more arrays to TRFData (a spectrogram is just an (n_samples, n_bands) feature) and name them in features, with tuples for interactions: ["envelope", ("envelope", "pitch")]. See Features.
  • A different window per feature — feature_windows={"onsets": (0, 0.8)}.
  • Smoother kernels — solver="ridge-laplacian" penalizes the difference between neighbouring delays instead of amplitude; not for a predictor with little signal. See Solvers and Recommendations.
  • Recordings split in trials or sessions — pass lists of arrays, one per segment; create_partitions() then stratifies the folds by segment.
  • MNE data — pass an mne.Raw as y to keep the montage, and get topographies with model.plot_joint("envelope").
  • A cohort — TRFGroup fits one specification across subjects and runs the group statistics. See Group analysis.

docs.text:

  • Plotting — inspect kernels and metrics at model / subject / cohort level.
  • Group analysis — fit a cohort and run TFCE.
  • Tutorials — four executed notebooks on synthetic data, from simulating a signal with a known answer to recovering it.
  • Examples — complete analyses on real recordings, including an 17-subject EEG cohort.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
TRFlearn leaves several choices to you: how to choose λ, how to validate, how to preprocess, which penalty to use. This page says what to choose in which case, and why. The why is theory wherever theory decides; where a choice depends on a crossover theory cannot place, the numbers come from simulations in which the true response is known:

  • two predictors fitted together, a speech-like envelope and a sparse onset train, at −20, −10 and 0 dB, with 2.5 to 30 minutes of data, white or 1/f noise, single subjects and cohorts of 16;
  • one spectrogram-like predictor of 1 to 32 bands whose bands correlate at 0, 0.5 or 0.9.

At −20 dB the held-out correlation is about 0.06, the range of speech-envelope TRFs in EEG. In the first set the onsets carry under 1 % of the response's variance: a weak predictor, which matters below.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
If the result is… Choose λ on Solver Preprocessing The TRF itself: its shape, amplitude, group average R² ridge Standardize Prediction accuracy (encoding or decoding r) Pearson ridge, or a banded ridge when one group of predictors is much weaker Standardize A weak predictor's TRF in one subject at EEG-like SNR Pearson ridge Standardize

In every case:

  • search λ: gridsearchCV() with no grid sweeps np.logspace(-3, 3, 13) and chooses on R²; pass metric="Pearson" when prediction is the result, and extend the grid when TRFlearn warns that the choice is on its edge;
  • validate with create_partitions(), which makes 5 folds, stratified by segment when the data come in segments;
  • leave metric_limit_percentage=None;
  • fit long recordings in float32 on the GPU;
  • fit a cohort with TRFGroup, with one λ for every subject (regularization_strategy="mean-curve") when subjects are compared, and compare them in original units, which is how TRFGroup hands its kernels out.

docs.title: What λ means here
docs.text:
TRFlearn solves the normal equations averaged per sample,

\[ \Big(\tfrac{1}{n} X^\top X + \lambda M\Big)\, w = \tfrac{1}{n} X^\top y , \]

where \(n\) is the number of samples and \(M = I\) for ridge. With Standardize every column of \(X\) has unit variance, so the diagonal of \(\tfrac{1}{n} X^\top X\) is 1: λ is measured against the variance of one predictor, and λ = 1 penalizes a coefficient as much as one standard deviation of its predictor weighs in the fit. Because of the \(1/n\), an λ means the same with 2 or with 30 minutes of data. The best λ still moves, for the reasons below.

docs.title: Which λ to expect
docs.text:
Ridge is the posterior mean of a Bayesian model in which the noise has variance \(\sigma^2\) and every coefficient is drawn independently with variance \(\tau^2\). That posterior mean solves the equations above with

\[ \lambda^\star = \frac{\sigma^2}{n\,\tau^2}. \]

With standardized predictors and target, the variance the response gets from the predictors is \(S = \tau^2 \operatorname{tr}(C)\), where \(C = \tfrac{1}{n} X^\top X\) is the correlation matrix of the lagged predictors. Its diagonal is 1, so \(\operatorname{tr}(C) = p\), the number of coefficients (predictors × lags), whatever the correlations between predictors. Writing \(\mathrm{SNR} = S / \sigma^2\):

\[ \lambda^\star = \frac{p}{n \cdot \mathrm{SNR}} = \frac{n_\text{predictors} \cdot n_\text{lags}}{n_\text{samples} \cdot \mathrm{SNR}} . \]

Four things move it:

  1. Noise. \(\lambda^\star \propto 1/\mathrm{SNR}\): one decade more for every 10 dB less. The noisier the data, the more of what the fit sees is noise, and the harder the prior has to pull.
  2. Data length. \(\lambda^\star \propto 1/n\): one decade less for every tenfold more data. The more data, the less the estimate needs the prior.
  3. Number of coefficients. \(\lambda^\star \propto p\). Spread the same response over more coefficients and each one carries less (\(\tau^2 = S/p\)), so the prior should pull harder: a 32-band spectrogram needs a larger λ than one envelope, and so does a longer window. The sample rate cancels out: doubling it doubles both the lags and the samples.
  4. Collinearity. It does not enter \(\lambda^\star\), since \(\operatorname{tr}(C) = p\) regardless, but it decides what the data can tell apart. Write \(C = \sum_i \mu_i v_i v_i^\top\). Along each direction \(v_i\), ridge keeps a fraction \(\mu_i / (\mu_i + \lambda)\) of the estimate. Correlated predictors put most of their variance in a few directions with large \(\mu_i\) — what they share — and leave many with small \(\mu_i\) — how they differ —, where noise is amplified by \(1/\mu_i\) unless λ suppresses it. A response the correlated predictors share lives in the large directions, so a larger λ costs it little and cross-validation picks one. A response in how they differ lives in the small directions, and no λ recovers it.

In simulation, λ chosen on R² follows all four directions: per decade of predictors it grows by 1.0 to 1.4 decades, per decade of data it falls by 0.6 to 1.4, and per 10 dB of SNR it falls by 0.5 to 1.2. It sits about one decade above \(\lambda^\star\), since real kernels are smooth and concentrated rather than independent coefficients. Correlated bands (0.5 to 0.9) add another 0.5 to 1.5 decades from four bands up. And with bands correlated at 0.9, a response carried by one band, or a different one by each band, comes out with a kernel error of 0.6 to 0.9 at 8 to 32 bands, against 0.3 to 0.5 when the bands share it.

docs.title: The grid
docs.text:
• np.logspace(-3, 3, 13), in standardized units, held every choice with one or two predictors, and 95 % of them for up to 32 correlated bands (between \(10^{-1.5}\) and \(10^{2}\)). It is what gridsearchCV searches when given no grid.
  • A grid denser than two points per decade changes nothing, and costs about the same: λ is scored from sums, so each extra point is cheap.
  • With many more coefficients, or a much lower SNR, than that, extend the top: about one decade per tenfold more coefficients or 10 dB less SNR.
  • TRFlearn warns when the selected λ is the smallest or the largest of the grid: the search stopped there instead of at a peak. At the top, extend upwards — or accept that the predictor is being shrunk away. At the bottom, extend downwards — or the metric curve is flat because the predictors explain almost nothing; the validation plot tells which.
  • Do not fix λ across datasets. In simulation λ = 1 matches the search at −10 and 0 dB and loses at −20 dB; 0.1 and 10 each lose badly somewhere.

docs.title: Pearson, R² or RMSE
docs.text:
Pearson's correlation is blind to the scale of a prediction:

\[ r(a\,\hat y,\, y) = r(\hat y,\, y) \qquad \text{for any } a > 0 . \]

As λ grows, ridge mostly shrinks the prediction, and until its shape changes Pearson does not notice: the curve is flat near its peak and the peak sits at a larger λ. R² charges for the shrinkage,

\[ R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_t (y_t - \hat y_t)^2}{\sum_t (y_t - \bar y)^2}, \]

since a prediction that is too small leaves residual. It selects the λ with the smallest held-out squared error, the loss ridge itself minimizes. RMSE is a monotone transform of the same error and selects the same λ.

  • The kernels are the result: R². It chooses about half a decade less λ. In simulation it recovers 0.85 of the envelope's amplitude against 0.66, and the 16-subject group average is better for both predictors: averaging removes noise, not shrinkage.
  • A weak predictor in one subject at EEG-like SNR: Pearson. There the extra shrinkage keeps the estimate from being mostly noise. With R², the weak onsets' kernel error at −20 dB rose by 0.95.
  • Prediction is the result: Pearson, which keeps a small edge of 0.001 to 0.005 in held-out r.

To collapse the folds' curves into one, keep the mean (the default) rather than the median (metric_aggregation_function).

  • The mean uses every fold at every λ. A fold spoiled by a bad segment has its whole curve scaled towards zero by one factor (for noise unrelated to the stimulus, in Pearson and in R² alike), which gives it less weight in the mean without dragging the peak elsewhere.
  • The median takes a different fold at different λ, as 'max' does, so its curve is rougher. It would only help against a fold whose curve has a different shape, which the simulations did not include.
  • In simulation, the median changed the λ chosen on Pearson for 38 % of subjects at −20 dB and 19 % at −10 dB. It improved no kernel; at −10 dB the envelope's error rose by 0.06 where λ changed. On R² it changed λ for 3–7 % of subjects, with no effect.

docs.title: metric_limit_percentage
docs.text:
It selects the largest λ whose metric is within a fraction of the best. Because a Pearson curve is flat near its peak, 0.01 buys a much larger λ, and 0.05 runs to the top of the grid. In simulation the envelope kept 0.34 of its amplitude at 0.01 and 0.005 at 0.05. An R² curve is steeper: 0.01 changes almost nothing, and 0.05 moves λ about half a decade up, back to where Pearson chooses, with the envelope's shrinkage that comes with it. The shape does not improve either: even at −20 dB with 2.5 minutes of data, the correlation between estimated and true kernel stays the same. Leave it None when the kernels are the result.

To decide from a pilot whether a response is there, test the held-out r against a permutation null and check that the kernel's shape is stable across folds or subjects; a more shrunken kernel looks smoother but carries no more information.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
What is recovered barely depends on the scheme. pooled and averaged, 3, 5 or 10 folds, stratified or contiguous, leave-one-segment-out, an inner split of 60 or 80 %: they choose the same λ and return the same kernels. The differences are elsewhere:

  • train_test loses. Its final fit sees 80 % of the data, and its kernels show it. Use it for quick looks.
  • Cost (relative to pooled, 5 folds): averaged 0.4–0.5×, 3 folds 0.6×, 10 folds 2.0×. Leave-one-segment-out costs as many folds as there are segments: the same as 5 folds with 5 segments, 6× with 30.
  • Stability. averaged chooses the same λ for more subjects.
  • Honesty. The cross-validated score is a fair estimate of the score on unseen data: in simulation they differ by at most 0.007 in r.

Recommended: create_partitions(), the default, which makes 5 folds stratified by segment (plain contiguous folds for one continuous recording), or n_folds=3 when time matters. With many short trials, keep stratified k-fold rather than leave-one-segment-out: same result, a fraction of the cost.

docs.title: From validation to the kernel you show
docs.text:
Cross-validation does two jobs, and the kernel you show is a third.

  1. Measuring predictive power. Report the cross-validated score: the metric on data that neither the fit nor the choice of λ saw, which pooled guarantees with its inner split. Never report the score of a fit on all the data: it is measured on the data it was fitted to, and is inflated. To ask whether a predictor adds anything, compare the two models' cross-validated scores on the same folds.
  2. Choosing λ. The validation curve's peak, on the metric that suits the question (see Pearson, R² or RMSE).
  3. Estimating the kernel. Fit with all the data at the chosen λ. This is not overfitting: λ is what controls overfitting, and holding data back would only make the kernel noisier. In TRFlearn, fit(regularization) stores in coef_ the average of the k folds' kernels, each fitted on \((k-1)/k\) of the data; with 5 folds it differs from a single fit on all of it by about 0.5 %.

docs.title: One λ for a whole group
docs.text:
When every subject hears the same stimulus, they share the lagged design \(X\) and \(C = \tfrac{1}{n} X^\top X\). For subject \(s\), with response \(w_s\) and noise \(\varepsilon_s\),

\[ \hat w_s(\lambda) = (C + \lambda I)^{-1}\, \tfrac{1}{n} X^\top y_s , \qquad \mathbb{E}\big[\hat w_s(\lambda)\big] = (C + \lambda I)^{-1} C\, w_s \equiv A_\lambda w_s . \]

The noise only adds variance; the expected kernel is the true one passed through an operator \(A_\lambda\) that depends on the stimulus and on λ, and on nothing about the subject.

With one λ for everyone, every subject's kernel goes through the same \(A_\lambda\), so anything a group analysis computes as a weighted sum of kernels keeps its expectation:

\[ \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_s c_s\, \hat w_s(\lambda)\Big] = A_\lambda \sum_s c_s\, w_s , \]

whether it is a group mean (\(c_s = 1/S\)), a difference between groups or a slope against a covariate. Two groups with the same response have the same expected kernel, whatever their noise; responses in a ratio of 0.8 keep that ratio.

With one λ per subject, \(\mathbb{E}[\hat w_s] = A_{\lambda_s} w_s\), and \(\lambda_s\) is not arbitrary: as above, the best λ grows with the subject's noise and falls with the size of its response. A noisier subject's kernel is shrunk more for the same response, a stronger responder's less: data quality turns into TRF amplitude, and real differences between subjects are exaggerated.

With different stimuli of the same kind (different stories, one speaker) \(C\) differs little between subjects and the argument holds approximately; that case was not simulated.

In simulation. Two groups of 12 subjects who hear one stimulus, 5 minutes each, at −20 and −10 dB, 60 cohorts per condition. The test is Welch's t on the envelope's peak (the eight channels and ±16 ms where the true response peaks), on kernels in original units:

λ Same response, noise 6 dB apart: p < 0.05 Mean t True ratio 0.8, estimated Power One for everyone, from the mean validation curve 9 % +0.04 0.80 82 % One per subject, on R² 54 % −2.5 0.75 77 % One per subject, on Pearson 8 % −0.5 0.78 42 % One per group, from each group's mean curve, on R² 71 % −5.1 0.78 85 %
  • With one λ the t statistics follow their null distribution (Kolmogorov–Smirnov p = 0.5). The 9 % is 11 cohorts of 120, which a test at 5 % produces by chance with p = 0.05.
  • With an λ per subject on R², the noisier group's kernel came out 22 % smaller for the same response, and a true ratio of 0.8 read as 0.75.
  • Pearson's per-subject λ hides that by shrinking everyone a lot: fewer false positives than R², but half the power, and its t statistics are still off-centre.
  • An λ per group is the worst: it lines the shrinkage up with the very label being tested.

Covariates. In cohorts of 16 whose gains spread over 0.7–1.3 and whose noise spreads over ±5 dB, regress log amplitude on log gain and on noise.

  • With one λ, the slopes are 1.00 and 0.00: the truth.
  • With an λ per subject on R² at −20 dB, they are 1.25–1.33 and −0.28 per 10 dB. Amplitude exaggerates real differences, and it loses about a quarter per 10 dB of noise. At −10 dB the distortion is much smaller (1.03–1.06 and −0.05).

Which common λ. The tests are valid because the λ is shared, not because of where it sits, so any λ chosen without looking at the groups serves them.

Where it sits does change the group-average kernel:

  • For the envelope and for weak onsets, the mean validation curve on R² matched the best λ in hindsight.
  • For a strong predictor, the average wants less shrinkage than one subject's fit, since averaging already cancels noise. Leave-one-subject-out finds it: take the λ at which the other subjects' average kernel best predicts each left-out subject. At −20 dB the group kernel of strong onsets had an error of 0.24 this way and 0.41 with the mean curve, against 0.23 at the best λ.

So:

  • for comparisons and covariates, use one λ for every subject, from the mean validation curve on R², chosen without looking at the groups;
  • for the average shape of a strong predictor, choose that λ leave-one-subject-out;
  • for a single subject, keep that subject's own λ.

In TRFGroup, regularization_strategy="mean-curve" shares the λ of the mean validation curve, in two passes: search_subject keeps each subject's curve, share_regularization picks the λ, and fit_subject fits everyone at it (see Group analysis). regularization_strategy="leave-one-out" chooses it leave-one-subject-out, in a single pass (see Leave-one-subject-out). Left unset, regularization_strategy fits each subject at its own λ and warns when they differ; regularization_strategy="subject" does the same without the warning, for an analysis that wants it.

docs.title: Compare subjects in original units
docs.text:
Standardize divides each subject's recording by its own standard deviation \(s_y\), and \(s_y^2 = g^2 v + \sigma^2\) holds the noise \(\sigma^2\) as well as the response's variance \(g^2 v\). A kernel in standardized units is the kernel in the recording's units divided by \(s_y\), so a noisier subject's kernel is smaller even with one λ. These are the units the plots label \(\sigma_y/\sigma_x\).

For a one-sample question — is there a response at all? — that is harmless: noise cannot create a mean. For comparing groups, or relating amplitude to a covariate, it is not. In the simulation above, standardized kernels told the two groups with the same response apart in 93–100 % of cohorts, whichever way λ was chosen. Use kernels in original units: the recording's unit per unit of each predictor. The model predicts \(\hat y = \mu_y + \sigma_y \sum_d w[d]\,(x[t-d] - \mu_x)/\sigma_x\), so \(w\,\sigma_y/\sigma_x\) is the same fitted model written in those units, and λ keeps its meaning. TRFGroup hands every kernel out that way by default (kernel_units="original"). For a single model, multiply coef_ by \(\sigma_y/\sigma_x\) from the training data, or fit with target_preprocess=None on recordings whose mean is zero (high-pass filtered, as EEG usually is).

Neither unit is neutral. Data units keep everything that multiplies a recording, such as skull thickness or electrode placement; standardized units keep the noise level. With one λ, original units at least treat every subject with the same estimator.

docs.title: Standardize, and why centring matters
docs.text:
TRFlearn fits no intercept, and centring the data is what stands in for one. For ridge with an unpenalized intercept \(b\),

\[ \min_{b,\,w}\ \lVert y - b\,\mathbf{1} - X w \rVert^2 + \lambda \lVert w \rVert^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b = \bar y - \bar x^\top w , \]

and substituting \(b\) back leaves exactly the centred problem

\[ \min_w\ \big\lVert (y - \bar y\,\mathbf{1}) - (X - \mathbf{1}\,\bar x^\top)\, w \big\rVert^2 + \lambda \lVert w \rVert^2 . \]

So centring a predictor does not change its kernel. When an onset train's zeros become slightly negative under Standardize, that is the intercept being absorbed, not a distortion of the onsets. Where zeros do carry meaning is a nonlinear expansion of event amplitudes, which spline_basis(scope="event") handles.

Scaling is what matters. With one λ for every predictor, dividing predictor \(j\) by \(s_j\) turns its penalty into \(\lambda / s_j^2\) in its own units. Standardize gives every predictor the same penalty per standard deviation. A kernel then maps one standard deviation of the predictor to one of the target; to read it in original units (µV per onset, say) multiply it by \(\sigma_y / \sigma_x\), both from the training data.

docs.title: Raw units
docs.text: Without scaling, a predictor's penalty depends on its units: a predictor with small variance is penalized more for the same response. In simulation, fitting in raw units silenced the onsets beside the envelope (0.06 of their amplitude) and, with the scales reversed, degraded the envelope instead. Use None only when the units are comparable on purpose.

docs.title: Normalize
docs.text:
Min–max scaling subtracts the minimum, not the mean: an offset an intercept would absorb, and TRFlearn has none.

On the target it breaks the fit. The target's mean, about 0.5, has to come from the predictors, so the kernels take on a large constant component. In simulation the held-out r fell to 0.34 of what the noise allows and the kernels were off by an order of magnitude. target_preprocess="Normalize" is therefore deprecated: it warns, and will be removed.

On the predictors, with a standardized target, it works, slightly worse than Standardize. Write an uncentred predictor as \(X = X_c + \mathbf{1}\mu^\top\), with \(X_c\) centred. With \(y\) centred too, the cross terms vanish and the loss becomes

\[ \tfrac{1}{n}\big\lVert y - X_c w - \mathbf{1}\,\mu^\top w \big\rVert^2 = \tfrac{1}{n}\lVert y - X_c w \rVert^2 + (\mu^\top w)^2 , \]

an extra penalty on each kernel's sum weighted by its predictor's mean. It pulls a predictor with a large mean, such as an envelope, towards a kernel of zero net area. In simulation, both predictors lost 0.05 to 0.14 of their amplitude against Standardize.

Min–max scaling also takes its scale from the two most extreme samples, so a single artefact sets it. Prefer Standardize.

docs.title: ridge
docs.text: The default, and the right one unless a case below applies: it pulls every kernel towards zero, which is what protects a weak predictor.

docs.title: Banded ridge
docs.text:
feature_groups gives each group of predictors its own λ (concepts). It pays off when groups differ a lot in how much they explain and each has many columns — acoustic against lexical features, say: the weaker group gets more shrinkage instead of a compromise λ for all. Know its costs:

  • It silences a weak group. Cross-validation only rewards prediction, so a group that adds little gets a very large λ and its kernel goes to almost nothing: in simulation, a weak predictor kept 9 % of its amplitude. Right for a nuisance regressor; wrong when you need that group's TRF.
  • Its λ varies more between subjects, by 0.6 to 1.1 decades in simulation, so a group average mixes kernels shrunk differently.
  • With groups of comparable strength it gains nothing over a single λ.
  • It costs more, by the number of band ratios searched: an 11 × 11 grid on two groups cost 1.1 to 2.2 times a single λ. A random search over ratios (random_bands) samples a few ratios instead of the full product.

When a band's λ lands on the edge of its grid, the warning names the band.

docs.title: ridge-laplacian
docs.text:
Its penalty is the squared difference between neighbouring lags,

\[ w^\top M w = \sum_d \big(w_{d+1} - w_d\big)^2 , \]

which charges roughness, not size: a constant kernel costs nothing and a slow one very little. It smooths without shrinking.

  • On a predictor with clear signal it helps: smoother kernels that keep more of their amplitude. In simulation it beat ridge on the envelope beside a weak predictor at every SNR; with two strong predictors it tied from −10 dB up and lost on both at −20 dB.
  • On a weak predictor it fails. Nothing pulls the kernel towards zero, so slow noise enters it as a large, smooth kernel. With 1/f noise, as in EEG, whose power sits in exactly those slow components, the weak onsets' kernel error rose from 1.5 to 5.9 at −20 dB.

Use it only when every predictor carries clear signal and the SNR is not at the floor.

docs.title: Precision and device
docs.text: float32 gives the same kernels and the same λ as float64, on CPU and GPU. It costs 0.6–0.7× on CPU; on a GPU, 0.2–0.35× of a CPU float64 fit from ten minutes of data up. float64 on a consumer GPU is slower than the CPU.

docs.title: Delay margins
docs.text: delay_margin only matters for a kernel that is still non-zero at the edge of its window. For kernels that decay inside it, it changed nothing in simulation; keep the window wide enough instead.

docs.title: Cohorts
docs.text: TRFGroup costs what a hand-written loop of TRFModel fits does (0.98–1.00×) and returns identical kernels. Asking it for diagnostics or criteria adds 12–19 %, a bootstrap 3–15 %.

docs.title: Public surface
docs.text:
Everything below is importable straight from trflearn; the pages above document each one in full.

TRFlearn -- Temporal Response Function estimation in PyTorch.

Public API

TRFData Data container: named features (+ interactions), segmented/lazy layout, per-feature windows, MNE Raw targets, cross-validation partitions. spline_basis / event_scoped A B-spline expansion to hand to feature_bases, with the lab's knot and order convention pinned. Any scikit-learn transformer works there; this is the one worth not re-deriving. scope="event" expands a sparse event feature at its events only, and event_scoped does the same for any other transformer. See trflearn.bases. TRFModel Single entry point to build a model; cv="pooled" (standard k-fold), cv="averaged" (Crosse-Lalor) or cv="train_test" (a single split) selects the backend and returns its instance. PooledTRF / AveragedTRF / TrainTestTRF The backend model classes, one per cv value, also usable directly. TRFGroup Cohort-level analysis: declare a spec once, fit it per subject, then summary / grand_average / tfce across subjects. TRFMixedModel One linear mixed model over a whole cohort: the population kernel, the between-subject spread at every lag and each subject's shrunk kernel, fitted from per-subject sufficient statistics. See trflearn.mixed. load Read back a model or a cohort written with its save method. See trflearn.io for what a saved file does and does not carry. compare Rank two or more fitted models by AIC and BIC -- the comparison the held-out metrics cannot make, since they do not price complexity. See trflearn.selection. band_grid / random_bands Search spaces for a banded ridge, where each group of features declared in feature_groups gets its own regularization. Pass either to gridsearchCV(regularization_grid=...); band_grid sweeps a per-band product and random_bands samples ratios, which is what scales past two or three bands. See trflearn.search. plot_* methods Figures are methods, not side-effects, and every one returns its figure and takes save_path / show. The same call works on all three owners::

    model.plot_joint("envelope")          # one fitted model
    group.plot_average("envelope")        # the cohort grand-average
    group("s01").plot_average("envelope") # one subject of that cohort

`trflearn.plots.TRFPlots` carries the table of which figure works on which
owner, which need a montage, and which are shaded by a cluster test. Five
of them pass through to ``mne.Evoked`` and list its parameters too.

set_verbosity / get_verbosity / verbosity_scope How much the package prints: "silent", "warning", "info" (the default) or "debug". Set it process-wide, scope it to a block with the verbosity_scope context manager, or override it for one object with the verbose argument every model, container and cohort accepts. See trflearn.verbosity.

docs.title: Basis expansions
docs.text:
feature_bases accepts any scikit-learn transformer, so this module exists for the two things scikit-learn does not provide: dropping a basis column, which a TRFlearn design needs and an ordinary regression does not, and expanding a sparse event feature at its events only.

See Features & windows for why the drop is mandatory, which rule to pick, and why an event feature reverses the default.

docs.title: bases
docs.text:
bases.py — The spline basis, with the lab's convention pinned.

models.TorchTRF accepts any scikit-learn transformer in feature_bases, and that mechanism needs nothing added to it. This module exists for the two things scikit-learn does not provide: dropping a basis column, which a TRFlearn design needs and an ordinary regression does not, and expanding an event feature at its events only::

spline_basis(n_functions=4, order=3, knots="quantile", drop="mean")
spline_basis(scope="event")          # a sparse event amplitude
event_scoped(transformer)            # the same scope, for any basis

A B-spline basis is a partition of unity: its columns sum to exactly 1 on every row it touches, and per-column standardization turns that into an exact linear dependency, repeated at every lag. Nothing crashes, because the ridge penalty covers a singular block, but regularization is then doing two jobs -- regularizing and keeping the block invertible -- so a tuned regularization is partly pricing an artificial redundancy that carries no information. Dropping costs nothing in expressiveness: the model has no intercept and the target is centered, so the remaining columns span the same space.

An event feature -- a saccade's amplitude at its onset sample, zero everywhere else -- turns that around. Its zero means no event, not an event of amplitude 0, so scope="event" places the knots from the event rows and leaves every other row at zero, as unfold's spl() does. The columns then sum to the onset indicator instead of to 1: the full basis is well conditioned on its own, and dropping a column would remove the part of the response that does not depend on the amplitude, hence drop=None by default under this scope. Beside an onset regressor for the same event the full basis repeats it exactly, and drop="mean" becomes an identifiability requirement.

A cohort -- TRFGroup or TRFMixedModel -- takes its bases already fitted and freezes them (freeze_bases), so that a spline column is the same function of the stimulus in every subject and its kernels can be averaged.

The rest of the argument -- which column goes and why the evidence is not one-sided, the knot padding this module inherits from scikit-learn, and composing a basis with an elementwise transform -- lives in the Features & windows concepts page (docs/concepts/features.md), which the API page for this module links rather than repeats.
