One name per column.

docs.title: spline_basis
docs.text:
spline_basis(
    n_functions: int | None = None,
    order: int = 3,
    *,
    knots: str | ndarray = "quantile",
    drop: str | None = "auto",
    scope: str = "sample",
    extrapolation: str = "constant"
) -> SplineBasis

A B-spline basis expansion with one column dropped per input feature.

The convention this package recommends, in one call. See the module docstring for why the drop is mandatory, why the default is "mean", and why an event feature reverses both.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_functions int or None

How many columns each input feature is expanded into -- after the drop. This is the number that reaches the design: the block's n_subfeatures, the second axis of coef_, and the count of plot labels. The underlying spline space is one larger whenever a column is dropped, and the helper works n_knots out backwards from it. None (the default) keeps the spline space at five functions whatever the drop -- 4 columns with one dropped, 5 without -- which at the default order is the lab's reference function (3 knots, cubic).

None order int

Polynomial order of the splines: 3 is cubic, 4 quartic, 1 piecewise linear. Passed to scikit-learn as degree.

3 knots (quantile, uniform)

Where the interior knots go. "quantile" places them at quantiles of the stimulus, so resolution follows where the data actually is -- the right default for the skewed amplitude distributions this is usually applied to. "uniform" spaces them evenly over the observed range. An array places them by hand, as SplineTransformer expects.

"quantile" drop (auto, mean, last)

Which column to remove per input feature. "mean" is unfold's rule (the column peaking nearest that feature's mean), "last" matches scikit-learn's include_bias=False. None keeps the whole basis, which leaves a per-sample block exactly singular under per-column standardization -- available on purpose, but not a neutral choice there. "auto" (the default) is "mean" under scope="sample" and None under scope="event"; pass "mean" when an onset regressor for the same event is in the model.

"auto" scope (sample, event)

Which rows the basis is fitted on and applied to. "sample" expands every row, zeros included -- right for a continuous feature, where 0 is a value (silence, in an envelope). "event" is for a sparse feature whose 0 means no event: the knots come from the rows where any column is non-zero, those rows are expanded, and every other row stays exactly zero.

"sample" extrapolation str

What transform does outside the fitted range, passed through to SplineTransformer. Relevant to predict on new stimulus.

'constant'

Returns:

Type Description SplineBasis

A transformer with fit/transform, usable directly as a feature_bases value and picklable, so save(with_bases=True) carries it.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If drop or scope is not a known value, or n_functions is too small for order -- the smallest spline space of a given order has order + 1 functions, so asking for fewer is a contradiction rather than a rounding matter, and it says so rather than quietly giving you something else.

Examples:

A continuous feature:

>>> model = TRFModel(
...     TRFDataset=data, features=["envelope"],
...     default_window=(-0.1, 0.4),
...     feature_bases={"envelope": spline_basis(n_functions=4)},
... )

A saccade's amplitude beside its onset, unfold's 1 + spl(amplitude):

>>> model = TRFModel(
...     TRFDataset=data, features=["saccade", "sac_amplitude"],
...     default_window=(-0.2, 0.4),
...     feature_bases={
...         "sac_amplitude": spline_basis(scope="event", drop="mean")
...     },
... )

docs.text:
event_scoped(transformer: Any) -> EventScoped

Any basis expansion, applied at the events of a sparse feature only.

What spline_basis(scope="event") does, for any other transformer: it is fitted on the rows where the feature is non-zero, applied to those rows, and every other row stays exactly zero.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default transformer sklearn-style transformer

Anything with fit/transform, pipelines included. It is cloned at fit, so the object passed in stays unfitted.

required

Notes

The wrapper goes outermost: it reads the events off the raw stimulus, so nothing inside it ever sees a zero. That makes np.log safe on an amplitude, where per sample it would map every empty row to -inf.

Examples:

>>> feature_bases = {"sac_amplitude": event_scoped(make_pipeline(
...     FunctionTransformer(np.log), spline_basis(drop=None)
... ))}

A digest of a basis's fitted state, equal for bases that transform alike.

docs.title: TRFData
docs.text: The lazy, window-agnostic data container. See the concept page for the narrative.

docs.title: TRFData
docs.text:
TRFData(
    features: dict[str, ndarray | list[ndarray]],
    y: ndarray | list[ndarray] | BaseRaw | list,
    sample_rate: int,
    precision: str = "float32",
    relevant_indexes: ndarray | list | None = None,
    target_names: list[str] | None = None,
    use_gpu: bool = False,
    info: Info | None = None,
    verbose: int | str | bool | None = None,
)

Bases: Dataset

Reusable, lazy container of named stimulus features, targets and folds.

Holds all candidate features by name, plus the targets and the cross-validation config, so a single instance can feed several models -- different feature subsets, different windows -- over the same recording.

It does not take tmin/tmax: the delay window lives on the model (default_window / feature_windows). Construction computes only the cheap, values-free segment layout; the NaN buffer between segments, the buffer-safe sample set and the folds all wait for materialize, which a model triggers once it knows its crop window. Re-materializing for a different window recomputes them and invalidates the feature cache.

Build a reusable, fully lazy TRF data container from named streams.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default features dict[str, ndarray | list[ndarray]]

Mapping name -> feature. Each feature is either a 2D array (n_samples, n_subfeatures) (single continuous recording) or a list of per-segment 2D arrays (samples_s, n_subfeatures) (segmented recording). All features must share the same layout as y (all 2D, or all lists with the same number of segments).

required y np.ndarray, list of np.ndarray, mne.io.Raw, or list of mne.io.Raw

Targets, in the same layout as the features: 2D (n_samples, n_channels) or a list of per-segment 2D arrays, or an MNE Raw / a list of Raw, one per segment. Raw input must match the features in length exactly, where plain arrays are trimmed to the per-segment minimum.

required sample_rate int

Sampling rate in Hz.

required precision str

"float32" or "float64".

"float32" relevant_indexes ndarray or list

Subset of samples used for folds and design. None = all buffer-free samples. Four forms are accepted:

  • an integer index array, already in concatenated coordinates;
  • a boolean mask with one entry per real sample, so its length is the sum of the segment lengths -- the inter-segment buffer is not part of it, since its width comes from the model's delay window and does not exist yet at construction time. A mask of any other length is an error;
  • in the segmented layout, a list of per-segment local index arrays, remapped to concatenated coordinates;
  • in the segmented layout, a list of per-segment boolean masks, each as long as its own segment. Entries are resolved one by one, so the list may mix both forms.

Whatever the form, the result is intersected with the buffer-free set at materialization.

These select rows of the design matrix and of the target, not samples of the raw feature: every feature is lagged over its whole series, in original time coordinates, and only then are these rows kept -- the same rows on both sides, so X and y stay aligned. A subset may therefore be arbitrarily gappy without its delays ever jumping across the gaps. Features and y must share the same original length for the indices to mean the same thing on both (see models.TorchTRF._make_gram_and_y for the full invariant).

None target_names list of str

Names for the targets (e.g. EEG channel labels). Ignored when info is given (or later attached): the channel names then come from it.

None use_gpu bool

If True, materialized features and targets live on CUDA.

False info Info

Channel info with a montage, for array-based targets. Equivalent to calling set_info afterwards, which documents what it unlocks and what degrades quietly without it.

None verbose (int, str, bool or None)

How much this container prints, overriding the process-wide setting: "silent", "warning", "info" or "debug". None (the default) follows the global one -- see trflearn.verbosity.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If precision is not one of the two supported values, if use_gpu is set without CUDA available, if features is empty or not a dict of string keys, if the feature and target layouts disagree, or if target_names does not match the channel count.

docs.title: set_info
docs.text:
set_info(info: Info) -> TRFData

Attach MNE channel info (montage, channel types) to this container.

The Raw ingestion path fills info on its own; this is the way in for array-based targets, whose montage would otherwise be missing for good. It unlocks models.TorchTRF.to_evoked, every montage-based figure, and -- the one that fails quietly rather than loudly -- the spatial adjacency of TRFGroup.tfce, which without a montage treats the channels as independent.

The info's channel names become target_names, mirroring what the Raw path already does. Nothing else is affected: info is pure metadata and takes no part in materialization, so it may be attached before or after materialize / create_partitions without recomputing anything.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default info Info

Must describe exactly n_channels channels at sample_rate Hz. Both are checked here so a mismatch surfaces now rather than several steps later inside a plotting call.

required

Returns:

Type Description TRFData

self, for chaining.

See Also

set_montage : build the info from a montage plus channel names.

Notes

TRFGroup copies the info from the first subject it fits, so attach it before fit_subject (or assign group.info yourself afterwards).

    ch_names: list[str] | None = None,

Build the channel info from a montage and attach it (see set_info).

The shortcut for the common case: no Raw at hand, but the electrode layout is known. Creates an mne.Info for ch_names at the container's sample_rate, applies montage to it and stores it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default montage str or DigMontage

A standard montage name (e.g. "standard_1020", "biosemi64") or a montage object.

required ch_names list of str

Channel names, in the order of the target columns. Defaults to the container's target_names — which only works if they are real electrode labels; the generated "Target i" placeholders are rejected with a message asking for explicit names.

None ch_types str or list of str

Channel types, forwarded to mne.create_info.

"eeg"

Returns:

Type Description TRFData

self, for chaining.

Examples:

>>> data = TRFData(features=feats, y=eeg_array, sample_rate=128)
>>> data.set_montage("standard_1020",

docs.title: set_source_positions
docs.text:
set_source_positions(
    positions: (
        dict[str, tuple[float, float, float]] | ndarray
    ),
    ch_names: list[str] | None = None,
) -> TRFData

Attach source-space region centroids as channel info (see set_info).

The source-space analogue of set_montage: for targets that are parcel or virtual-electrode timecourses rather than sensors, where a montage does not exist and MNE's own machinery has nothing to work with. The centroids are written into the channel positions of an mne.Info, so from here on the regions travel through the package exactly as sensors do -- mne.pick_info keeps them aligned when group.TRFGroup restricts a cohort to its common channels, and io.save stores them.

What they unlock is the spatial adjacency of group.TRFGroup.tfce, which for parcels comes from statistics.source_adjacency (proximity) instead of a montage, and plots.TRFPlots.plot_source_butterfly. Topomaps stay unavailable: they need a head surface to interpolate onto, which region centroids are not.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default positions (dict or array - like, shape(n_channels, 3))

{region_name: (x, y, z)} or an array in the order of the target columns. Coordinates in metres, as MNE stores them (the frame only has to be consistent -- adjacency and colouring use relative distances). A dict is matched on the channel name, falling back to the name stripped of MNE's -0/-1 uniqueness suffixes, which appear whenever several centroids share a parcel name.

required ch_names list of str

Region names, in the order of the target columns. Defaults to the existing info's names, else target_names.

None

Returns:

Type Description TRFData

self, for chaining.

See Also

set_info : attach a ready-made mne.Info. statistics.source_adjacency : the graph these positions feed.

Examples:

>>> data = TRFData(features=feats, y=parcel_timecourses,
...                sample_rate=128)
>>> data.set_source_positions(label_positions, ch_names=label_names)

Positions may also be added to targets ingested as an mne.Raw of region timecourses, which keeps that Raw's channel names and types:

>>> data = TRFData(features=feats, y=raw_src, sample_rate=128)
>>> data.set_source_positions(label_positions)

docs.title: create_partitions
docs.text:
create_partitions(
    n_folds: int | None = None,
    stratify_by_segment: bool | None = None,
    segments_as_folds: bool = False,
    train_size: float | None = None,
) -> TRFData

Record the cross-validation partition config (lazy).

This does not build the folds: the fold indices depend on the buffer-safe sample set, which is only known once a model fixes the crop window and triggers materialize. Here the cheap, values-free constraints are validated and the config stored; the folds are built at materialization, or immediately if the container is already materialized.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_folds int or None

The number of folds; None means DEFAULT_N_FOLDS (5). Ignored when segments_as_folds=True -- the fold count is then the number of segments, and a disagreeing value warns at materialization.

None stratify_by_segment bool or None

Block-stratified CV: within each segment, divide its sample positions into n_folds contiguous sub-blocks; fold k's test set is the union of sub-block k across all segments, so every fold sees every segment. None (the default) stratifies whenever the container is segmented and uses plain contiguous KFold otherwise; True requires the segmented layout; False always uses plain contiguous KFold. With a single segment it falls back to plain contiguous KFold.

None segments_as_folds bool

Leave-one-segment-out CV (the Lalor/mTRF paradigm). Fold s's test set is exactly segment s, so the fold count is the number of segments and n_folds is ignored. Requires the segmented layout with at least 2 segments. Takes precedence over stratify_by_segment.

False train_size float

A single contiguous train/test split: the first train_size fraction of the buffer-safe samples is the train fold, the rest the test fold, one fold in total. Used by the cv="train_test" paradigm; takes precedence over every other argument, which are then ignored.

None

Returns:

Type Description TRFData

self, for chaining.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If train_size is not a fraction in (0, 1), or if a segment-based scheme is explicitly asked of a single recording.

Notes

Folds are always contiguous in time, with no sample-level shuffling: shuffling scatters near-in-time neighbours across train and test and, on autocorrelated signals like EEG, produces severe leakage. Use stratify_by_segment to balance segments without that contamination, or segments_as_folds for leave-one-segment-out CV.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
What a fitted design says about itself: how well conditioned it is, how much its feature blocks overlap, and what the fit costs in effective parameters. Mixed into every paradigm, so these are methods of the model you already have.

None of it is computed by fitting — see diagnostics for why — and all of it is cached, so a model loaded from disk reports the numbers its file carried without recomputing anything.

docs.title: ModelDiagnosticsMixin
docs.text:
The design report of models.TorchTRF, kept out of the estimator itself.

Mixed into models.TorchTRF beside plots.ModelPlots, on the same reasoning: reporting on a fit is not fitting, and the class is easier to read when the two are not interleaved.

Every *_ attribute below reads the cache and, on a miss, computes it through the method that owns it -- diagnostics for the first five, information_criteria for the last three. All eight are None for solver="cross_corr", which has no penalized normal system.

It holds no state of its own. What it needs from the host:

_diagnostics The cache every value is stored in and read from. _fitted_regularization Refused when None: there is no regularized design to report on. _require_data and _full_design_pass The full-design assembly, and the guard that explains how to get the data back when a model was loaded without it. _build_block_penalty, _coef_matrix, _trim_blocks and _feature_column_slices The design's own geometry, which the criteria and the per-block GVIF are computed against.

docs.title: diagnostics
docs.text:
diagnostics(
    *,
    vif: bool = True,
    criteria: bool = False,
    recompute: bool = False
) -> dict

Compute the numerical diagnostics of the design, once, and cache them.

Diagnostics are a report on the fit, not a product of it: nothing here runs during fit/gridsearchCV. The reason is cost. The numbers are defined on the full design -- the normal matrix over every relevant sample, not a single fold -- so that they are single, well defined quantities that do not depend on an arbitrary fold and are identical for the pooled and averaged paradigms. Assembling it is a whole extra pass over the data, on top of the ones the fit already made fold by fold and discarded, and it was being paid by every fit whether or not anyone ever read the result. Asked for explicitly, it is paid once, by whoever wants the answer.

The cache is keyed by name, and a stored None counts as computed: with solver="cross_corr" there is no penalized normal matrix, so all five are legitimately None and asking again would not help.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default vif bool

Compute the collinearity report: vif_, vif_columns_ and vif_aliased_, which come out of one decomposition and are therefore cached together. This is the one extra (n_columns, n_columns) eigendecomposition on top of the two the condition number needs; vif=False skips it and leaves the keys uncomputed, so a later read of any of the three can still fill them in.

True criteria bool

Also fill the information criteria (see information_criteria) from the same assembly. They are a different report, and asking for them separately is a second identical pass over the design -- which is nothing on one model and one pass per subject on a cohort. This method is the one entry point for "walk the full design once", and vif / criteria say what to compute while it is in memory; information_criteria remains the direct entry when the criteria are all that is wanted.

False recompute bool

Recompute even if the values are cached. Only useful after something about the design changed, and impossible on a model loaded without its data.

False

Returns:

Type Description dict

{"condition_number": float | None, "effective_rank": float | None, "vif": ndarray | None, "vif_columns": ndarray | None, "vif_aliased": ndarray | None}. The three vif keys are absent when vif=False and they had not been computed before, and the criteria keys are present only with criteria=True.

Warns:

Type Description UserWarning

When the condition number exceeds ILL_CONDITIONED_ABOVE. This is the one thing fitting used to say on its own; it now waits until someone asks.

UserWarning

When the design carries exactly aliased columns, naming both how many take part in a dependency and how many are redundant. Only with vif=True, which is the default.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

If the model has not been fitted, or if it was loaded without its data and the values are not already cached from the file.

Examples using diagnostics

  • 2 · Natural speech TRF

docs.title: information_criteria
docs.text:
information_criteria(
    *, recompute: bool = False
) -> CriteriaReport

AIC and BIC of the fitted model, computed once and cached.

What they are for: the metrics in metrics say how well this model predicts, and cannot rank two different models, since adding a feature block almost never makes the fit worse. AIC and BIC put the fit and a price for complexity in one number, so they can. Lower is better for both. To compare, use selection.compare, which also refuses the pairs that are not comparable.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default recompute bool

Recompute even if cached. Same meaning and same limits as in diagnostics.

False

Returns:

Type Description CriteriaReport

The nine keys, their shapes and when they are None, are on that class.

target_ss is y'y of the raw target over the rows that entered the fit, and it is what selection.compare fingerprints to refuse two models that are not describing the same response. Raw and not standardized on purpose: with the default target_preprocess="Standardize" the standardized y'y is approximately n for any recording whatsoever, so it would pass two entirely different datasets as the same one.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

If the model has not been fitted, or was loaded without its data and the values are not already cached from the file.

Notes

Computed like the rest of the design report -- on demand, on the full relevant design at the fitted regularization, assembled in float64 -- and cached in the same store, so diagnostics() and this share a pass' worth of discipline but not the pass itself.

The three ingredients.

The likelihood is in-sample. That is the definition, not an oversight: AIC exists because the in-sample fit is optimistic, and the penalty is the correction. See trflearn.selection for why penalizing a held-out likelihood would count that correction twice.

The complexity is the effective degrees of freedom, the trace of the ridge hat matrix H = X (X'X + n a M)^-1 X', computed here as tr((XTX + a M)^-1 XTX) on the per-sample-averaged normal matrix -- which is already the right quantity, since the package solves (X'X/n + a M), i.e. (X'X + n a M), so the n cancels. It runs from n_columns at λ -> 0 down to 0 as λ grows. The column count would be wrong: a penalized fit does not spend n_columns parameters, and counting columns would make two models with the same windows equally complex however differently they were regularized.

The residual sum of squares is read off the same normal matrices, N * (y'y - 2 b'X'y + b'X'X b), so scoring the fit costs no second pass over the design and no prediction.

Two widths, on purpose.

With delay_margin > 0 the margin lags are estimated and then trimmed away. The residuals are those of the reported filter, so rss uses the trimmed design and coef_; the effective degrees of freedom describe the estimation that produced it, so edf is computed at fit width -- those parameters were fitted from the data and did spend its information, whatever happened to them afterwards. At the default delay_margin=0 the two widths are the same and the distinction is moot.

docs.title: TRFGroup
docs.text: Cohort-level analysis. See the concept page for the narrative.

docs.title: TRFGroup
docs.text:
TRFGroup(
    features: list,
    default_window: tuple,
    *,
    cv: str = "pooled",
    feature_windows: dict | None = None,
    feature_bases: dict | None = None,
    feature_groups: dict | None = None,
    feature_preprocess: str | None = "Standardize",
    target_preprocess: str | None = "Standardize",
    solver: str = "ridge",
    delay_margin: float = 0.0,
    drop_zero_rows: bool = False,
    drop_warn_fraction: float = 0.25,
    diagnostics: bool = False,
    criteria: bool = False,
    regularization_grid: (
        list | ndarray | dict | None
    ) = None,
    metric: str = "r2",
    score_on: str | list | dict | None = None,
    bootstrap: bool = False,
    n_resamples: int | None = None,
    random_state: int | None = None,
    fit_method: str = "gridsearch",
    regularization: float | None = None,
    regularization_strategy: str | None = None,
    keep_kernels_by_regularization: bool = False,
    n_subjects: int | None = None,
    kernel_units: str = "original",
    train_size: float | None = None,
    inner_train_cutoff: float | None = None,
    metric_aggregation_function: str | int | None = None,
    metric_limit_percentage: float | None = None,
    per_fold_metric: bool = False,
    validation_plot: bool | None = None,
    plot_dir: str | PathLike | None = None,
    verbose: int | str | bool | None = None
)

Bases: GroupPlots

Fit one model spec across a cohort and aggregate the results.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default features list

Feature specs (strings / interaction tuples), exactly as for TRFModel.

required default_window tuple of float

(tmin, tmax) in seconds — the fallback delay window, forwarded to each subject's TRFModel. Required.

required cv str

Cross-validation paradigm passed to TRFModel ("pooled", "averaged" or "train_test").

"pooled" feature_windows dict or None

Per-feature delay windows, forwarded to TRFModel.

None feature_bases dict or None

Per-feature basis expansions, already fitted, which every subject shares unchanged. That is what makes a spline column the same function of the stimulus in every subject, and so what lets the cohort average its kernels; refitted per subject, the knots would follow each subject's own stimulus. Fit each basis once on a stimulus that covers the whole cohort -- the subjects' feature arrays concatenated, say -- and pass it fitted. A subject whose bases differ from the ones the cohort was fitted with is refused.

None feature_groups dict or None

{band: [spec, ...]} grouping features into bands with their own regularization (a banded ridge), forwarded to TRFModel. Every subject of a cohort shares one band structure, so the per-band λ values each of them selects are comparable across the cohort; summary reports the scalar summary and each subject's record keeps the per-band detail.

None feature_preprocess str

Standardization choices, forwarded to TRFModel.

'Standardize' target_preprocess str

Standardization choices, forwarded to TRFModel.

'Standardize' solver str

Solver, forwarded to TRFModel.

"ridge" delay_margin float

Ridge edge margin (seconds), forwarded to TRFModel.

0.0 drop_zero_rows bool

Estimate coefficients only where some feature block has a predictor, forwarded to TRFModel. Part of the cohort spec on purpose: it rescales what regularization means, so a cohort must not mix the two settings across subjects. See models.TorchTRF for the derivation.

False drop_warn_fraction float

Threshold above which the dropped-sample warning fires, forwarded to TRFModel. Warned once per subject model.

0.25 diagnostics bool

Compute each subject's design diagnostics and record them. Off by default because they are not a product of fitting: each one costs a full extra pass over that subject's design (see models.TorchTRF.diagnostics), and a cohort pays it once per subject. With it off, condition_number, effective_rank, vif and n_aliased are None in every record. With it on, the collinearity report is included -- one more (n_columns, n_columns) decomposition on a pass that is already being paid for -- because a diagnostic that cannot be read across subjects does not say whose design is the odd one out. Overridable per subject via fit_subject(..., diagnostics=True).

False criteria bool

Record each subject's information criteria (AIC, BIC, the effective degrees of freedom, and the two quantities that identify the data they were computed on). Off by default for the same reason: it is a full extra pass over each subject's design. With diagnostics also on, both reports come out of one pass rather than two.

This is what compare_to needs, and it has to be decided before fitting: the cohort discards each subject's model, so a comparison cannot be assembled after the fact without refitting. Overridable per subject via fit_subject(..., criteria=True).

False regularization_grid array - like or None

Regularization grid searched per subject when fit_method="gridsearch". None searches search.DEFAULT_REGULARIZATION_GRID, np.logspace(-3, 3, 13).

None metric str

Chooses each subject's λ and scores each subject. R² suits the kernels a cohort is fitted for; pass "Pearson" when prediction accuracy is the result.

"r2" score_on (str, list, dict or None)

Which held-out samples every subject's metric is computed on, as in models.TorchTRF.fit: "informative", a list of features or a {feature: (tmin, tmax)} window. None (the default) scores every sample. Only these declarative forms are shared by a cohort; a boolean array or a callable describes one recording, so it goes to that subject's fit_subject. The figures' metric label is marked with it, and each record keeps scored_on.

None bootstrap bool

If True, store each subject's bootstrap metric distribution.

False n_resamples optional

Forwarded to the backend's bootstrap when bootstrap=True. None (the default) leaves the backend's own values in place -- 10,000 resamples and a fixed seed, so every subject's interval is reproducible and, since the seed does not vary with the subject, comparable across the cohort. Overridable per subject in fit_subject.

None random_state optional

Forwarded to the backend's bootstrap when bootstrap=True. None (the default) leaves the backend's own values in place -- 10,000 resamples and a fixed seed, so every subject's interval is reproducible and, since the seed does not vary with the subject, comparable across the cohort. Overridable per subject in fit_subject.

None fit_method (gridsearch, fit)

How each subject is fitted. "gridsearch" sweeps regularization_grid with the paradigm's gridsearchCV and refits at the selected λ; "fit" skips the search and fits directly at regularization.

"gridsearch" regularization float or None

Fixed regularization used when fit_method="fit". Required in that mode (here or per subject).

None regularization_strategy str or None

How the subjects' λ values relate when fit_method="gridsearch". A noisier subject selects a larger λ and is shrunk more, so with a λ per subject a difference between subjects partly reflects their noise (see One λ for a whole group in docs/recommendations.md).

"mean-curve", "median" One λ for the whole cohort, in two passes: search_subject on every subject, share_regularization, then fit_subject on every subject at that λ. "mean-curve" selects on the subjects' mean validation curve; "median" takes the geometric median of the λ values they chose on their own. fit_subject raises if it is called before share_regularization. "leave-one-out" One λ for the whole cohort, the one at which the other subjects' average kernel best predicts each subject, scored with metric. It needs every subject's kernels at every λ, so it keeps them whatever keep_kernels_by_regularization says, together with the sums of each subject's design. "subject" Each subject is searched and fitted at its own λ, in one loop of fit_subject. None (the default) As "subject", but the cohort warns once when its subjects end up at different λ values. Following the two-pass pattern shares one λ instead, by "mean-curve".

None keep_kernels_by_regularization bool

Have search_subject also fit each subject at every λ searched and keep those kernels in memory, so that share_regularization fills every subject's record at the shared λ and the second loop of fit_subject is not needed. Same compute as the two passes; what it saves is loading every subject twice, and what it costs is memory -- logged at INFO for the first subject, and refused before any fit past half of the memory available. The kernels are read with kernels_by_regularization and are not written by save. With bootstrap, diagnostics or criteria, which need the data, the second loop stays.

False n_subjects int or None

How many subjects the cohort will search, so that the memory the kept kernels take is checked for all of them before the first one is fitted. None checks the subjects searched so far, one at a time.

None kernel_units (original, standardized)

Units of every kernel the cohort hands out: results, subjects, grand_average, the cluster tests, the contrasts and the figures. "original" undoes the standardization, coef_ · σ_y / σ_x, giving the recording's unit per unit of each feature. "standardized" keeps the coefficients as fitted, in target standard deviations per feature standard deviation; since each subject is divided by their own σ_y, which contains their noise, a noisier subject's kernel comes out smaller. It can be changed after fitting: the grand average follows, and cluster tests run in the other units are cleared.

"original" train_size float or None

Train proportion of the single split, forwarded to the backend constructor. Only valid with cv="train_test".

None inner_train_cutoff float or None

Inner train/validation cutoff of the regularization search. Only valid with cv="pooled"; None keeps the backend default (0.8).

None metric_aggregation_function (str, int or None)

How per-fold validation metrics are aggregated for λ selection ("median"/"mean"/"max"/fold index). Not available with cv="train_test"; None keeps the backend default, which is "mean" in every paradigm.

None metric_limit_percentage float or None

If set, select the largest λ within this fraction of the best metric. It shrinks the kernels without improving their shape; leave it None when the kernels are the result.

None per_fold_metric bool

Report the metric per fold instead of over the concatenated folds. The cohort still stores the channel-wise metric, so aggregation is unaffected.

False validation_plot bool or None

Whether each subject's regularization search plot is saved. Defaults to False (the cohort loop is not interactive).

None plot_dir (str, Path or None)

Directory those plots go in, one validation_plot_<subject>.png per subject, created if it does not exist. A directory rather than a path because a cohort writes one figure per subject -- the single-figure TRFModel.gridsearchCV is the one that takes a plot_path. None writes them into the working directory.

None verbose (int, str, bool or None)

How much every subject's model prints, overriding the process-wide setting: "silent", "warning", "info" or "debug". None (the default) follows the global one. "warning" is the usual choice for a cohort -- numeric problems still surface, the per-subject status chatter does not. See trflearn.verbosity.

None Notes

Every parameter above is a default: fit_subject accepts the same names as per-subject overrides, plus any other keyword the selected paradigm's fit/gridsearchCV accepts (e.g. as_evoked). Parameters that the chosen cv does not support raise a TypeError naming what is available. A subject fitted with fit_method="fit" ignores the defaults that only configure the regularization search (inner_train_cutoff, metric_aggregation_function, metric_limit_percentage), so a group set up for the search can still fit a subject at a known λ; passed to that call explicitly, they raise.

Subjects need not share a montage. Each one records its channel names, and every aggregate is computed over common_channels -- the intersection, in the first subject's order -- matching channels by name rather than by position. A cohort whose subjects all share the same montage is unaffected; one that does not warns once, naming the channels it drops.

See Also

call : the per-subject plotting view, group("s01").plot_*(...). plots.GroupPlots : the cohort's own figures, and the table of which figure works on which owner.

Attributes:

Name Type Description shared_regularization_ (float, dict or None)

The cohort's λ after share_regularization: a float, or {band: value} for a banded search. None before, and in a cohort that does not share one. What it was chosen from is in regularization_search_.

grand_average_ dict or None

{spec: {"mean","std","sem","n"}} after grand_average, over common_channels.

stats_ dict

{spec: (t_obs, pvals)} after permutation_test / tfce.

contrast_stats_ dict

{spec: (t_obs, pvals)} after permutation_test_contrast, and {(spec_a, spec_b): ...} after permutation_test_contrast_features.

info Info or None

Channel info inherited from the first subject's TRFData (montage/types for adjacency and Evoked export). Restricted to common_channels wherever it labels an aggregate.

common_channels list or None

The channels every subject contributes; None for unnamed (array) targets, which are aligned by position instead.

Examples using TRFGroup

  • 1 · OPM sensor TRF
  • 2 · Natural speech TRF
  • 3 · OPM source TRF

docs.title: kernel_units property writable
docs.text:
kernel_units: str

Units of every kernel the cohort hands out; see the class Parameters.

Setting it recomputes the grand average on its next use and clears the cluster tests, which were run in the other units.

docs.title: subject_ids property
docs.text:
subject_ids: list

Subject identifiers, in the order they were added.

docs.title: subjects property
docs.text:
subjects: MappingProxyType

Read-only view of every fitted subject's stored result.

{subject_id: {"coef_", "metric", "scored_on", "regularization", "bootstrap", "delays", "scales", "condition_number", "effective_rank", "vif", "n_aliased", "aic", "bic", "edf", "n", "target_ss", "ch_names"}} -- see results for what each entry holds. The mapping (and each record) rejects assignment, so the cohort cannot be mutated by accident; the arrays inside are the stored ones, not copies, so .copy() them before modifying in place. The kernels are the exception when kernel_units is "original": they are computed on each call.

docs.title: regularization_search_ property
docs.text:
regularization_search_: MappingProxyType | None

What the cohort's λ was chosen from; None before any search.

Returns:

Type Description MappingProxyType or None

regularization (n_values,), each λ searched: the value itself, or the global scale of a banded one -- the axis the curves are drawn over. metric The metric the curves are in, marked by score_on. curves {subject: (n_values,)}, each subject's validation curve. chosen {subject: λ}, what each subject's own search chose: a float, or {band: value} for a banded search. strategy The strategy share_regularization used, None before. cohort_curve (n_values,), the curve the shared λ was selected on: the mean curve or the leave-one-out one. None for "median", which selects on the choices, and before sharing.

docs.title: common_channels property
docs.text:
common_channels: list | None

Channels in every fitted subject, in the first subject's order.

The cohort does not require its subjects to share a montage: each one contributes the channels it has, and every aggregate (grand_average, summary, permutation_test, the group plots) is computed over this intersection. Channels missing from even one subject are dropped from all of them -- the same convention as picking a common set before a permutation test.

Returns None when at least one subject was fitted from plain arrays with no channel names: nothing can be matched by identity there, so aggregation falls back to positional alignment and simply requires every subject to have the same number of channels.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

If no subject has been fitted yet.

ValueError

If the intersection is empty -- the cohort has no shared channel and there is nothing to average.

Examples using common_channels

  • 2 · Natural speech TRF
  • 3 · OPM source TRF

docs.title: results
docs.text:
results(subject_id: str | tuple) -> MappingProxyType

Read-only access to one subject's stored result.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default subject_id str or tuple

An id passed to fit_subject. Unknown ids raise KeyError listing the cohort.

required

Returns:

Type Description MappingProxyType

Everything below is the subject's own, in the subject's own channel order -- not picked to common_channels.

coef_ {spec: (n_channels, n_subfeatures, n_delays)}, the fold-averaged kernels, in the cohort's kernel_units. metric (n_channels,), the channel-wise held-out metric. scored_on {"score_on", "fraction"}: what the metric was restricted to and the fraction of held-out samples kept, or None when it covers every sample (see models.TorchTRF.fit). regularization, regularization_bands The regularization actually fitted, as a scalar summary and, for a banded ridge, the {band: value} detail. regularization_bands is None when the bands never varied. bootstrap {"n_samples", "distribution", "random_state"}, or None. delays {spec: lags} in samples. scales {"target": (n_channels,), "features": {spec: (n_subfeatures,)}}, what the subject's standardization divided by (None where nothing was divided). They take the fitted coefficients to original units. condition_number, effective_rank The design diagnostics, None unless the cohort was built with diagnostics=True. vif, n_aliased {spec: float}, each block's generalized VIF (Fox & Monette, 1992, as GVIF^(1/2d)), and how many design columns are exact linear combinations of the rest. Read them together: the GVIF is computed on a full-rank subset of the columns, so an exact dependency shows up in n_aliased rather than as a large GVIF -- two duplicated blocks read 1.0 each once the duplicate columns are set aside. 1.0 means nothing shared, nan the degenerate single-block case, 0 a healthy design. Both follow diagnostics=True. The per-column arrays behind them stay on the model and are not recorded; refit the odd subject to inspect them. aic, bic, edf (n_channels,) information criteria and the effective degrees of freedom, None unless the cohort was built with criteria=True. Lower is better, and a criterion means something only as a difference against another model of the same response -- which is what compare_to is for. n, target_ss How many rows entered this subject's fit and the raw y'y over them. They identify the data those criteria describe, and compare_to refuses a comparison when they disagree. ch_names This subject's channel labels, None for unnamed array targets. The axis order of coef_ and metric.

See Also

subjects : the same view for the whole cohort. call : the plotting view (group(subject_id).plot_*()).

Examples:

>>> res = group.results("s01")
>>> res["regularization"], res["metric"].mean()
>>> res["coef_"]["envelope"].shape

Examples using results

  • 2 · Natural speech TRF

docs.title: save
docs.text:
save(
    path: str | PathLike, *, with_bases: bool = False
) -> None

Write the cohort to path (see trflearn.io).

Nothing is lost: the cohort already keeps only compact arrays per subject, so one read back with trflearn.load(path) aggregates, tests, plots and keeps fitting subjects exactly like this one. The per-subject bootstrap distributions and the cluster-test results travel with it -- expensive to recompute, and the second is what shades the figures.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str or PathLike

Destination file; parent directories are created. .pkl is the convention, but the path is used verbatim.

required with_bases bool

Embed the feature_bases transformers, the only thing that ties a file to a library version. Without them a cohort that used bases still reads back whole; only fitting further subjects needs them set again, and trflearn.load says so.

False See Also

trflearn.io.save : the format, and what a version bump costs.

Examples using save

  • 2 · Natural speech TRF

docs.title: search_subject
docs.text:
search_subject(
    TRFDataset: TRFData,
    subject_id: str | tuple,
    **overrides: Any
) -> TRFGroup

Run one subject's regularization search and keep only its curve.

The first of the two passes that fit a cohort at one λ::

for subject_id in subject_ids:
    group.search_subject(load(subject_id), subject_id)
group.share_regularization()
for subject_id in subject_ids:
    group.fit_subject(load(subject_id), subject_id)

The search is the one fit_subject would run, without the final fit. The model is discarded and the cohort keeps n_values floats per subject, from which share_regularization picks the λ.

When the cohort keeps its kernels (keep_kernels_by_regularization or regularization_strategy="leave-one-out"), the subject is also fitted at every λ, as fit_subject would at each one, and the kernels and the metric are kept for share_regularization to fill the record with; leave-one-out keeps the sums of the subject's design too. The memory this takes is known before the fit: it is logged at INFO for the first subject and refused past the budget.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default TRFDataset TRFData

The subject's container, already partitioned.

required subject_id str or tuple

The key the curve is kept under, the same fit_subject takes.

required **overrides Any

Any keyword of fit_subject that configures the search (inner_train_cutoff, score_on, validation_plot, ...). Not regularization_grid or metric: the curves are averaged, so they must share one grid and one metric.

{}

Returns:

Type Description TRFGroup

self, so calls chain over a cohort.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the cohort fits each subject at its own λ (regularization_strategy="subject") or at a fixed one (fit_method="fit"), if the subject has already been searched, or if its search space differs from the other subjects'.

TypeError

If regularization_grid, metric, diagnostics, criteria or a keyword of the final fit is passed.

RuntimeError

If share_regularization has already run.

MemoryError

If the kernels the cohort keeps would pass the budget: half of the memory available, over n_subjects or the subjects so far.

docs.title: share_regularization
docs.text:
share_regularization(
    strategy: str | None = None,
) -> float | dict

Choose the cohort's λ from every searched subject.

The second of the two passes (see search_subject); fit_subject then fits every subject at the result. A cohort that kept its kernels is filled here instead, every searched subject's record at the shared λ, unless it asks for bootstrap, diagnostics or criteria, which need the data and leave the fit_subject loop in place.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default strategy (mean - curve, median, leave - one - out)

"mean-curve" selects on the subjects' mean validation curve, the way one subject's search selects on its own curve, so metric_limit_percentage applies. "median" takes the geometric median of the λ values the subjects chose on their own, snapped to the nearest λ searched. "leave-one-out" selects on how well the other subjects' average kernel predicts each subject, in the cohort's kernel_units, over common_channels, and also takes metric_limit_percentage; it needs the kernels and sums a cohort built with that strategy keeps. None uses the cohort's regularization_strategy, or "mean-curve" when that is unset. See group_regularization for the arithmetic.

"mean-curve"

Returns:

Type Description float or dict

The λ, also kept as shared_regularization_: a float for a plain grid, {band: value} for a banded search, which shares the whole vector. The curve it was selected on is in regularization_search_.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the strategy is not one of the three, the cohort fits each subject at its own λ (regularization_strategy="subject"), or "median" meets a λ that is not positive.

RuntimeError

If no subject has been searched, some were already fitted at their own λ, or "leave-one-out" lacks a subject's kernels.

docs.title: kernels_by_regularization
docs.text:
kernels_by_regularization(
    subject_id: str | tuple,
) -> MappingProxyType

One subject's kernels at every λ searched, not only the shared one.

Kept by search_subject when the cohort is built with keep_kernels_by_regularization=True or regularization_strategy="leave-one-out". They show how a subject's kernel changes with the regularization, and are what the leave-one-out and the one-pass fill read.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default subject_id str or tuple

An id passed to search_subject.

required

Returns:

Type Description MappingProxyType

regularization (n_values,), each λ searched: the value itself, or the global scale of a banded one, as in regularization_search_. coef_ {spec: (n_values, n_channels, n_subfeatures, n_delays)}; entry i is the kernel fit_subject would store at the i-th λ, in the cohort's kernel_units. metric (n_values, n_channels), the cross-validated metric at each λ.

Raises:

Type Description KeyError

If the subject was not searched.

RuntimeError

If the cohort did not keep the subject's kernels.

docs.title: fit_subject
docs.text:
fit_subject(
    TRFDataset: TRFData,
    subject_id: str | tuple,
    **overrides: Any
) -> TRFGroup

Fit the group's spec on one subject and store the minimal result.

Builds a TRFModel with the group's spec, fits it the way the group was configured -- fit_method="gridsearch" (the paradigm's gridsearchCV, refitting at the selected λ) or fit_method="fit" (a direct fit at regularization) -- then extracts the fold-averaged kernels, the channel-wise metric, the fitted regularization and, if requested, the bootstrap distribution, and discards the model.

After share_regularization, the search is not repeated: the subject is fitted directly at shared_regularization_. With a shared regularization_strategy it must come first, and this raises until it has. A cohort that kept its kernels has every searched subject filled by then, and does not need this call at all.

Any group-level fit default can be overridden here, and so can any other keyword the selected paradigm's fit/gridsearchCV accepts::

group.fit_subject(data, "s1", metric_limit_percentage=0.05)
group.fit_subject(data, "s2", fit_method="fit", regularization=1e3)
group.fit_subject(data, "s3", per_fold_metric=True, as_evoked=True)

Keywords belonging to fit are routed through run_fit_kwargs when the regularization search runs, so both stages are reachable from one call and run_fit_kwargs itself is not accepted. A direct fit ignores the group's search-only defaults (see the class Notes).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default TRFDataset TRFData

The subject's container, already partitioned.

required subject_id str or tuple

The key this subject is stored and later looked up under.

required **overrides Any

Any group-level fit default (regularization_grid, metric, bootstrap, fit_method, regularization, ...), plus any other keyword the selected paradigm's fit / gridsearchCV accepts.

{}

Returns:

Type Description TRFGroup

self, so calls chain over a cohort.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If a keyword the chosen cv does not support is passed (the message lists what it does accept), or run_fit_kwargs is.

ValueError

If the subject has already been fitted, or feature_bases is unfitted or differs from the bases the cohort was fitted with.

RuntimeError

If the cohort shares its λ (regularization_strategy="mean-curve" or "median") and share_regularization has not run yet.

Warns:

Type Description UserWarning

Once per cohort, when regularization_strategy is unset and the subjects end up fitted at different λ values.

Examples using fit_subject

  • 1 · OPM sensor TRF
  • 2 · Natural speech TRF
  • 3 · OPM source TRF

docs.text:
summary() -> dict

Descriptive statistics of the cohort.

Computed by statistics.descriptive_summary over common_channels, so the per-channel entries line up with the cohort's shared montage rather than with one subject's.

Carries a "diagnostics" entry when every subject was fitted with diagnostics=True: the spread of each block's generalized VIF across subjects, and the subjects whose design has exactly aliased columns. That is the reading the per-subject numbers cannot give -- whose design is the odd one out.

docs.title: grand_average
docs.text:
grand_average() -> dict

Grand-average the per-subject kernels; cache and return the result.

Returns {spec: {"mean","std","sem","n"}} (see statistics.grand_average). Subjects are matched channel by channel by name over common_channels, so a cohort recorded with different montages averages the electrodes it shares instead of averaging position i with position i.

Examples using grand_average

docs.title: permutation_test
docs.text:
permutation_test(
    spec: str | tuple,
    threshold: float | dict | None = None,
    test_window: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any
) -> tuple[ndarray, ndarray]

Cluster permutation test that a feature's kernel differs from zero.

Assembles the per-subject kernel maps for spec -- (n_subjects, n_delays, n_channels) for a scalar feature, or (n_subjects, n_delays, n_subfeatures, n_channels) for a multi-column one (no averaging: the sub-features enter the clustering as their own lattice dimension) -- builds the full adjacency (delay/sub-feature lattices x channel adjacency), and calls statistics.cluster_1samp. Stores and returns (t_obs, pvals) in stats_, each shaped like the map's non-subject dimensions.

Subjects are aligned over common_channels, so a cohort recorded with different montages is tested on the electrodes it shares.

See permutation_test_contrast for the paired version, which asks whether two cohorts' kernels differ from each other rather than from zero.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default spec str or tuple

The feature whose kernel is tested.

required threshold (float, dict or None)

A float runs the cluster-mass flavour with that cluster-forming t; a dict or None runs TFCE. See statistics.t_threshold for picking the float -- the degrees of freedom are len(group) - 1 -- and statistics.cluster_1samp for what each flavour's p-values mean.

None test_window tuple of float or None

(tmin, tmax) in seconds restricting the test to part of the kernel's delay axis, both ends inclusive. Narrowing an a-priori window shrinks the multiple-comparison space and buys power, at the cost of saying nothing about the delays left out. The result keeps the full delay length either way: untested delays come back with pvals = 1.0 and t_obs = NaN, so the figures shade a windowed result without knowing one was run.

None **kwargs Any

Forwarded to statistics.cluster_1samp (n_permutations, tail, seed, n_jobs, progress).

{}

Examples:

>>> from trflearn.statistics import t_threshold
>>> t = t_threshold(0.01, df=len(group) - 1)
>>> t_obs, pvals = group.permutation_test("envelope", threshold=t)

permutation_test_contrast(
    other: TRFGroup,
    spec: str | tuple,
    threshold: float | dict | None = None,

    **kwargs: Any

Paired cluster permutation test between two cohorts.

The standard group-level TRF contrast: both cohorts hold the same subjects fitted under two conditions, and the question is whether the kernels differ from each other. Taking the per-subject difference turns that into a one-sample test against zero, which is what statistics.cluster_1samp performs -- so this is a paired test, and the subject pairing is the whole point.

The sign follows the subtraction: a positive t_obs means self exceeds other at that point.

required spec str or tuple

The feature whose kernel is contrasted. Must be present in both.

required threshold (float, dict or None)

The flavour, exactly as in permutation_test: a float is the cluster-forming t of a cluster-mass test, a dict or None runs TFCE.

None **kwargs Any

{}

Type Description ValueError

docs.title: compare_to
docs.text:
compare_to(other: TRFGroup) -> CohortComparison

Rank two cohorts by AIC and BIC, subject by subject.

The group-level version of selection.compare: both cohorts hold the same subjects fitted under two different model specs -- envelope alone against envelope + onsets, say -- and the question is which spec describes this group of people better. A held-out metric cannot answer it, since adding a feature block almost never makes the fit worse; the criteria price the complexity, so they can.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default other TRFGroup

The cohort to compare against. Must hold exactly the same subject ids as self; subjects are paired by id, never by position.

required

Returns:

Type Description CohortComparison

The per-subject deltas and both aggregations of them, which documents every field. The sign is self - other and lower is better, so a positive delta favours other.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

If either cohort has no fitted subject.

ValueError

If the cohorts do not hold the same subjects, if either was fitted without criteria=True, or if any subject's two fits do not describe the same response -- different n, channel count or target_ss. A criterion difference across different data is not interpretable, and nothing in the arithmetic would notice.

Notes

Both cohorts must have been fitted with criteria=True, and that is a decision made before the loop: the cohort discards each subject's model after fitting, so the criteria cannot be assembled afterwards without refitting.

The Wilcoxon is the honest test here, and for a reason worth stating: the per-subject criteria are overconfident, because both assume independent samples and EEG residuals are autocorrelated. That inflation is within a subject. Asking whether N independent subjects fell on the same side does not inherit it -- each subject contributes one observation, however overconfident their own number was.

See docs/group-analysis.md for how to read the two aggregations against each other.

Examples:

>>> lean = TRFGroup(["envelope"], (-0.1, 0.4), criteria=True)
>>> rich = TRFGroup(["envelope", "onsets"], (-0.1, 0.4), criteria=True)
>>> ...  # fit the same subjects into both
>>> table = lean.compare_to(rich)
>>> table.best["bic"], table.n_favouring_self["bic"]
('self', 12)
>>> print(table.summary())

docs.title: permutation_test_contrast_features
docs.text:
permutation_test_contrast_features(
    spec_a: str | tuple,
    spec_b: str | tuple,
    threshold: float | dict | None = None,
    test_window: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any
) -> tuple[ndarray, ndarray]

Paired cluster permutation test of two features of the same model.

The within-model counterpart of permutation_test_contrast. Where that one compares the same feature across two cohorts, this compares two features that were fitted jointly, in one design and one solve, for every subject.

That joint fit is what makes the comparison clean, and it is the reason to prefer this over two separate models when the question allows it:

  • the two kernels are estimated controlling for each other, so shared variance between correlated regressors is split rather than handed whole to whichever regressor happens to be in the model;
  • they come from the same regularization, the same normalization, the same folds and the same sample count, so their difference carries no trace of a difference in regularization.

The canonical use is a pair of condition-coded versions of one regressor -- attended vs unattended stream, left vs right, target vs distractor -- entered as two features of a single model.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default spec_a str or tuple

The two features to contrast, both present in the fitted model. The sign follows the subtraction: positive t_obs means spec_a exceeds spec_b.

required spec_b str or tuple

The two features to contrast, both present in the fitted model. The sign follows the subtraction: positive t_obs means spec_a exceeds spec_b.

required threshold (float, dict or None)

The flavour, exactly as in permutation_test.

None test_window tuple of float or None

Restricts the tested delays exactly as in permutation_test. Both features are required to share a delay window here, so one range means the same thing on each.

None **kwargs Any

Forwarded to statistics.cluster_1samp.

{}

Returns:

Type Description (t_obs, pvals) : tuple of ndarray

Shaped like the kernel map's non-subject dimensions. Also stored in contrast_stats_ under the key (spec_a, spec_b).

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If either feature is missing, if they are the same feature, or if their kernels differ in shape -- different delay windows or sub-feature counts make the difference undefined.

Notes

Commensurability is the caller's responsibility. Nothing here can check that subtracting the two kernels means something. Two envelopes are regression weights against the same kind of regressor in the same units, so their difference is interpretable; an envelope and a spectrogram are not, and the difference would be a number without a referent. Same window and same sub-feature count are enforced below because they are checkable; same kind of regressor is not.

CohortComparison(
    subject_ids: list,
    delta_aic: ndarray,
    delta_bic: ndarray,
    delta_aic_per_channel: ndarray,
    delta_bic_per_channel: ndarray,
    n_favouring_self: dict[str, int],
    median: dict[str, float],
    total: dict[str, float],
    wilcoxon: dict[str, tuple[float, float]],
    best: dict[str, str],
)

Two cohorts ranked by AIC and BIC, subject by subject.

What TRFGroup.compare_to returns. Every per-criterion field is a {"aic": ..., "bic": ...} mapping, so one lookup reads the same quantity for both criteria. Frozen, so the fields cannot be reassigned -- shallowly, since the dicts and arrays they hold stay mutable.

The sign is self - other and lower is better, so a positive delta favours other. That is the opposite of TRFGroup.permutation_test_contrast, where a positive t_obs favours self.

Attributes:

Name Type Description subject_ids list

The pairing order every vector below follows.

delta_aic, delta_bic (n_subjects,) np.ndarray

self - other per subject, summed over the shared channels.

delta_aic_per_channel, delta_bic_per_channel (n_channels,) np.ndarray

The mean over subjects. Descriptive, and meant for a topomap: there is deliberately no per-channel test, which would be one test per electrode.

n_favouring_self dict of str to int

How many subjects each criterion puts on self's side.

median, total dict of str to float

The two aggregations, both reported; see the Notes.

wilcoxon dict of str to tuple of float

(statistic, p) of the paired signed-rank test of the per-subject deltas against zero. p is nan below statistics.MIN_SIGNED_RANK_SUBJECTS subjects.

best dict of str to str

{"aic": "self" | "other", "bic": ...} by the median.

Notes

Each subject contributes one number -- their criterion summed over channels -- and what to do with the resulting (n_subjects,) vector is a modelling choice, so both answers are given rather than one chosen silently. median, n_favouring_self and wilcoxon read it as random effects, one observation per subject; total reads it as fixed effects, the cohort as one large model. When the two disagree, that is the finding: it is the signature of an atypical subject.

docs.title: How a cohort chooses one λ
docs.text: The arithmetic behind share_regularization, on plain arrays.

docs.title: group_regularization
docs.text:
group_regularization.py -- how a cohort chooses one λ.

Kernels compared across subjects need one λ for all of them: a noisier subject selects a larger λ and is shrunk more, so a λ per subject turns data quality into amplitude (One λ for a whole group in docs/recommendations.md). group.TRFGroup runs the loops over subjects and keeps their records; this module holds the arithmetic of the choice, on plain arrays -- no data, no model, no cohort -- so it can be read and tested on its own.

Three strategies

"mean-curve" (mean_curve, then select_index) Each subject's validation curve -- the metric of their own search at every λ, averaged over channels and aggregated over folds -- is averaged across subjects, each with the same weight, and the best point of that mean is chosen the way one subject's search chooses on its own curve. A noisy subject has a flat curve, so it moves the peak little although it weighs the same. "median" (median_index) The geometric median of the λ values the subjects chose on their own, snapped to the nearest λ searched. "leave-one-out" (leave_one_out_curve, then select_index) At every λ, the average kernel of the other subjects predicts each subject's recording, and the curve is that score averaged over channels and subjects. It asks the question the group-average kernel is for: how well a kernel estimated without a subject describes them. The inner benchmark found it closest to the best λ in hindsight for a strong predictor in heavy noise, where the mean curve over-regularizes.

The leave-one-out needs every subject's kernel at every λ and the sums of every subject's design, which a cohort keeps in memory while it searches. kept_nbytes says exactly how much that takes per subject, and check_budget refuses before any fit when the cohort would not fit.

Kernel layout

A cohort records kernels as {spec: (n_channels, n_subfeatures, n_delays)}. The arithmetic here wants one coefficient matrix (n_columns, n_channels) in the column order of the design -- block after block, delay-first within a block. stack_kernels and column_scales translate.

docs.title: Saving and loading
docs.text: save / load for fitted models and cohorts, and the limitations of a saved file.

docs.title: io
docs.text:
io.py — Saving and loading fitted models and cohorts.

Two verbs. A model or a cohort writes itself with save, and load brings it back, deciding what it is from the file's own manifest::

model.save("s01.pkl")
group.save("cohort.pkl")
lmm.save("mixed.pkl")

model = trflearn.load("s01.pkl")                  # predicts new stimulus
model = trflearn.load("s01.pkl", TRFDataset=data) # + refit and predict()
group = trflearn.load("cohort.pkl")               # a fully live cohort
lmm = trflearn.load("mixed.pkl")                  # fitted, and refittable
What is in the file

A model saves its fitted state, not its data. The live object holds the container, the targets and every block's raw stimulus, so pickling it would write the whole dataset to disk once per subject. What predict actually reads is kilobytes: the kernels, each block's predict-time normalizer statistics, the block metadata (spec, sub-feature count, delays) and the bases. That -- plus the metric, the diagnostics and the cross-validation figure's ingredients -- is what the file carries.

A cohort saves everything it has. TRFGroup already discards each model after fitting and keeps only compact arrays, so there is no fitted state to restore: a reloaded cohort does everything a live one does, including fitting more subjects. Its per-subject bootstrap distributions and cluster-test results travel with it: both are expensive to recompute, and the second is what shades the figures. (A model has no bootstrap to save -- fit(bootstrap=True) returns the distribution rather than storing it; the cohort is what keeps it.)

A mixed model saves its sums and its search. mixed.TRFMixedModel keeps every subject's sufficient statistics and nothing else of the recordings, so the file carries them whole, with the settings, the channel info and the variance-parameter search of the last fit (mixed.optimize.ParameterFit). Every other estimate is read off the likelihood at that optimum on load, without searching again, so a loaded model tests, plots, refits and takes more subjects like the one that was saved.

The format

A pickle of a plain dictionary -- nested dicts, strings, numbers and NumPy arrays, and nothing else. Pickling the live objects would embed this package's class paths, so any later rename would break every file already written; a payload with no class in it survives refactors, and load rebuilds the object from it. The file is called .pkl because that is what it is: no private extension is invented, and dispatch reads the manifest rather than the suffix, which stops being true as soon as someone renames the file.

format_version is written into every file, and anything but the current version is refused outright rather than half-read.

Within a version, keys are added but never removed or repurposed. The version is bumped only for a change that would make an old file unreadable -- version 2 renamed a block descriptor's key -- because a bump orphans every file already on disk, while a new key orphans nothing: a reader that does not find it has lost only what did not exist when the file was written. A payload of the current version is therefore a lower bound on what it holds, and every key added since the last bump is read with .get and treated as "never computed" when absent. Removing or repurposing a key is what the version number is for.

Keys outlive renames. A key keeps the name it was first written under even when what it stores is renamed in the code: _STORED_AS maps the two, and save and load translate through it. The regularization was called alpha when the format was set, so the files still say alpha and every file written before the rename keeps loading.

Limitations

Worth knowing before relying on a saved file:

  • A pickle executes code when it is read. Only load files whose origin you trust. This is a property of the format, not of this package.
  • A loaded model has no data. predict(X_new), every plot including validation_plot(), to_evoked and all the reported numbers work. Calling fit, gridsearchCV or predict() with no arguments raises and tells you to reload with TRFDataset=, which re-materializes the container and gives you a fully live model again.
  • A loaded cohort has no limitations. It aggregates, tests, plots and keeps fitting subjects.
  • Diagnostics travel as a frozen report. condition_number_, effective_rank_, vif_, vif_columns_, vif_aliased_ and the information criteria (aic_, bic_, edf_ and the rest of TorchTRF.information_criteria) are saved as they stood, and a loaded model reports those numbers without recomputing anything. Whatever had not been computed at save time -- they are on demand, see TorchTRF.diagnostics -- is saved as None and reads back as None, on a live model too. Reload with TRFDataset= and call diagnostics(recompute=True) to get them.
  • with_bases=True files are tied to library versions. Bases are sklearn transformers, the one part of the state that is not an array. By default they are not embedded: the payload records what each block had, and load asks for them, so the file stays pure data. Embedding them is one flag away and couples the file to the sklearn and Python versions that wrote it.
  • The MNE info is rebuilt, not preserved. Channel names, types, sampling rate and sensor positions are stored and reassembled on load -- enough for topomaps, to_evoked and the cluster test's adjacency; the rest of the Info is dropped. Storing the object itself would put an MNE class in the payload and make mne -- an optional dependency here -- mandatory to open the file. If mne is missing at load time the file still opens, with a warning, and everything except montage-dependent plotting works.

docs.text: The evaluation metrics and the registry that owns them: Pearson, R² and RMSE.

docs.title: metrics
docs.text:
metrics.py — Evaluation metrics for TRF models.

Every metric the package can report lives here, registered by name in the :data:METRICS registry with the register decorator. Adding a metric is writing its functions and decorating them; nothing in models.py needs editing. Pearson, R² and RMSE ship with the package.

Two functions per metric

A metric is evaluated on two very different inputs, and the registry names both so the two paths cannot drift apart.

fn(y_pred, y_true, sample_dim) is the direct computation. It reduces sample_dim and broadcasts the remaining dimensions right to left, so the gridsearch can score a whole regularization grid at once -- (n_values, n_samples, n_channels) against (n_samples, n_channels).

from_sums(n, sum_x, sum_y, sum_x2, sum_y2, sum_xy) recovers the same value from sufficient statistics, which is what makes the block bootstrap affordable: bootstrap precomputes those five sums per block once and every resample is a sum over blocks, so the data is read once however many resamples are drawn. Arguments arrive as (batch, n_channels) tensors with n already broadcast to (batch, 1) and clamped to at least 1, so the body is plain elementwise algebra.

from_sums is optional. Not every metric has a closed form in those five sums -- Spearman needs the ranks of the full resample, spectral metrics need the signal -- and leaving it None is what lets the bootstrap refuse a metric up front instead of silently reporting something else.

bootstrap is that routine, and it lives here rather than on the model because nothing in it is about TRFs: it cuts two lists of held-out tensors into blocks, reduces each block once, and resamples the blocks. All it needs from a caller is where to put the tensors. The model keeps the one rule that is its own -- a block may not be coarser than a cross-validation fold -- and calls in here.

Conventions

The degenerate case belongs to the metric. A channel with no variance is undefined for Pearson and for R², both reporting 0 here, and perfectly well posed for RMSE -- which must not inherit that convention, since 0 is an error's best possible score and a flat channel would read as a perfect fit.

higher_is_better is consumed only where the package chooses something -- the λ of _select_regularization, the fold of _aggregate_folds('max') -- through as_score. Everything stored, returned or plotted stays in native units: RMSE is always displayed as RMSE.

Two things worth knowing before reporting these

R² is not Pearson squared. On held-out data Pearson is invariant to any affine rescaling of the prediction and R² is not, so ridge shrinkage leaves r untouched while costing R² directly: R² sits below r² systematically, responds to regularization in a way r does not, and can select a different λ. Held-out R² can also be negative, so plots.plot_metric_topomap -- which defaults to a sequential colormap -- needs a diverging cmap for it.

RMSE is in standardized target units, not microvolts: it is computed inside fit on the normalized targets, and the inverse transform only happens in predict. Under the default target_preprocess="Standardize" that keeps it comparable across channels and subjects, but it also makes it a near-monotone transform of R² (RMSE ~ sigma * sqrt(1 - R2)), so the two select nearly the same λ. RMSE earns its place when target_preprocess=None.

What scoring design @ coef takes from a design and its target.

from_sums reads five sums of a prediction x and a target y. When x = X b, the three involving x are, channel by channel, s'b, b'Gb and b'h, with G = X'X, h = X'y and s the column sums of X. These sums, read once, score any number of coefficient matrices without forming a prediction.

The five sums from_sums reads, for several predictions at once.

Every field but n is (n_coefs, n_channels): one row per coefficient matrix the prediction x = X b was formed with. Sums over disjoint rows add, so the folds of a cross-validation can be reduced one at a time and scored once, as if their predictions had been concatenated.

docs.title: pearson
docs.text:
pearson(
    y_pred: Tensor, y_true: Tensor, sample_dim: int = -2
) -> Tensor

Channel-wise Pearson correlation between prediction and target.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default y_pred Tensor

Prediction, broadcastable against y_true.

required y_true Tensor

Target.

required sample_dim int

Dimension reduced over, the samples axis.

-2

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

Correlation with sample_dim removed; 0 where either side is flat.

Notes

Pearson is a ratio, so the divisor of the second moments cancels -- but only if it is the same on both sides. Writing the covariance over a and the deviations over b yields (b/a) * r. Here both are n (.mean() for the covariance, unbiased=False for the deviations), so the result matches np.corrcoef and scipy.stats.pearsonr exactly -- which is the point, since a TRF correlation is meant to be comparable with values from mTRF, MATLAB or R.

Do not switch one side to unbiased=True: Bessel's correction unbiases a variance, not a correlation, and does nothing for the real downward bias of r towards rho. Applied to one side only it silently scales every reported metric by (n-1)/n.

Notes

SS_tot uses the mean of y_true over the samples being scored, so on held-out data this is the usual out-of-sample R² and can be negative: a model that predicts worse than the test set's own mean scores below 0. That is informative rather than a failure, and it is the difference from Pearson, which cannot see a mis-scaled prediction at all.
