    y_pred_folds: list[Tensor],
    y_test_folds: list[Tensor],
    n_blocks: int,
    *,
    device: device,
    dtype: dtype
) -> dict[str, Tensor]

Reduce held-out folds to per-block sufficient statistics.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default y_pred_folds list of torch.Tensor

Per-fold predictions, each (n_samples_fold, n_channels).

required y_test_folds list of torch.Tensor

Per-fold targets, matching those shapes.

required n_blocks int

Contiguous blocks to cut the concatenated folds into.

required device device

Where the reduced statistics are accumulated.

required dtype dtype

Precision the sums are taken in.

required

Returns:

Type Description dict of str to torch.Tensor

n_per_block of shape (n_blocks,) and sum_x, sum_y, sum_x2, sum_y2, sum_xy, each (n_blocks, n_channels). x is the prediction, y the target.

Notes

The folds are concatenated and cut into n_blocks contiguous blocks -- the last one absorbing the remainder, so no sample is discarded -- and each block is reduced to five sums plus its length. This is what makes the bootstrap affordable at all: the data is read once, here, and every resample afterwards is a sum over blocks, so the cost stops depending on how many resamples are asked for.

docs.title: sample_block_indices
docs.text:
sample_block_indices(
    n_blocks: int,
    n_resamples: int,
    random_state: int | None,
) -> ndarray

Draw block indices with replacement, one row per resample.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_blocks int

How many blocks exist, and how many each resample draws.

required n_resamples int

How many resamples to draw.

required random_state int or None

Seed.

required

Returns:

Type Description np.ndarray of shape (n_resamples, n_blocks)

Block indices, with repetition.

Notes

This is the resampling scheme itself, kept on its own so it can be checked without running a fit. Each of the n_blocks positions in a resample is drawn uniformly and independently, so the block multiplicities of a resample are Multinomial(n_blocks, 1/n_blocks). That is what makes the resulting sample equally weighted, and therefore its percentiles bootstrap percentiles -- see bootstrap for why enumerating the distinct resamples instead does not.

Drawing through NumPy rather than a torch generator keeps the same random_state producing the same indices on CPU and on GPU.

docs.title: bootstrap
docs.text:
bootstrap(
    y_pred_folds: list[Tensor],
    y_test_folds: list[Tensor],
    metric: str = "Pearson",
    n_blocks: int = 8,
    n_resamples: int = 10000,
    random_state: int | None = 42,
    *,
    device: device,
    dtype: dtype,
    verbose: int | None = None
) -> tuple[int, Tensor]

Estimate a channel-wise bootstrap distribution by resampling blocks.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default y_pred_folds list of torch.Tensor

Per-fold predictions, each (n_samples_fold, n_channels).

required y_test_folds list of torch.Tensor

Per-fold targets, matching those shapes.

required metric str

Any name, label or alias in the registry. It must declare a from_sums form: this routine never revisits the data, it sums per-block sufficient statistics, and a metric without a closed form in those sums (Spearman, anything spectral) is rejected up front rather than approximated.

'Pearson' n_blocks int

Contiguous segments to split the data into before resampling. A caller holding a cross-validation split should keep this at or above its fold count, so that a block is never coarser than a fold.

8 n_resamples int

How many resamples to draw. A few thousand already resolve a 95% percentile interval; raise it for narrower quantiles.

10000 random_state int or None

Seed for the resampling. Fixed by default, so two runs of the same model report the same interval; pass a different value to see how much the interval owes to the resampling itself.

42 device device

Where the statistics and the resamples are computed.

required dtype dtype

Precision the sums are taken in.

required verbose int or None

A resolved verbosity level overriding the global one. The progress bar over the resamples is shown at DEBUG only. See trflearn.verbosity.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description n_resamples int

Echoed back, so a caller can record what the interval rests on.

distribution Tensor

(n_resamples, n_channels), on the CPU.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If n_blocks or n_resamples is not positive.

NotImplementedError

If metric declares no from_sums form.

Notes

The held-out predictions and targets are cut into n_blocks contiguous blocks, and n_resamples resamples are drawn -- each one n_blocks blocks sampled independently with replacement. Every resample is evaluated from precomputed per-block sufficient statistics, so the data is read once and the cost is linear in n_resamples, independent of how many folds produced it.

This replaced an exhaustive enumeration of every combination-with-replacement of the blocks, and the change is not only about cost: the intervals it reports are narrower. Enumerating each distinct resample once weights them uniformly, while the bootstrap weights each by how many ordered draws produce it. The two measures differ most in the tails, which is where the percentiles are -- the degenerate resamples (every draw landing on the same block) are a large share of the uniform measure and a negligible share of the bootstrap one. The old intervals were therefore conservative rather than wrong in direction, but they were not bootstrap intervals. Sampling draws from the right measure and returns an equally weighted sample, which is also what lets every consumer keep taking plain percentiles and medians of distribution.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: TRFModel(...) is the factory; it returns a PooledTRF, AveragedTRF or TrainTestTRF, all of which inherit the estimator API below. See the concept page for the narrative.

docs.title: TRFModel
docs.text:
TRFModel(
    TRFDataset: TRFData,
    features: list,
    *args: Any,
    cv: Literal["pooled"] = ...,
    **kwargs: Any
) -> PooledTRF

    TRFDataset: TRFData,

    cv: Literal["averaged"],
    **kwargs: Any
) -> AveragedTRF

TRFModel(
    TRFDataset: TRFData,
    features: list,
    *args: Any,
    cv: Literal["train_test"],
    **kwargs: Any
) -> TrainTestTRF

TRFModel(
    TRFDataset: TRFData,
    features: list,
    *args,
    cv: str = "pooled",
    **kwargs
) -> PooledTRF | AveragedTRF | TrainTestTRF

Build a TRF model, choosing the cross-validation paradigm with cv.

A single entry point that dispatches to the paradigm class and returns its instance:

  • cv="pooled" -> PooledTRF (standard k-fold): for each test fold, one model is fit on the pooled complement and predicts the held-out set. The default; recommended for everyday use.
  • cv="averaged" -> AveragedTRF (Crosse-Lalor): one model is fit per partition and each fold is predicted by the leave-one-out average of the other partitions' models. Mildly optimistic -- the held-out fold is standardized with its own statistics (see AveragedTRF).
  • cv="train_test" -> TrainTestTRF: a single contiguous train/test split; the λ that scores best on the test fold is kept, and train_size sets the split. The simplest option, but optimistic -- λ is selected on the reported set (see TrainTestTRF).

Forwarded unchanged to the paradigm's constructor -- every argument of models.TorchTRF, plus train_size for cv="train_test".

docs.title: The estimator API
docs.text: Every paradigm shares these methods, defined on the base estimator TorchTRF (fit, gridsearchCV, predict, to_evoked, …). The design report (diagnostics, information_criteria, vif_, aic_, …) is documented under Diagnostics, and the plotting methods under Plotting.

docs.title: TorchTRF
docs.text:
TorchTRF(
    TRFDataset: TRFData,
    features: list,
    default_window: tuple,
    feature_windows: dict | None = None,
    feature_bases: dict | None = None,
    feature_groups: dict | None = None,
    feature_preprocess: str | None = "Standardize",
    target_preprocess: str | None = "Standardize",
    solver: str = "ridge",
    delay_margin: float = 0.0,
    drop_zero_rows: bool = False,
    drop_warn_fraction: float = 0.25,
    verbose: int | str | bool | None = None,
)

Base TRF estimator: delayed linear models with regularization.

Fits at a fixed λ (fit), or selects one over a grid and refits (gridsearchCV); either can also return a block-bootstrap distribution of the channel-wise metric. predict and to_evoked read the result, and save writes it.

The design report (diagnostics, information_criteria, vif_, aic_, …) comes from diagnostics.ModelDiagnosticsMixin and the figures from plots.ModelPlots.

Initialize a delayed ridge-style TRF estimator over named features.

The design is assembled block-by-block (feature-first): each selected feature (a base key or an interaction tuple) contributes its own lagged sub-design with its own delay window, concatenated horizontally. The penalty is block-diagonal (one penalty per feature over its own delays); for a single feature with the global window this is identical to the classic single-block design.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default TRFDataset TRFData

The (already partitioned) data container. Provides y, folds, relevant_indexes, the global delays window, device/precision, and lazy get_feature(name) access.

required features list

Selected features: each entry is a base key (str) or a tuple of keys (("k1","k2")) for an interaction (outer product of the raw features). An interaction expands to the product of its constituents' column counts.

required default_window tuple of float

(tmin, tmax) in seconds, the delay window every feature uses unless feature_windows overrides it.

required feature_windows dict

{spec: (tmin, tmax)} in seconds overriding the window of a feature/interaction. Defaults: a base feature without an entry uses the global window; an interaction without an entry uses the union of its constituents' specified windows (or the global window if none were specified). Windows are independent: a feature may extend beyond default_window. The container's crop window is the union of default_window and every entry here, so every resolved window is covered by construction. Keys must be among the selected features (a key that is not raises KeyError).

None feature_bases dict

{spec: transformer} attaching a basis expansion to a feature's amplitude, keyed like feature_windows. transformer is any scikit-learn-style object with fit/transform: the raw columns (n_samples, n_subfeatures) are mapped to (n_samples, n_subfeatures * k) before lagging, so a scalar feature becomes k smooth basis channels. Fitted once on the relevant stimulus (knots never see the target) and reused across folds and in predict.

For splines, prefer trflearn.bases.spline_basis over a bare SplineTransformer: it drops one column per input feature, without which the block is exactly singular under feature_preprocess and regularization ends up holding it together rather than only regularizing it. Any other transformer is accepted, pipelines included. See Features, interactions & windows in the docs for the full argument and for composing a basis with an elementwise transform.

An event feature -- zero wherever no event occurred, like a saccade's amplitude -- takes spline_basis(scope="event"), or trflearn.bases.event_scoped around any other transformer: the basis is fitted on the events and the empty rows stay zero. Expanded per sample instead, every empty row reads as an event of amplitude 0 and the quantile knots collapse onto those zeros.

None feature_groups dict

{band: [spec, ...]} grouping the selected features into bands, each of which gets its own regularization -- a banded ridge. The canonical use is two bands, an acoustic one and a linguistic one, so that a 16-column spectrogram and a 1-column surprisal are not forced to share a regularization strength their very different column counts and signal-to-noise ratios do not justify.

One rule covers every case: a spec that is not listed in any band is its own band. So None (the default) makes every feature a band, and a partial mapping needs no filler entries for the features left out. Band order is the declaration order of feature_groups first, then the unlisted specs in features order -- deterministic, so it can be serialized and reported against.

That the default is one band per feature rather than one band overall costs nothing: a scalar regularization broadcasts to every band, so a model built and fitted without ever mentioning bands is the same model, to the bit, that it was before bands existed. Bands are the resolution available, not a resolution imposed.

Keys of the lists are specs, written exactly as in features (a string, or a tuple/list for an interaction). A spec listed twice, or a spec that is not among the selected features, is an error.

See trflearn.search for how the per-band grid is then swept, and gridsearchCV for what regularization_grid accepts once bands exist.

None feature_preprocess str or None

'Standardize', 'Normalize', or None for no normalization. Applied per feature block and to the targets respectively. target_preprocess='Normalize' is deprecated and will be removed: with no intercept, a target that is not centred cannot be fitted.

'Standardize' target_preprocess str or None

'Standardize', 'Normalize', or None for no normalization. Applied per feature block and to the targets respectively. target_preprocess='Normalize' is deprecated and will be removed: with no intercept, a target that is not centred cannot be fitted.

'Standardize' solver str

'ridge', 'ridge-laplacian' or 'cross_corr' (see solvers). 'ridge-laplacian' smooths without shrinking: do not use it for a predictor that carries little signal.

'ridge' delay_margin float

Margin in seconds added on each side of every feature's window to absorb ridge edge-ringing (converted to lags via the sample rate). Trimmed off the kernel before predicting. Sizes the container's inter-segment buffer at materialization.

0.0 drop_zero_rows bool

Exclude from the coefficient estimation the samples at which no feature block has any predictor -- the entirely-zero design rows that sparse features (word onsets, fixations, blinks) produce when no continuous feature accompanies them. Off by default, matching mTRF-Toolbox and Eelbrain, which fit on every sample. Prediction and scoring are unaffected either way; score_on in fit is what restricts the scored samples.

It does not change the family of fitted models, only what regularization means: with k the surviving fraction, coef(λ, drop=True) == coef(k * λ, drop=False). A grid tuned with one setting does not carry over to the other. See Features, interactions & windows in the docs for why the mask is read before standardization and before any basis.

False drop_warn_fraction float

docs.text:
fit(
    regularization: float | dict | ndarray,
    metric: str = "Pearson",
    per_fold_metric: bool = False,
    bootstrap: bool = False,
    as_evoked: bool = False,
    n_resamples: int = 10000,
    random_state: int | None = 42,
    score_on: ScoreOn = None,
) -> tuple[dict, Tensor] | tuple[dict, Tensor, dict]

Fit one TRF per fold at a fixed λ, and score the held-out folds.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default regularization (float, dict or ndarray)

The regularization strength. A scalar applies to every band, a {band: value} mapping or a vector in band order sets them individually.

required metric str

Any name, label or alias in the metrics registry.

'Pearson' per_fold_metric bool

Score each fold separately instead of scoring the concatenated predictions once. Cannot be combined with bootstrap.

False bootstrap bool

Also return a block-bootstrap distribution of the metric.

False as_evoked bool

Also export the fitted kernels to MNE Evoked in coef_as_evoked_. The return value is unchanged.

False n_resamples int

Resamples to draw. Only consulted when bootstrap=True.

10000 random_state int or None

Seed for the resampling, fixed by default so two runs of the same model report the same interval. Only consulted when bootstrap=True.

42 score_on (str, list, dict, ndarray, callable or None)

Which held-out samples the metric is computed on. None (the default) scores every one: how much of the recording the model explains. The other forms keep the samples where a sparse feature can predict something, which is what an event-locked question asks:

"informative" where any block has an event within its delay window. [spec, ...] where one of the named blocks has an event within its delay window. The form to use when a continuous feature beside them makes every sample informative. {spec: (tmin, tmax)} from tmin to tmax seconds after each event of spec, a window of its own inside the model's delay range. spec may be a container feature the model does not fit, so that two models can be scored on the same samples. boolean array one entry per real sample of the container, as for relevant_indexes. callable called with the held-out samples' real sample numbers, and returning one boolean per number.

An event is a sample where the raw feature, before any basis, is non-zero. Only the scoring changes: the estimation and predict do not, and drop_zero_rows stays independent. The bootstrap and per_fold_metric see the same samples. scored_on_ records the selection and the fraction of held-out samples it kept, and metric_name_ is marked, e.g. "Pearson (onsets)": such a metric is not comparable to one over every sample.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description trfs dict

{spec: (n_folds, n_channels, n_subfeatures, n_delays)}, one kernel per selected feature.

metric Tensor

(n_folds, n_channels) with per_fold_metric=True, otherwise (n_channels,) over the concatenated predictions.

distribution dict

Only with bootstrap=True, and appended third: {"n_samples", "distribution", "random_state"}.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If per_fold_metric and bootstrap are both set, or score_on is malformed or keeps fewer than two samples of a fold.

KeyError

If score_on names a feature the model does not fit (list) or the container does not hold (dict).

TypeError

If score_on is none of the forms above.

RuntimeError

If the model was loaded without its data.

Notes

coef_ (the fold-averaged kernels) is populated afterwards. The numerical diagnostics are not: they are computed on demand by diagnostics.

docs.text:
gridsearchCV(
    regularization_grid: (
        list | ndarray | dict | None
    ) = None,
    inner_train_cutoff: float = 0.8,
    metric: str = "r2",
    metric_aggregation_function: str | int = "mean",
    metric_limit_percentage: float | None = None,
    validation_plot: bool = True,
    plot_path: str | PathLike = "validation_plot.png",
    run_fit: bool = True,
    run_fit_kwargs: dict | None = None,
    score_on: ScoreOn = None,
) -> tuple

Select one λ by aggregating inner-validation metrics across folds.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default regularization_grid (list, ndarray, dict, BandSearch or None)

The λ values to try. search.as_search decides between:

None (the default) search.DEFAULT_REGULARIZATION_GRID, np.logspace(-3, 3, 13). 1-D sequence the ordinary regularization grid. This is always its meaning, even for a model whose band count happens to equal the grid length; per-band values go one of the other two ways. {band: grid} a Cartesian product per band (search.band_grid). search.BandSearch a prepared space, e.g. from search.random_bands, which is what to reach for past two or three bands.

None inner_train_cutoff float

Fraction of each training partition that estimates; the rest scores the λ values.

0.8 metric str

Any name, label or alias in the metrics registry. It chooses λ and, with run_fit=True, is the metric the refit reports. The default, 'r2', suits kernels that are interpreted: R² charges for shrinkage, which Pearson's correlation cannot see. Pass 'Pearson' when prediction accuracy is the result.

'r2' metric_aggregation_function str or int

How to collapse the per-fold metrics: 'mean', 'median', 'max' or a fold index. See _aggregate_folds for what each does and for the caveat on 'max'. 'mean' is the package-wide default, shared by every paradigm so that the λ each one selects -- and therefore the metric each one reports -- is arrived at the same way and stays comparable across them. It is less robust than 'median' to a single bad fold.

'mean' metric_limit_percentage float or None

Prefer the largest λ whose metric is within this fraction of the best. See _select_regularization. It shrinks the kernels without improving their shape: a Pearson curve is nearly flat over decades of λ, so even 0.01 can buy a much larger λ and 0.05 can shrink the kernels to almost nothing. Leave it None when the kernels themselves are the result.

None validation_plot bool

Save the validation figure. The figure's ingredients are recorded either way, so validation_plot() can render it on demand.

True plot_path str or PathLike

Where to save it; parent directories are created.

'validation_plot.png' run_fit bool

Refit at the selected λ, populating coef_.

True run_fit_kwargs dict or None

Forwarded to fit on that refit.

None score_on (str, list, dict, ndarray, callable or None)

Which held-out samples are scored, as in fit. It applies to the samples that select λ as well as to the refit, so λ is tuned for the same question the reported metric answers.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description best_regularization float or dict

A float for a plain grid, a {band: value} mapping once the bands were actually varied -- so a caller that never asked for bands never has to unpack one.

result tuple or float

fit's output with run_fit=True, otherwise the selected λ's aggregated metric.

Raises:

Type Description (ValueError, KeyError, TypeError)

As in fit for a malformed score_on; a ValueError too if run_fit_kwargs also sets it.

RuntimeError

If the model was loaded without its data.

predict(X_new: dict | None = None) -> Tensor

Predict the neural response from a stimulus using the fitted kernels.

Sums each feature block's contribution: the (base or interaction) raw feature is standardized with the block's predict-time normalizer, lagged over its own delays, multiplied by coef_[spec], and accumulated; the total is mapped back to target units with the target normalizer.

docs.text:
to_evoked(info: Info | None = None) -> dict

Return the fitted kernels as MNE Evoked objects.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default info Info

Channel info (with montage) to attach. Defaults to the info captured from the input Raw (TRFData.info). Pass one explicitly when the dataset was built from plain arrays, or to override the montage. Its channel count must match coef_ and its sfreq the model's sample_rate.

None

Returns:

Type Description dict

{spec: Evoked} for a single-column feature, and {spec: list of Evoked} for a wider one -- see below.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

If the model has not been fitted.

ValueError

If there is no channel info to attach.

Warns:

Type Description UserWarning

When a feature has more than one sub-feature, since a list comes back where a single object might be expected.

Notes

Each kernel is (n_channels, n_subfeatures, n_delays) and an Evoked is strictly channels x time, so the response channels become the Evoked channels (inheriting the montage) and the feature's delays become the time axis (delays / sample_rate seconds, possibly negative). The sub-feature axis has nowhere to go in a single Evoked, so a feature with more than one column comes back as a list of them, one per column, tagged in comment.

Simple single train/test split TRF (the cv="train_test" paradigm).

One contiguous split: the model is fit on the train fold across the whole regularization grid and each λ is scored by its metric on the test fold; the λ that scores best there is kept. No inner validation, no fold aggregation -- the simplest possible workflow. Built via TRFModel(..., cv="train_test").

Caveat. λ is selected on the same set whose metric is reported, so the reported metric is optimistic: the max over the grid, not an unbiased generalization estimate. Recommended only for a quick look; use cv="pooled" or cv="averaged" when the metric must be trustworthy.

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text: The shared plotting API. See the Plotting guide for usage.

docs.title: TRFPlots
docs.text:
Every figure its owners share, plus the table of which one works where and the contract for adding a new one.

The five mne.Evoked passthroughs carry MNE's own parameter list under Other Parameters, read from the installed MNE rather than copied — which is why this block is rendered by inspection.

docs.title: TRFPlots
docs.text: Every shared figure, and the contract its owners implement.

docs.title: What you can draw, and where
docs.text:
Six owners inherit this: a fitted model (models.TorchTRF), a cohort (group.TRFGroup), one stored subject reached as group("s01"), a cohort mixed model (mixed.TRFMixedModel, drawing its population kernel), a view of that mixed model -- lmm("s01") for a subject's own kernels, lmm.variability for the between-subject SD -- and the kernels a simulation injected (simulation.GroundTruth). Most figures work on all of them; the exceptions are worth knowing before reaching for one.

Figure Model Cohort Subject Mixed Mixed view Truth Needs plot, plot_image, plot_psd ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ — plot_joint, plot_psd_topomap ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ montage plot_average ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ — plot_contrast ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ montage if kind="joint" plot_features, plot_feature ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ montage plot_metric_topomap ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ montage plot_source_butterfly, to_stc ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ centroids plot_bootstrap ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ — validation_plot ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ — plot_subjects ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗ — plot_variance_components ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗ montage plot_fit_diagnostics ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗ montage

"Needs a montage" means sensor positions, which arrive with an mne.Raw target or through core.TRFData.set_montage. Those figures draw topomaps, and without positions they raise saying so. The others need no channel info at all: on an owner fitted on arrays the channels are drawn as Target 0, Target 1 and so on. Source-space targets carry centroids instead, via core.TRFData.set_source_positions; they place the source figures, and no topomap.

The green/red significance shading is cohort only. It comes from a statistic over subjects -- a cluster permutation test on a group, a Wald test on a mixed model -- and it is drawn by plot, plot_joint, plot_image, plot_average, plot_contrast, plot_features and plot_source_butterfly once that test has run. On every other owner show_stats=True is accepted and quietly does nothing -- the figure is the same as with show_stats=False. MixedPlots says what its shading means.

Every ✗ is a plain AttributeError: plot_bootstrap needs per-subject distributions, validation_plot a grid search, plot_metric_topomap a held-out metric, and plot_subjects, plot_variance_components and plot_fit_diagnostics a fitted mixed model, so none exists on an owner that cannot have one -- a ground truth was never scored, so it has no metric either.

Every figure returns its figure and accepts save_path (written, creating parent directories) and show; see _finalize_figure for what survives the close. Two settings, read by every figure of an object rather than passed per call: plot_baseline and plot_sphere, both below.

docs.title: Adding a figure
docs.text:
Write it against the hooks, never against the owner's own attributes -- that is what keeps one method working for every owner. Take spec first, read the kernel through _baselined_kernel (not _plot_kernel, so the display baseline applies), end with _finalize_figure, and return what it returns. If the figure only makes sense for one owner, define it on that owner's subclass instead of here.

Display-only baseline; see the class body for the accepted forms.

Fixed head sphere for every topomap.

plot_average(
    spec: str | tuple,
    show_stats: bool = True,
    channel_reduce: str = "mean",
    x_units: str = "ms",
    title: str | None = None,
    sub_labels: list | None = None,
    alpha_level: float = 0.05,
    min_sig_channels: int | float = 1,
    color: str = "C0",
    style: str = "mne",
    save_path: str | PathLike | None = None,
    show: bool = False,
) -> Figure

Butterfly and channel summary -- the figure that always works.

A single axis for a scalar feature; for a multi-column one, two axes sharing the time axis: the kernel averaged over its sub-features on top, and a sub-features x time heatmap of the channel-collapsed coefficient below, with the non-significant cells attenuated.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default spec str or tuple

The feature to draw; a tuple names an interaction.

required show_stats bool

Shade the significant delay intervals green (positive) or red (negative) on the top axis. Cohort only: a model and a single subject have no cluster result, so this is accepted and does nothing there.

True channel_reduce (mean, gfp)

How the bottom panel collapses its channel axis -- not its sub-feature axis, which is what the rows are, and not the top panel, which always shows the sub-feature average. "mean" is the signed average, which keeps the polarity and is drawn on a diverging scale centred at zero. "gfp" is the RMS: reach for it when the response is dipolar, positive over some sensors and negative over others, where the signed mean cancels a real effect toward zero. It is non-negative, so it is drawn on a sequential scale and it discards the sign. No effect on a scalar feature, which has no such panel.

"mean" x_units (ms, s)

Unit of the time axis.

"ms" title str or None

Overrides the default, which is the subject id and the feature when there is a subject, else the feature alone.

None sub_labels sequence or None

Tick labels for the heatmap's sub-feature rows; must have one entry per sub-feature.

None alpha_level float

Significance cutoff applied to the p-value map.

0.05 min_sig_channels int or float

Channels that must reach alpha_level for a delay to count. A float in (0, 1) is read as a fraction of them.

1 color str

Colour of the native butterfly's channel-mean line.

"C0" style (mne, native)

How the top axis is drawn; see the Notes.

"mne" save_path (str, PathLike or None)

Where to write the figure; parent directories are created.

None show bool

Display the figure instead of closing it in pyplot.

False

Returns:

Type Description Figure

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If style or channel_reduce is not one of its two values, or if sub_labels does not match the sub-feature count.

Notes

style="mne" draws the top axis with mne.Evoked.plot -- the same butterfly every other MNE figure uses, spatially coloured from the montage, with the GFP trace. What it plots is unchanged; only the rendering differs. It needs a montage, so without one it falls back to the native drawing: thin per-channel traces, a bold channel mean and a one-standard-deviation band. That fallback is why this figure is the one that always works. style="native" opts out and draws it that way regardless.

The shading and the heatmap are drawn here in both styles; only the butterfly ever comes from MNE. The vertical axis and the colorbar are labelled in coefficient units, which under the default standardization are σ_target/σ_feature.

docs.title: plot_contrast
docs.text:
plot_contrast(
    spec_a: str | tuple,
    spec_b: str | tuple,
    kind: str = "average",
    *,
    show_stats: bool = True,
    channel_reduce: str = "mean",
    x_units: str = "ms",
    title: str | None = None,
    sub_labels: list | None = None,
    alpha_level: float = 0.05,
    min_sig_channels: int | float = 1,
    color: str = "C0",
    style: str = "mne",
    save_path: str | PathLike | None = None,
    show: bool = False,
    **kwargs: Any
) -> Figure

Draw the difference between two features of one model.

kind="average" (the default) gives the figure plot_average produces: a butterfly for a scalar feature, and for a multi-column one the sub-feature-averaged butterfly over a sub-features x time heatmap. It needs no montage, so it is the one that always works.

kind="joint" gives the plot_joint figure instead -- MNE's butterfly with topographies at its peaks -- of the sub-feature-averaged difference. That is usually the figure a contrast is for: it answers "where and when do the two conditions diverge" in one panel. It needs a montage, and grid / mean / std / sem / ts_args / topomap_args may be passed through to it; channel_reduce and sub_labels do not apply to it.

This is the picture behind TRFGroup.permutation_test_contrast_features / TRFGroup.tfce_contrast_features, and its reason to exist: those return a p-value for spec_a - spec_b while the difference itself was not drawable, so the effect could be tested and never looked at. With show_stats (the default) a stored result for this exact pair shades the butterfly green (spec_a above spec_b) or red (below), the same convention the test reports its sign in. Nothing is shaded when the pair has not been tested -- always the case for a single TRFModel, where cluster tests do not apply.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default spec_a str or tuple

The two features, both in the fitted model. The sign follows the subtraction. They must share a delay window and a sub-feature count; whether the difference means anything is the caller's to judge (see _resolve_contrast).

required spec_b str or tuple

The two features, both in the fitted model. The sign follows the subtraction. They must share a delay window and a sub-feature count; whether the difference means anything is the caller's to judge (see _resolve_contrast).

required kind (average, joint)

Which figure to draw, as above.

"average"

Returns:

Type Description Figure

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the two are the same feature, if their kernels disagree in shape or delay window, or if kind is not one of the two.

RuntimeError

If kind="joint" and the channels have no sensor positions.

Notes

x_units, title, style, color, alpha_level, min_sig_channels, save_path and show mean exactly what they mean in plot_average.

Both kernels are partial coefficients from the same design and solve, so they share a λ, a normalization, the folds and the sample count, and each is estimated controlling for the other. Their difference therefore carries no trace of a difference in regularization -- which is exactly what subtracting two separately fitted models would give you. The canonical use is a pair of condition-coded versions of one regressor (attended vs unattended, target vs distractor) entered as two features.

plot_features(
    specs: list | None = None,
    *,
    show_stats: bool = True,
    alpha_level: float = 0.05,
    min_sig_channels: int | float = 1,
    channel_reduce: str = "mean",
    x_units: str = "ms",
    ylims: list | tuple | None = None,
    vlim_topo: tuple = (None, None),
    topo_times: dict | float | None = None,
    sub_labels: dict | list | None = None,
    title: str | None = None,
    figsize: tuple | None = None,
    save_path: str | PathLike | None = None,
    show: bool = False
) -> Figure

One column per feature: butterfly, masked image and peak topomap.

The summary figure of a fitted model or cohort. Each feature gets a column of three stacked rows sharing a delay axis:

  1. the butterfly of the kernel (averaged over sub-features), with the significant delay intervals shaded green/red;
  2. for a scalar feature, the channels x time image with the non-significant region greyed out; for a multi-column one, a sub-features x time heatmap of the channel-collapsed coefficient (channel_reduce; see plot_average for what the two reducers mean and why they are drawn on different colour scales). A black curve on a twin axis traces how many channels are significant at each delay;
  3. a topomap at the delay carrying the most significant channels (falling back to the GFP peak when nothing is significant), significant sensors marked, with its own colorbar.

Needs sensor positions, for the topomap of row 3; without them, use plot_average. Significance comes from _plot_stats, so the figure renders unshaded -- and rows 2/3 unmasked -- for a lone TRFModel or a SubjectPlots, where a cohort cluster test does not exist.

plot_bootstrap(
    subject_ids: list | None = None,
    kind: str = "violin",
    channel_reduce: str | int = "mean",
    ci: float | None = 95,
    sort: bool = False,
    title: str | None = None,
    save_path: str | PathLike | None = None,
    show: bool = False,
) -> Figure

Compare the per-subject bootstrap metric distributions side by side.

Each subject fitted with bootstrap=True carries a (n_resamples, n_channels) distribution of the held-out metric, built by resampling contiguous blocks with replacement. This figure puts one violin (or box) per subject on a shared axis, so the cohort is read as a whole: who is reliable, who is noisy, and how far apart they really are relative to their own spread.

Three things are drawn on top of the distributions, because a violin alone is easy to over-read:

  • the observed metric (the one the subject actually scored) as a marker. It is not the centre of its bootstrap distribution in general, and the gap is worth seeing;
  • the percentile interval at ci as a vertical line -- the number one would report, drawn where it can be compared across subjects;
  • the cohort mean of the observed metrics, as a horizontal reference.

Subjects to show, in this order. Default: every fitted subject, in fitting order.

How the channel axis is collapsed to one value per resample. An int selects a single channel. The observed metric is collapsed the same way, so marker and distribution stay commensurate.

Order subjects by the median of their distribution instead of by fitting order. Ignored when subject_ids is given explicitly.

As in the other figures.

As in the other figures.

As in the other figures.

evoked_to_stc(
    evoked: Evoked, labels: list, src: SourceSpaces
) -> SourceEstimate

Paint a region-wise Evoked onto the cortex as a SourceEstimate.

Parcellated results have one value per region, but MNE's brain rendering wants one per vertex. Every vertex of a label therefore takes its region's value, giving the flat, uniformly-coloured parcels that make a parcellation figure readable as such.

Rendering is deliberately left out: the returned stc takes the whole of mne.SourceEstimate.plot (hemispheres, views, colormaps, time viewer) without this package wrapping and re-exposing any of it, and no 3D backend is pulled in unless you call it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default evoked Evoked

Channels named after the labels -- e.g. models.TorchTRF.to_evoked output for source-space targets. Names carrying MNE's -0/-1 uniqueness suffixes also match, the first such channel winning.

required labels list of mne.Label

The parcellation, e.g. from mne.read_labels_from_annot. Labels with no matching channel are left at zero.

required src SourceSpaces

The surface source space (two hemispheres) defining the vertices to paint. Its vertno sets the stc's vertices.

required

Returns:

Type Description SourceEstimate

Examples:

>>> labels = mne.read_labels_from_annot(
...     "fsaverage", parc="aparc", subjects_dir=sd)
>>> stc = evoked_to_stc(
...     group.to_stc("envelope", labels, src), labels, src)
>>> brain = stc.plot(subject="fsaverage", subjects_dir=sd, hemi="split")

docs.title: Search
docs.text: Hyperparameter search spaces: the per-band regularization grids of a banded ridge, factored into a band ratio and a global scale so one eigendecomposition serves a whole scale sweep. Why that split is what makes a banded search affordable is below; Solvers covers the solve it feeds.

docs.title: search
docs.text:
search.py — Which regularization strengths to try.

models owns how a model is fitted and solvers owns the numeric solve; this module owns the third question: which hyperparameters get tried, and in what order. It knows nothing about designs, folds or targets -- everything here is arithmetic on small arrays of regularization strengths.

A BandSearch is that list of strengths, plus the band names its columns refer to. Nothing more: a search says what to try, and solvers decides how to solve it. An ordinary regularization grid is the case where every vector is uniform, and is built as exactly that rather than as a special shape.

Why a λ vector gets split in two

A banded ridge gives each group of features its own regularization strength, so the hyperparameter stops being a number and becomes an (n_bands,) vector. Searching over vectors is where the cost explodes: five values over four bands is 625 λ values, and the naive way to run them is 625 separate solves per fold.

Most of that work is avoidable, and seeing why is the point of this module. Write any positive λ vector as ::

λ = scale * ratio        ratio normalized to geometric mean 1

The ratio says which band is penalized harder than which -- the direction of the vector. The scale says how strongly the model is regularized overall -- its size. Normalizing the ratio makes the split unique: scale = geomean(λ).

The split earns its place because the two halves cost completely different things to change. Moving the scale is nearly free: with the ratio held fixed, every scale in a sweep comes out of one eigendecomposition of the design, reused. Moving the ratio is not: a new direction needs a new factorization. So what a search costs is governed by how many ratios it holds, not by how many λ values -- and two searches of the same size can differ by an order of magnitude.

That is what random_bands exploits and what band_grid cannot: a random search draws a handful of ratios and sweeps the whole scale grid at each, where a Cartesian product spends most of its ratios on corners carrying a single scale. band_grid has the arithmetic.

The factorization is derived, not stored. BandSearch keeps the λ vectors and computes the split on demand, for the two questions that need it: what single number puts a banded fit on the x axis of the validation figure, and which λ values belong to the same curve. solvers recovers its own grouping from the per-column weights it receives, and never reads this one.

Vocabulary

band A named group of design blocks sharing one λ, from the model's feature_groups. With no feature_groups every feature is its own band. ratio The direction of a λ vector: (n_bands,), positive, geometric mean 1. The banded-ridge literature writes it gamma. scale The size of a λ vector: one positive number, the geometric mean of its entries. It is what random_bands(scales=...) sweeps and what the search reports as best_scale; for an ordinary ridge it is λ itself. regularization One regularization strength to try, λ -- here always an (n_bands,) vector. n_values counts them; an ordinary scalar λ is the uniform case.

Axis names follow the package glossary in docs/concepts/notation.md.

docs.title: summary_scale
docs.text:
summary_scale(regularization: Strengths) -> float

One number standing for a per-band λ vector: its geometric mean.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default regularization sequence of float or np.ndarray

An (n_bands,) λ vector. Zeros are tolerated here, unlike in normalize_ratio.

required

Returns:

Type Description float

The scale. 0.0 for an empty input; the arithmetic mean when any band is unpenalized.

Notes

The same lambda the search is parametrized by, which is what makes it the right summary rather than merely a defensible one -- a scalar fit and a banded fit are then reported on the same axis.

Arithmetic would be wrong here, and not subtly. Regularization strengths live on a log scale and routinely span orders of magnitude, so the mean of {10, 10000} is 5005 -- a number nearer the larger band than to anything the model does -- where the geometric mean is 316, the scale a single-λ fit of comparable shrinkage would have used.

It falls back to the arithmetic mean if any band is unpenalized, where the geometric mean collapses to zero and stops distinguishing anything.

required

The global multiplier, geomean(λ).

ratio ndarray

(n_bands,), geometric mean 1.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If regularization is empty, non-finite, or not strictly positive.

Notes

The inverse of λ = scale * ratio, and unique: taking the geometric mean of both sides gives geomean(λ) = scale * 1. The scale comes from summary_scale, so the two functions cannot disagree about what a vector's scale is.

from_values(
    values: ndarray | Sequence, band_order: BandNames

Build a search from explicit λ vectors.

(n_values, n_bands), one row per λ vector, strictly positive.

required band_order sequence of str

The model's band order; names the columns.

required

Notes

Rows are normalized before being stored: grouped by ratio in first-appearance order, and sorted ascending by scale within each group, with duplicates dropped. The λ numbering is therefore a function of the set of vectors handed in, not of the order they happened to be written in -- so two callers who list the same space differently get the same figure and the same best_index.

docs.title: band_grid
docs.text:
band_grid(
    grids: dict[str, Strengths] | Strengths,
    band_order: BandNames,
    *,
    max_values: int = MAX_VALUES
) -> BandSearch

Cartesian product of a per-band grid.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default grids dict of str to sequence, or sequence of float

{band: values}. A band left out of the dict reuses the grid of the single band that was given, if exactly one was; otherwise its absence is an error, since silently regularizing a band at one fixed value while sweeping the others is a search a caller would not notice they had asked for. A bare sequence is applied to every band.

required band_order sequence of str

The model's band order; fixes the column order of the result.

required max_values int

Refuse products larger than this. n_bands bands at n_values each is n_values ** n_bands solves per fold, which passes "large" quickly: 10 values over 4 bands is 10,000.

MAX_VALUES

Returns:

Type Description BandSearch

The product, in the ratio order from_values imposes.

Raises:

Type Description KeyError

If grids names a band the model does not have, or leaves one without a grid when more than one was given.

ValueError

If the product would exceed max_values, or a grid is empty, non-finite or not strictly positive.

Notes

The product is generated directly, because {band: grid} is how a caller thinks about it, and from_values then puts it in ratio order. That ordering exposes the structure a product hides: an n_values by n_values log-spaced grid over two bands contains only 2 * n_values - 1 distinct ratios, its diagonals.

Be aware that a product is nonetheless the worst shape for the eigendecomposition path in solvers, which needs a run of scales at one ratio to pay for itself: the diagonals of a product are long but its corners hold a single scale each, so most groups fall back to an ordinary solve. random_bands sweeps the whole lambda grid at every ratio and is the shape that path was built for. Prefer it when the search is large enough for the difference to matter.

docs.title: random_bands
docs.text:
random_bands(
    band_order: BandNames,
    *,
    n_ratios: int = 20,
    scales: Strengths | None = None,
    concentration: float = 1.0,
    random_state: int | None = 42
) -> BandSearch

Random search: ratios drawn uniformly on the simplex, times a lambda grid.

Draws n_ratios Dirichlet samples and sweeps the full scales grid at each, for n_ratios * len(scales) λ values whose cost does not grow with the number of bands -- the reason to prefer this over band_grid past two or three of them. It is the strategy of Nunez-Elizalde et al. (2019), on the Bergstra & Bengio argument that for a fixed budget random draws cover the directions that matter better than a grid does as the dimension rises.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default band_order sequence of str

The model's bands; sets the dimension of the simplex.

required n_ratios int

How many ratio vectors to draw.

20 scales sequence of float or np.ndarray

Global scales swept at every ratio. Defaults to np.logspace(-2, 6, 20), the span an unnormalized ridge on standardized features usually needs.

None concentration float

Dirichlet concentration. 1.0 is uniform over the simplex; below 1 favours lopsided ratios (one band carrying most of the penalty), above 1 favours near-equal ones.

1.0 random_state int or None

Seed. Fixed by default for the same reason models.TorchTRF._bootstrap_metric fixes its own: two runs of the same model should select the same λ and report the same metric, and a search whose result moves between runs is not one a paper can cite.

42

Returns:

Type Description BandSearch

(n_ratios * len(scales), n_bands), one ratio's whole sweep after another.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If n_ratios is below 1, or scales is empty, non-finite or not strictly positive.

Notes

A Dirichlet sample sums to 1, so it is rescaled to geometric mean 1 to match the module's convention. That is a relabelling of the same direction: what the draw fixes is the proportion between bands, and the overall size is what scales sweeps.

docs.title: Model selection
docs.text:
Information criteria (AIC, BIC) and the comparison between fitted models — the ranking the held-out metrics cannot make, since they do not price complexity.

See Models & paradigms for what the numbers mean and when not to trust them.

docs.title: selection
docs.text:
selection.py — Information criteria, and comparing two fitted models.

The metrics in trflearn.metrics answer "how well does this model predict?". They cannot answer "which of these two models should I report?", because adding a feature block almost never makes the fit worse: a comparison between different models needs the fit and a price for complexity in the same number. That is what AIC and BIC are, and this module owns both -- the arithmetic here, the quantities they are computed from on the model (models.TorchTRF.information_criteria)::

log_likelihood(rss, n)    Gaussian log-likelihood from a sum of squares
aic(log_lik, edf)         Akaike information criterion
bic(log_lik, edf, n)      Schwarz / Bayesian information criterion
check_comparable(reports) refuse a set that cannot be differenced
compare(models)           two or more fitted models, side by side,
                          as a `Comparison`

Lower is better for both criteria.

The Gaussian constant is included. n*log(2*pi) cancels in any delta, so many implementations drop it; keeping it means the absolute value is a real AIC, comparable with what statsmodels or R print for the same residuals.

What the three parts of the number are -- an in-sample likelihood, effective degrees of freedom rather than a column count, channels that add up -- and the two limits worth knowing before reporting them -- autocorrelated residuals, and an regularization selected by cross-validation -- are in the Models & paradigms concepts page (docs/concepts/models.md), which the API page for this module links rather than repeats.

docs.title: CriteriaReport
docs.text:
Bases: TypedDict

What models.TorchTRF.information_criteria returns, key by key.

Every value is None together for solver="cross_corr", which has no penalized normal system and therefore no hat matrix to take a trace of.

The per-channel arrays are (n_channels,). The two totals are the sums over channels -- the multivariate criterion under independent channels, the assumption the rest of the package already makes.

docs.title: log_likelihood
docs.text:
log_likelihood(rss: ndarray | float, n: int) -> ndarray

Gaussian log-likelihood at the maximum-likelihood noise variance.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rss ndarray or float

Residual sum of squares, typically (n_channels,).

required n int

Samples the residuals were computed over.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Log-likelihood, shaped like rss.

Notes

-n/2 * (log(2*pi) + log(rss/n) + 1), the value of the normal log-likelihood once sigma^2 has been set to its MLE rss/n. It works elementwise, so a vector of residual sums of squares gives a vector of log-likelihoods.

A channel with rss == 0 is a perfect fit, whose likelihood diverges; -inf then propagates as inf through both criteria. It is reported that way rather than clamped, because a perfectly fitted channel of real data means the design is degenerate and silently returning a large finite number would hide that.

docs.title: aic
docs.text:
aic(
    log_lik: ndarray | float, edf: ndarray | float
) -> ndarray

Akaike information criterion, -2*log_lik + 2*k.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default log_lik ndarray or float

Log-likelihood, from log_likelihood.

required edf ndarray or float

Effective degrees of freedom, tr(H). A scalar for a model fitted at one regularization, which is what models.TorchTRF.information_criteria passes; broadcast against log_lik either way.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

The criterion, shaped like the broadcast of the two arguments.

Notes

k = edf + 1: the effective degrees of freedom of the mean, plus one for the noise variance, which is estimated too. Forgetting that +1 is harmless when comparing models whose edf differ but not when comparing a model against a null one, so it is included here rather than left to the caller.

docs.text:
bic(
    log_lik: ndarray | float, edf: ndarray | float, n: int
) -> ndarray

Schwarz information criterion, -2*log_lik + log(n)*k.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default log_lik ndarray or float

Log-likelihood, from log_likelihood.

required edf ndarray or float

Effective degrees of freedom, as in aic.

required n int

Samples the fit was computed over.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

The criterion, shaped like the broadcast of log_lik and edf.

Notes

Same k as aic. The penalty grows with the sample size, so BIC prefers smaller models than AIC does and increasingly so as the recording gets longer -- with the tens of thousands of samples a continuous EEG design has, log(n) is around 10 and the two criteria routinely disagree. That disagreement is information: AIC targets predictive accuracy, BIC targets identifying the true model among the candidates, and they are not the same question.

docs.title: check_comparable
docs.text:
check_comparable(reports: dict[str, dict]) -> None

Refuse a set of criteria that cannot legitimately be differenced.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default reports dict of str to dict

{name: report}. Only three keys of each report are read, and they are the whole input contract: aic (None marks a model with no penalized system), n, and target_ss. A full models.TorchTRF.information_criteria report satisfies it, and so does any narrower mapping carrying those three -- which is how group.TRFGroup.compare_to reuses this guard over stored per-subject records rather than over models.

required

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If any model has no effective degrees of freedom, or if two of them disagree on the sample count, the channel count, or y'y.

Notes

This is the point of compare, not a formality. An information criterion is an absolute number attached to one dataset: a difference between two of them means "which model describes this response better" and means nothing at all if the two were not fitted to the same response, over the same rows. Nothing about the arithmetic notices -- it happily subtracts -- so the check has to be here.

The three quantities catch the realistic mistakes between them: n (a different row subset, e.g. one model with drop_zero_rows=True), the channel count (a different montage or subject), and y'y over the fitted rows (a different target, a different target_preprocess, or the same subject's data reloaded differently). That last one is the fingerprint that catches what the first two miss.

docs.title: compare
docs.text:
compare(
    models: ModelSet, names: list[str] | None = None
) -> Comparison

Rank two or more fitted models by AIC and BIC.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default models dict or sequence

{name: model}, or a sequence of models. Given a sequence, names come from names or, failing that, from each model's feature specs ("envelope + onsets").

required names list of str

Names for a sequence of models. Redundant, and refused, when models is already a mapping.

None

Returns:

Type Description Comparison

The ranking, one field per quantity; see the class for what each holds.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the models are not comparable -- see check_comparable, which is where the real work of this function is.

Notes

Both criteria are reported because they answer different questions and routinely disagree on long recordings: AIC targets predictive accuracy and BIC targets identifying the true model, and BIC's penalty grows with log(n). Reporting only the one that agrees with you afterwards is the thing to avoid; that is why neither is the default here.

Read the Models & paradigms concepts page before acting on a small difference: EEG residuals are autocorrelated, so both criteria are overconfident.

Examples:

>>> table = compare({"envelope": m1, "envelope + onsets": m2})
>>> table.best["bic"]
'envelope'
>>> print(table.summary())

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text:
trflearn.simulation builds recordings whose answer is known: the only data on which recovering a kernel can be checked instead of argued. It is opt-in (import trflearn.simulation, never imported by the rest of the package) and its event tables need pandas, which comes with the simulation extra; see Installation. The tutorials use every part of it.

Two ways to build a recording:

  • simulate, multichannel and for any features: a continuous stimulus from envelope / spectrogram, impulse trains from an event table, or both. It returns the TRFData a model is built from and the GroundTruth that model should recover.
  • EEGSimulator, one channel, event by event, where each event's covariates can modulate the response through a kernel's modifier.

docs.title: simulate
docs.text:
simulate(
    features: dict[str, ndarray | list[ndarray]],
    kernels: dict[str, ndarray],
    sample_rate: int,
    *,
    info: Info | None = None,
    snr_db: float = 0.0,
    noise_colour: str = "white",
    rng: Generator | int | None = None,
    **data_kwargs: Any
) -> tuple[TRFData, GroundTruth]

Simulate one recording with known kernels, ready to model.

Each feature with a kernel is convolved with it, the responses add up, and noise is added at snr_db against that sum. Features without a kernel are kept: they reach the model and carry no response.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default features dict of str to np.ndarray or list of np.ndarray

The stimulus, as TRFData takes it: per feature an (n_samples, n_subfeatures) array, or a list of them, one per segment.

required kernels dict of str to np.ndarray

Per feature, (n_channels, n_subfeatures, n_delays) at lags 0, 1, ... samples: the layout of a fitted model's coef_. spatiotemporal_kernel builds one from waveforms and topographies.

required sample_rate int

Sampling rate in Hz.

required info Info or None

Channel info with the montage, one channel per kernel row. Passed to TRFData, so the montage-based figures work. None leaves the targets as plain arrays.

None snr_db float

Signal-to-noise ratio in dB, measured on the noise-free signal over every segment and channel. np.inf adds no noise.

0.0 noise_colour (white, pink, brown)

Colour of the noise, independent across channels.

"white" rng (Generator, int or None)

Source of randomness for the noise, or a seed for one.

None **data_kwargs Any

Passed on to TRFData, e.g. precision or use_gpu.

{}

Returns:

Name Type Description data TRFData

The features and the simulated targets, in the layout of features.

truth GroundTruth

The injected kernels.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If a kernel names a feature not in features, is not 3-D, does not match its feature's columns, or the kernels and info disagree on the number of channels.

Examples:

>>> info = make_info(["Fz", "Cz", "Pz", "Oz"], 128)
>>> p1n1 = (
...     CompoundKernel("envelope", 128)
...     .add(0.05, 1.0, 0.02)
...     .add(0.1, -1.5, 0.03)
... )
>>> kernel = spatiotemporal_kernel(
...     p1n1.waveform, gaussian_topography(info, [0, 0, 1])
... )
>>> data, truth = simulate(
...     {"envelope": envelope(128 * 60, 128, rng=0)},
...     {"envelope": kernel}, 128, info=info, snr_db=-5, rng=0,
... )

docs.title: Continuous stimuli
docs.text:
continuous_stimuli.py — Speech-like predictors: an envelope, a spectrogram.

Both are band-limited noise, rectified: not speech, but with the property that matters for a TRF, energy confined to the syllabic modulation band, so the lagged design is as ill-conditioned as a real envelope's. envelope is one column. spectrogram is one envelope per acoustic band, and the bands share part of their modulation, as they do in speech: band_correlation sets how much, as the expected correlation between any two bands.

Both return float arrays of shape (n_samples, n_columns), non-negative and of unit standard deviation per column, and the same rng seed gives the same stimulus.

docs.title: Discrete stimuli
docs.text:
discrete_stimuli.py — Event tables: when events happen and what they carry.

An experiment is a table with one row per event: its type, its onset latency in samples, and any covariates. TrialStructure draws the covariates from TrialVariable specifications, an ISI sampler spaces the onsets (assign_event_latencies), and ExperimentDesign does both in one call, then turns the table into one impulse train per event type: the features a TRFData takes. to_features does that conversion for any table, and adds each covariate as an amplitude at its event's onsets, the input spline_basis(scope="event") expects.

The tables are pandas DataFrames. pandas is imported where it is used and ships with the simulation extra.

kernels.py — The responses a simulation injects.

An ERPKernel is one component, a Gaussian or Hann bump at a peak latency, whose amplitude can depend on the event through a modifier. A CompoundKernel sums several of them under one name, and is what recordings.EEGSimulator registers. Kernels are causal: their time axis starts at the event onset.

docs.title: Montage helpers
docs.text:
recordings.py — Continuous recordings with known kernels buried in them.

simulate builds a multichannel recording from any features: per feature a kernel of shape (n_channels, n_subfeatures, n_delays), the layout of a fitted model's coef_, convolved with the stimulus and summed, plus noise at a requested signal-to-noise ratio. It returns the TRFData a model is built from and the GroundTruth the model should recover. simulate_cohort repeats it for subjects who share the stimulus and the kernels, each with their own noise and gain.

EEGSimulator builds one channel, event by event: per event and per kernel component, a stick whose height is 1 + modifier(**event_row), convolved with the component's waveform and summed, plus white, pink or brown noise.

The montage helpers spread a time course or a kernel over a scalp layout: make_info builds an mne.Info with sensor positions, and gaussian_topography / project_to_channels give it a smooth spatial distribution, e.g. posterior for a visual response or fronto-central for a motor one. mne is imported where it is used.

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text: Penalty matrices and the penalized solve. See the concept page.

docs.title: solvers
docs.text:
Penalty matrices and the regularized linear solve for TRF models.

Every regularized TRF solver builds a penalty matrix M and solves the normal equations (X^T X + λ M) coef = X^T y. This module owns three concerns so the model classes in models.py stay thin.

Penalty construction. Each penalty is a pure function of the design shape (n_subfeatures, n_delays) -- no dependence on the stimulus data -- registered by name in the :data:PENALTIES registry with the register decorator. Adding a penalty is writing the function and decorating it; nothing else needs editing.

ridge            : Tikhonov regularization (``M = I``).
ridge-laplacian  : temporal Laplacian smoothness penalty. It penalizes
                   differences between adjacent lags, not the kernel's
                   size, so it smooths without shrinking.

cross_corr is not a registered penalty: it has no M (unregularized cross-correlation baseline) and is the penalty is None case of solve_penalized.

The solve. solve_penalized is the one entry point, and picks among three strategies: one eigendecomposition reused across every scale sharing a ratio, one batched LU over the stacked grid, or one factorization per λ. The first needs a diagonal penalty, the second enough VRAM, and the third always works -- which is why it is where the other two fall back. Which of them wins is partly a hardware question, and the sweep behind the numbers is recorded in development/measured-constants.md, which ships with the source rather than with this documentation.

A caller states the problem and never the method: nothing outside this module chooses a strategy, or needs to know there is more than one.

Banded ridge

In a banded ridge the design's columns are partitioned into bands -- groups of features sharing one regularization strength -- so regularization is a vector, one entry per band, instead of a scalar. This module never sees bands: models expands a per-band λ into one weight per design column before calling, and search decides which vectors to try. What arrives here is always per-column weights, and an ordinary scalar ridge is just the case where every column carries the same weight -- one row of scales either way.

Vocabulary

regularization One regularization strength to solve at. A scalar for an ordinary ridge, a vector with one entry per band for a banded one -- n_values counts either kind, and both arrive here as one row of the (n_values, n_columns) scales matrix. scale, ratio A vector λ factored as λ = scale * ratio, with scale the global strength (lambda) and ratio the relative weighting between bands. Rows sharing a ratio are what the eigendecomposition path serves in one factorization; _ratio_groups recovers them, and search generates them that way to begin with.

Scope

Everything here is per block -- one selected feature (or interaction) with its own delay window. The model's full penalty is the block diagonal of these, assembled in models._build_block_penalty, so n_columns in this module is one block's width and models sums it over blocks. Axis names follow the package glossary in docs/concepts/notation.md.

docs.title: laplacian_penalty
docs.text:
laplacian_penalty(
    n_subfeatures: int,
    n_delays: int,
    *,
    device: device,
    dtype: dtype
) -> Tensor

Temporal Laplacian penalty, for delay-first column ordering.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_subfeatures int

Raw stimulus columns of the block, before lagging.

required n_delays int

Lags in the block's window.

required device (device, dtype)

Where and at what precision to build the matrix.

required dtype (device, dtype)

Where and at what precision to build the matrix.

required

Returns:

Type Description Tensor

(n_columns, n_columns) Laplacian, with n_columns = n_subfeatures * n_delays.

Notes

Adjacent delays of the same subfeature sit n_subfeatures apart in the flat coefficient vector, so the off-diagonals land at +/- n_subfeatures. The first and last delay have one temporal neighbour instead of two, hence a main diagonal of 1 there and 2 elsewhere.

Equivalently M = L_{n_delays} (x) I_{n_subfeatures}: the 1-D Laplacian over the delays, replicated per subfeature.

w^T M w = sum_d (w[d+1] - w[d])**2, a first-difference penalty: a constant kernel costs nothing and a slowly varying one very little. Ridge protects a weak predictor by pulling its kernel towards zero; this penalty does not, so slow noise -- where 1/f noise such as EEG's has its power -- can enter such a predictor as a large, smooth kernel.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text: Pure, stateless helpers consumed by TRFGroup and usable standalone.

docs.title: statistics
docs.text:
statistics.py — Group-level statistics for TRF kernels.

Pure, stateless helpers consumed by group.TRFGroup and usable standalone. Nothing here holds class state or imports models/core, so the dependency graph stays acyclic: the classes import this module, never the reverse.

Four groups of function:

Descriptives. grand_average averages per-subject kernels across a cohort; descriptive_summary counts the cohort and summarizes its metrics, its selected regularization, and -- when it was fitted with diagnostics=True -- how the collinearity of the design varies between subjects.

The paired test. paired_signed_rank is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test of per-subject differences against zero, behind group.TRFGroup.compare_to.

The cluster test. cluster_1samp runs a one-sample permutation test against zero in either of its two flavours, cluster mass at a fixed t threshold or TFCE; tfce_1samp is the TFCE flavour under its own name, and t_threshold turns a p into the t the other flavour needs. delay_positions and restore_full_delays restrict a test to a window of delays and put the result back on the whole axis. mne is imported lazily, so the rest of the module carries no hard MNE dependency. The permutation loop is the one place in the package worth a progress bar.

Spatial adjacency, which the cluster test needs when the channels are source parcels rather than sensors and mne.channels.find_ch_adjacency therefore has no montage to read. source_adjacency builds the graph from centroid proximity, surface_adjacency from shared borders on the cortex.

Axis names follow the package glossary in docs/concepts/notation.md.

docs.title: source_adjacency
docs.text:
source_adjacency(
    positions: ndarray,
    n_neighbors: int = 6,
    dist_factor: float = 1.5,
) -> csr_matrix

Neighbourhood graph of source-space regions from their centroid positions.

The sensor-space counterpart of this is mne.channels.find_ch_adjacency, which needs a montage and so cannot describe parcels. Here proximity stands in for anatomy: two regions are neighbours when their centroids are close, which is what lets a cluster test group a spatially contiguous effect instead of treating every region as independent.

Two rules are unioned, because either alone fails at one end of the range. A distance threshold (dist_factor x the median nearest-neighbour distance) captures genuine local structure but leaves outlying regions with no neighbours at all; a k-nearest floor (n_neighbors) guarantees every region is connected but, alone, would link distant regions in sparse areas.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default positions np.ndarray of shape (n_regions, 3)

Centroid coordinates, in the order of the data's channels. Typically read off an mne.Info built by core.TRFData.set_source_positions.

required n_neighbors int

Nearest-neighbour floor: how many neighbours every region gets even when the distance threshold would leave it isolated.

6 dist_factor float

Distance threshold, as a multiple of the median nearest-neighbour distance. Larger values give larger, more permissive clusters.

1.5

Returns:

Type Description csr_matrix

(n_regions, n_regions) boolean adjacency, symmetric and including the diagonal -- the form mne.stats.combine_adjacency expects.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If positions is not (n_regions, 3), holds a non-finite coordinate, or if either knob is out of range.

Notes

The graph is geometric, not anatomical: it does not know about the cortical surface, so two regions facing each other across a sulcus (or across the midline) count as neighbours if their centroids are close.

docs.title: surface_adjacency
docs.text:
surface_adjacency(
    ch_names: Sequence[str],
    labels: Sequence,
    surfaces: dict[str, tuple],
) -> csr_matrix

Neighbourhood graph of cortical regions from their borders on the surface.

The anatomical alternative to source_adjacency. Proximity is a proxy for adjacency and a leaky one: centroids that are close in space may sit on opposite banks of a sulcus, or on opposite sides of the midline, and a cluster is then free to jump a gap it should not cross. Here two regions are neighbours only when an edge of the surface triangulation actually joins a vertex of one to a vertex of the other -- they share a border.

Hemispheres are never linked, since no edge crosses between them.

The surfaces and labels are passed in rather than read here, so this package keeps no knowledge of FreeSurfer layouts and the graph can be built for any parcellation the caller can load::

labels = mne.read_labels_from_annot(subject, parc, subjects_dir)
surfaces = {
    h: mne.read_surface(f"{subjects_dir}/{subject}/surf/{h}.white")
    for h in ("lh", "rh")
}

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ch_names sequence of str

docs.title: cluster_1samp
docs.text:
cluster_1samp(
    data: ndarray,
    adjacency: csr_matrix | None = None,
    threshold: float | dict | None = None,
    n_permutations: int = 1024,
    tail: int = 0,
    seed: int | None = None,
    n_jobs: int = 1,
    progress: bool | None = None,
    verbose: int | None = None,
) -> tuple[ndarray, ndarray]

One-sample cluster permutation test against zero, wrapping mne.stats.

Both flavours of the test are here, chosen by threshold, because they differ only in that argument and in how the p-values map back onto the grid:

  • threshold=float -- cluster mass. Points whose t exceeds the threshold are grouped into clusters and each cluster's summed t is compared against the permutation null of the largest cluster. The result is one p-value per cluster; every point in a cluster shares it. Cluster inference does not localize: the honest statement is "this cluster is significant", not "this delay/channel is". Use t_threshold to pick the float.
  • threshold=dict (or None -> dict(start=0, step=0.2)) -- threshold-free cluster enhancement, which integrates over every threshold and yields a genuine per-point p-value, so no cluster-forming threshold has to be guessed.

mne.stats.spatio_temporal_cluster_1samp_test accepts data of shape (n_observations, p[, q], n_vertices), so a multi-column feature is handled natively -- no need to collapse its sub-features.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data ndarray or Tensor

Per-subject kernel maps, shaped (n_subjects, n_delays, n_channels) or (n_subjects, n_delays, n_subfeatures, n_channels). Channels (the dimension the adjacency describes) must be last; the middle dimensions form regular lattices.

required adjacency csr_matrix or None

The full adjacency over prod(data.shape[1:]) locations, as built by mne.stats.combine_adjacency (lattice over the middle dims x channel adjacency). None lets MNE assume a lattice along the last dimension only, which is valid only for the 3D case with lattice channels.

None threshold (float, dict or None)

Cluster-forming t threshold (cluster mass), TFCE parameters (dict), or None for the default TFCE settings.

None n_permutations int

Sign-flip permutations for the null.

1024 tail int

0 = two-sided, 1 = positive, -1 = negative.

0 seed int or None

RNG seed for reproducibility.

None n_jobs int

Parallel jobs for the permutation loop, forwarded to mne.stats. The loop is the whole cost of the test -- at a few thousand permutations over a channels x lags grid this is the difference between seconds and minutes -- so raise it on a multi-core machine.

1 progress bool or None

Show MNE's permutation progress bar. None follows the verbosity level and shows it at DEBUG; True/False decides for this call alone, which is how a quiet cohort run still gets a bar on the one test that takes minutes. MNE gates the bar on its own log level, so showing it also prints MNE's four setup lines -- the two cannot be separated.

None verbose int or None

A resolved verbosity level overriding the global one when progress is left at None. See trflearn.verbosity.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description t_obs ndarray

The t statistic, shaped data.shape[1:], TFCE-enhanced in the TFCE flavour.

pvals ndarray

The same shape: a per-point p-value under TFCE, and under cluster mass the p-value of the cluster each point belongs to (1.0 where a point joined no cluster). Thresholding it therefore recovers the significant-cluster mask in either flavour.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If data is neither 3-D nor 4-D.

docs.title: Verbosity
docs.text: How much the package prints. See the concept page.

docs.title: verbosity
docs.text:
verbosity.py -- One switch for everything the package prints.

Every message TRFlearn writes to stdout passes through report, which drops it unless the effective verbosity is at least the level the message was tagged with. Four levels, ordered by importance so a single threshold is enough:

SILENT  (0)  nothing.
WARNING (1)  a computation degraded: a singular system fell back to
             ``lstsq``, a batched solve ran out of memory, an argument was
             coerced. Nothing failed, but the result was not obtained the
             intended way.
INFO    (2)  status: what the library decided on the user's behalf, such as
             creating default partitions. **The default.**
DEBUG   (3)  diagnostics only useful while working on the package itself,
             e.g. the per-stage GPU/CPU memory report.
Two ways in

A process-wide default, set once::

trflearn.set_verbosity("warning")

and a per-object verbose argument on TRFData, the model classes and TRFGroup, which overrides the global for that object alone. Leaving it at None (the default) means the object follows the global at call time, so a later set_verbosity still reaches an object built before it.

For a cohort loop -- the case this exists for, where one message per subject buries whatever the user is actually reading -- verbosity_scope scopes the change instead of leaving it set::

with trflearn.verbosity_scope("warning"):
    for subject_id, data in cohort.items():
        group.fit_subject(data, subject_id)
Not Python warnings

This governs the package's own messages, not warnings.warn. The UserWarning sites (a dropped-sample fraction, a missing montage, an ill-conditioned design) keep Python's machinery -- stacklevel, per-site deduplication, pytest.warns -- which a print cannot reproduce. SILENT therefore does not silence them; warnings.simplefilter("ignore") does. user_stacklevel gives the stacklevel for a warning raised several calls deep.

Examples using verbosity

  • 2 · Auditory pipeline
  • 2 · Natural speech TRF
