docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The moving parts, and how they fit together.

  • TRFData container

    A lazy, window-agnostic store of named features and the response; segment-aware, MNE-native, materialized on demand.

  • Cross-validation

    create_partitions records a fold config; time-contiguous KFold, per-segment stratification, leave-one-segment-out, or a single train/test split.

  • Models & paradigms

    TRFModel(cv=...) picks pooled, averaged or train_test; all share the same spec, solvers and diagnostics.

  • Features & windows

    Names, interactions, per-feature delay windows, spline bases, and the crop window.

  • Solvers

    Ridge, temporal Laplacian, or an unregularized cross-correlation baseline.

  • Preprocessing

    Per-column standardization / normalization (or none), fit on each fold's train set.

  • Verbosity

    How much the package prints: four levels, set globally or per object, so a cohort loop can turn the chatter down.

docs.title: The pipeline in one line
docs.text:
TRFData(features, y, sample_rate)  →  create_partitions(...)  →  TRFModel(cv=...)
     →  gridsearchCV / fit  →  coef_ / predict / to_evoked  →  plots

Scale it to a cohort with TRFGroup, which fits one spec per subject and aggregates (grand average, TFCE).

docs.title: Cross-validation — create_partitions
docs.text:
create_partitions only records the config — it is lazy. The fold indices are built later, when a model materializes the container for its crop window. Folds are always contiguous in time: there is no sample-level shuffling, which would leak autocorrelated neighbours across the train/test boundary.

Call Paradigm create_partitions() The default: 5 folds, stratified by segment when the data come in segments, plain contiguous KFold for one continuous recording. A model built on an unpartitioned container uses it too. create_partitions(n_folds, stratify_by_segment=True) Each fold draws a contiguous chunk from every segment — balances segments without leakage. Requires segmented data. create_partitions(n_folds, stratify_by_segment=False) Plain contiguous KFold, segments or not. create_partitions(segments_as_folds=True) Leave-one-segment-out (the Lalor/mTRF paradigm for many short segments): fold s tests on segment s, trains on the rest. n_folds is ignored. create_partitions(train_size=0.8) A single contiguous train/test split (one fold), for cv="train_test". Takes precedence over the other args. 
data.create_partitions()   # 5 folds, stratified by segment; then build a model

Partitioning is index-level and independent of which features a model later uses, so one partitioned container can drive several different model specs.

Lazy folds

Right after create_partitions(...), data.folds is still None; it is populated when the first model is instantiated (materialization). This is expected.

See also: train_size and the train_test paradigm and the full API for TRFData.create_partitions.

docs.title: Features, interactions & windows
docs.text:
When building a model, features is a list of specs:

  • a string selects a base feature by name;
  • a tuple ("k1", "k2") is an interaction — the outer product of the raw features (d1·d2 columns).

docs.title: Per-feature delay windows
docs.text:
The model always takes a default_window=(tmin, tmax) (seconds) — the fallback for any feature without its own window. Each feature can override it with feature_windows={spec: (tmin, tmax)} (for an interaction, the union of its constituents' windows). Windows are independent — a feature window may extend beyond default_window — and the container's crop window is their union, so no subset rule applies. Keys must name a selected feature: an unknown key (a typo, or a feature you did not select) raises KeyError rather than being ignored.

model = TRFModel(
    TRFDataset=data,
    features=["envelope", "spectrogram", ("envelope", "spectrogram")],
    default_window=(-0.2, 0.6),
    feature_windows={"envelope": (-0.1, 0.4)},
    solver="ridge-laplacian",
)

docs.title: Basis expansions (feature_bases)
docs.text:
To model a nonlinearity in the stimulus, attach a basis expansion to a feature's amplitude via feature_bases={spec: transformer} — keyed exactly like feature_windows. The transformer is any scikit-learn-style object with fit/transform (canonically SplineTransformer): each raw column (n_samples, n_subfeatures) is mapped to (n_samples, n_subfeatures·k) before lagging, so a scalar feature becomes k smooth basis channels.

For splines, use spline_basis, which pins the recommended convention in one call:

from trflearn import spline_basis

model = TRFModel(
    TRFDataset=data,
    features=["envelope"],
    feature_bases={"envelope": spline_basis(n_functions=4, order=3,
                                            knots="quantile", drop="mean")},
)

n_functions is the number of columns the design actually receives — the block's n_subfeatures, the second axis of coef_, the count of plot labels — after the dropped column. Left out, it keeps the spline space at five functions whatever the drop — 4 columns with one dropped, 5 without — which at the default order is the lab's reference function (3 knots, cubic). order is the polynomial order (3 cubic, 4 quartic), knots is "quantile" (resolution follows where the data is — the right default for skewed amplitudes), "uniform", or an explicit array.

docs.title: Why a column is dropped
docs.text:
A whole B-spline basis makes the block exactly singular

B-splines are a partition of unity: the k basis columns sum to 1 in every row, and feature_preprocess centres each column, so the centred columns sum to zero — an exact linear dependency, repeated at every lag. Nothing raises, because the ridge penalty covers the deficiency, but regularization is then holding the block together as well as regularizing it, and the tuned value is chosen partly to fix an artificial redundancy that carries no information. Measured on one spline block: condition number 1.6e+07 against 3.3e+04 for the same design with a column removed.

The collinearity report catches it, but the other two diagnostics do not, so read the right one. condition_number is computed on the regularized matrix and cannot tell the two apart at a working regularization; effective_rank is a participation ratio, not a rank, and does not see exact singularity. What does see it is vif_columns_, which reads inf for every column of the block, and vif_aliased_, which lists them — with a UserWarning naming the count and the rank deficit, which are far apart here: every column takes part in the dependency while only one per lag is redundant. The block's vif_ stays unremarkable on purpose: the redundancy is inside the block, and the generalized VIF measures what a block shares with the others.

Dropping the column costs nothing. The model has no intercept and the target is centred, so the remaining k-1 columns span exactly the same space — this is the same reason unfold and other event-based toolboxes remove one spline from a basis that accompanies an intercept.

Which one, and how many. drop="mean" removes the column peaking nearest the predictor's mean (unfold's rule, the default); drop="last" matches sklearn's include_bias=False; drop=None keeps the whole basis. This is a documented choice, not an obvious one: with ridge and no intercept the two rules are different models rather than reparametrizations, and the evidence points both ways — conditioning strongly favours "mean" (VIF 2.5 against 195 on a skewed stimulus), while one synthetic test scored marginally better with "last". Conditioning is the reproducible half, which is why it wins the default.

The drop is per input feature, not one column overall. sklearn lays the expansion out feature-major and the partition of unity holds within each feature's group, so a feature with several columns (a spectrogram, an interaction) loses one column per group. Removing a single one overall would leave every other group's dependency standing.

docs.title: Event features: scope="event"
docs.text:
A sparse event feature — a saccade's amplitude at its onset sample, zero everywhere else — needs the basis applied at the events only. Its zero means no saccade, not a saccade of amplitude 0, and a per-sample expansion gets both halves wrong: the quantile knots are placed from a column that is mostly zeros, so they pile up at 0 and leave the amplitudes in a single polynomial piece; and a spline evaluated at 0 is not 0, so every empty sample enters the design as a small event.

feature_bases={"sac_amplitude": spline_basis(scope="event")}

fits the knots on the rows where the feature is non-zero, expands those rows and leaves every other row at exactly zero — what spl() means in unfold. A row counts as an event when any of its columns is non-zero, the same test drop_zero_rows applies. For any other transformer, event_scoped does the same, and goes outermost: nothing inside it ever sees a zero, so even np.log is safe on an amplitude.

from trflearn import event_scoped

feature_bases={"sac_amplitude": event_scoped(make_pipeline(
    FunctionTransformer(np.log), spline_basis(drop=None)))}

The drop turns around. At the events the columns sum to 1, elsewhere to 0: their sum is the onset indicator, which centring does not cancel. So the whole basis is well conditioned on its own, and it needs every column, because the part of the response that does not depend on the amplitude — the average response to a saccade — lives in that sum. With one column dropped the block can no longer represent it, and that part of the response is forced into shapes that vary with the amplitude. Hence drop=None is the default under this scope, and the two ways of writing the same model are:

Model features feature_bases["sac_amplitude"] Columns Amplitude alone ["sac_amplitude"] spline_basis(scope="event") 5 Onset + amplitude (unfold's 1 + spl(a)) ["saccade", "sac_amplitude"] spline_basis(scope="event", drop="mean") 1 + 4

They span the same space. Beside an onset regressor for the same event — a feature of ones at the event samples — the whole basis would repeat it exactly, so there the drop is an identifiability requirement and has to be asked for. Pick the second form when the onset kernel is wanted as a term of its own, as in unfold.

docs.title: Composition: log, and anything else
docs.text:
feature_bases takes any transformer, so an elementwise transform and its composition with a basis need nothing new:

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer
import numpy as np

feature_bases={"sac_amplitude": make_pipeline(FunctionTransformer(np.log1p),
                                              spline_basis(n_functions=4))}

Use log1p, not log: with rectified envelopes zero is frequent and np.log maps it to -inf without complaining. And a lambda is not picklable, so it would fail at save(with_bases=True) rather than at fit time — wrap a named function.

docs.title: Two things to know
docs.text:
The basis is fit once on the relevant stimulus samples (knots come from the stimulus, never the response — no target leakage) and reused across folds and in predict. The expanded n_subfeatures flows through coef_, the diagnostics and to_evoked unchanged (a feature with more than one column exports one Evoked per basis channel).

Fitting once means the quantile knots see the held-out folds. The leak is mild — the basis never sees the target — but it is why spline_basis defaults to sklearn's knot padding with extrapolation="constant" rather than the unfold-exact clamped construction. In range the two span the same space (measured maximum principal angle ~1e-13); outside it, clamped boundary functions have nothing to continue into and evaluation raises. So if the basis is ever tightened to per-fold fitting, held-out stimulus beyond the training range becomes reachable during the grid search, and only the sklearn padding survives it. Choosing it now is what keeps that door open.

drop_zero_rows is unaffected by any of this: it reads its mask from the pre-basis stimulus, because informativeness is a property of the stimulus rather than of how it was parametrized — and a per-sample basis maps 0 to something non-zero.

docs.title: In a cohort
docs.text:
A cohort averages each basis column across subjects, which only means something if column k is the same function of the stimulus in every subject. Refitted per subject it is not: quantile knots follow each subject's own amplitudes, so the same column peaks at a small saccade in one subject and at a larger one in the next. So TRFGroup takes its bases already fitted and never refits them. Fit each one once, on a stimulus that covers the whole cohort:

amplitudes = np.concatenate([features["sac_amplitude"]
                             for features, _ in cohort.values()])
group = TRFGroup(
    features=["saccade", "sac_amplitude"],
    default_window=(-0.2, 0.4),
    feature_bases={"sac_amplitude": spline_basis(scope="event", drop="mean")
                   .fit(amplitudes)},
)

An unfitted basis is refused when the cohort is built, and a subject whose bases differ from those the cohort was fitted with is refused at fit_subject — after reloading a cohort saved without its bases, set group.feature_bases back to the same fitted ones.

docs.title: delay_margin
docs.text: An optional margin (seconds) added on each side of every feature's window to absorb ridge edge effects; it is trimmed off the kernel before predicting.

docs.title: Models & paradigms
docs.text:
TRFModel(...) is a single entry point; the cv argument picks the cross-validation paradigm and returns the matching backend instance.

cv Backend Paradigm "pooled" (default) PooledTRF Standard k-fold: for each test fold, one model is fit on the pooled complement and predicts the held-out set. "averaged" AveragedTRF Crosse–Lalor: one model per partition; fold j is predicted by the leave-one-out average of the others. "train_test" TrainTestTRF A single contiguous train/test split; the λ that scores best on the test fold is kept. 
model = TRFModel(TRFDataset=data, features=[...])                  # pooled (default)
model = TRFModel(TRFDataset=data, features=[...], cv="averaged")   # Crosse–Lalor
model = TRFModel(TRFDataset=data, features=[...], cv="train_test", # 80/20 split
                 train_size=0.8)

All paradigms share the same features / interactions / windows / bases, solvers and diagnostics.

docs.title: Fitting
docs.text:
• gridsearchCV(regularization_grid, ...) selects a single λ by cross-validation (an inner train/validation split), then — with run_fit=True — refits at that λ. With no regularization_grid it searches np.logspace(-3, 3, 13); it chooses on R² unless metric says otherwise, and the refit reports the same metric (see Recommendations for when Pearson is the better choice). Aggregation across folds defaults to "mean" in every paradigm, so the λ they select is comparable across them ("median" — more robust to an outlier fold — "max" or a fold index are one argument away); metric_limit_percentage biases toward a larger λ, which shrinks the kernels without improving their shape (see Recommendations). It records a validation figure (see validation_plot).
  • fit(regularization, ...) fits at a fixed λ and stores coef_ and the predict-time normalizers.
  • predict(X_new=None) applies coef_ to a stimulus (the model's own by default, or a dict{name: array} of base features), returning the response in target units.

docs.title: Scoring on a subset of samples
docs.text:
The held-out metric covers every sample of each fold. A sparse model — word onsets, fixations, with no continuous feature beside them — predicts the mean wherever its design row is all zero, and those stretches still enter the correlation. Its r then answers how much of the recording the model explains, which is the honest default. It does not answer the event-locked question, how well the response is predicted given that an event occurred. score_on, on fit and gridsearchCV, restricts the held-out samples the metric is computed on:

score_on= scores on None (default) every sample "informative" samples where any block has an event within its delay window ["onsets"] the same, for the named blocks only — beside a continuous feature every sample is informative, so this is the form to use there {"onsets": (0.0, 0.5)} 0 to 0.5 s after each event, a window of its own inside the model's delay range boolean array / callable exactly those samples, one entry per real sample (as for relevant_indexes); a callable receives the held-out samples' numbers

An event is a sample where the raw feature, before any basis, is non-zero. The window of the dict form may belong to a feature the model does not fit, so two models can be scored on the same samples — an envelope model and an onset model both on {"onsets": (0.0, 0.5)}:

model.gridsearchCV(grid, score_on={"onsets": (0.0, 0.5)})
model.metric_name_    # "R² (onsets 0 to 0.5 s)"
model.scored_on_      # {"score_on": {"onsets": (0.0, 0.5)}, "fraction": 0.31}
  • Only the scoring changes. The estimation and predict are untouched, and drop_zero_rows stays independent: it decides which rows fit the kernels, score_on which ones score them, and together they fit and score on the event windows.
  • Every metric of the call sees the same samples — per fold, concatenated and bootstrapped, in all three paradigms. In gridsearchCV that includes the metric that selects λ, so λ is tuned for the question the reported metric answers; pass it there, not in run_fit_kwargs.
  • The result says what it is. A Pearson over a subset is not comparable to one over every sample, nor to a literature value, so metric_name_ is marked and scored_on_ keeps the selection and the fraction of held-out samples it kept. Both are saved with the model.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
diagnostics() returns condition_number_ (of the regularized normal system), effective_rank_ (participation ratio of the design) and a three-part collinearity report. All of them are computed on the full relevant design at the fitted λ, so they are single, well-defined values — identical across the two cv paradigms.

attribute what it answers vif_ per block: how much of it is explained by the other blocks, as the generalized VIF of Fox & Monette (1992), GVIF^(1/2d). 1.0 means nothing shared vif_columns_ per column, the textbook VIF; inf where the column is an exact combination of the others vif_aliased_ which columns take part in a linear dependency — the actionable one

vif_ is per block rather than per column because a lagged design is collinear within a block by construction: contiguous lags of an autocorrelated signal are correlated, that is not a defect, and any per-column average reports it as one — large for every block, separating nothing. The generalized VIF is invariant to how a block is parametrized internally, which is exactly what removes lag collinearity from the answer. A block with no other block to share with (a single-feature design, or one wholly redundant given the rest) reads nan.

Read vif_ next to vif_aliased_ rather than on its own. The block number is computed on a full-rank subset of the columns, so one aliased column cannot zero a determinant and take the whole report with it — which also means an exact dependency does not inflate it: two duplicated blocks read 1.0 each once the duplicates are set aside. The per-column half is what catches those.

They are not computed by fitting. Assembling the full design is an extra pass over the data — in float64, because an exact dependency is not distinguishable from a merely collinear direction at float32 — and a diagnostic is a report on the model rather than a part of it, so it is computed when asked for and cached:

model.diagnostics()              # everything
model.diagnostics(vif=False)     # skip the (n_columns, n_columns) decomposition
model.condition_number_          # computes on first access, then reads the cache

Two UserWarnings come with them, on the first read rather than at the end of every fit: the 1e6 ill-conditioning one, and one naming both the number of aliased columns and the rank deficit when the design carries an exact dependency.

A cohort records them per subject under TRFGroup(..., diagnostics=True) (off by default — it is one extra pass per subject). The record keeps the per-block vif keyed by spec and n_aliased, the count; group.summary() then carries a "diagnostics" entry with the spread across subjects, which is what says whose design is the odd one out.

docs.title: Comparing two models: AIC and BIC
docs.text:
A held-out metric says how well one model predicts. It cannot rank two different models — envelope alone against envelope + onsets — because adding a feature block almost never makes the fit worse, and with ridge it is not even obvious how many parameters were added. information_criteria() puts the fit and a price for complexity in one number, and compare() ranks a set of them. Lower is better for both criteria.

model.information_criteria()   # {"aic", "bic", "edf", "n", "rss", ...} per channel
model.aic_, model.bic_, model.edf_          # on demand, then cached

table = trflearn.compare({"envelope": m1, "envelope + onsets": m2})
table.best["bic"]                           # by the summed criterion
table.best_per_channel["aic"]               # (n_channels,) of names — topoplottable
table.delta_bic_total                       # {name: ΔBIC against the winner}
print(table.summary())                      # one printable row per model

Three things decide the number, and each is a deliberate choice:

  • The likelihood is in-sample, on the full design at the fitted λ. That is the definition rather than an oversight of the package's held-out discipline: AIC exists because the in-sample fit is optimistic and the penalty is the correction. Penalizing a held-out likelihood would apply that correction twice.
  • The complexity is the effective degrees of freedom tr(H), not the column count. A penalized fit does not spend n_columns parameters — edf_ runs from n_columns at λ → 0 down to 0 as λ grows — and counting columns would make two models with the same windows equally complex however differently they were regularized.
  • The channels add up. Each criterion is (n_channels,), and the total is their sum, which is the multivariate criterion under independent channels — the assumption the rest of the package already makes.

compare() refuses models that are not comparable rather than differencing them anyway: different n (one of them with drop_zero_rows), a different channel count, or a different y'y over the fitted rows — the fingerprint that catches a different target or a different target_preprocess. A criterion is an absolute number attached to one dataset, and nothing in the arithmetic notices when the dataset changed. solver="cross_corr" has no penalized system and therefore no tr(H): all of them are None there, and compare() says so.

Two limits

EEG residuals are autocorrelated. Both criteria assume independent samples; continuous EEG is nowhere near that, so the effective sample size is a fraction of the row count and both are overconfident — they call a difference decisive sooner than the data warrant. BIC suffers less, since its penalty grows with log(n). Use them to rank models fitted on the same data, not as a significance test.

λ was chosen by cross-validation, and this is an in-sample criterion, so the data does double duty, mildly.

Across a cohort the same comparison is TRFGroup.compare_to, which pairs subjects by id and turns each one's criteria into a single observation — and that framing escapes the autocorrelation warning above, since it does not depend on the sample size inside a subject. It needs TRFGroup(..., criteria=True), decided before fitting.

docs.title: The train_test paradigm
docs.text:
The simplest option: a single contiguous split whose "CV" just sweeps the grid, fits on train and keeps the λ that scores best on the test fold. The split is set by train_size (on the model, or via create_partitions(train_size=...); defaults to 0.8).

It is optimistic

There is no inner validation and no fold aggregation: λ is chosen on the very set whose metric is then reported, so the reported metric is the maximum over the grid, not an unbiased estimate. Use it for a quick, straightforward look; prefer pooled / averaged when the number must be trustworthy.

averaged caveat

The leave-one-out average is itself clean — a fold's coefficients never see its own data — but each partition is standardized once with its own statistics, a mild feature-scale leakage into the CV estimate (no target leakage). pooled avoids this by standardizing the test fold with training statistics.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text: Every array dimension in TRFlearn has one name, used identically in code, docstrings and comments. A shape written in a docstring uses the same tokens as the variables around it, so the two cannot drift apart unnoticed.

docs.title: Axis names
docs.text: Name What it counts n_samples Time samples (rows of the target, of a stimulus, of a design). n_kept_samples Samples surviving a row selection, when both counts coexist. n_channels Columns of the target y — sensors, or source vertices. n_features Named features: the keys of the feature dict. n_subfeatures Raw stimulus columns of one feature, before lagging. 1 for an envelope, 5 for a 5-band spectrogram, 8 after a spline expansion. n_delays Lags in a block's window (len(blk["delays"])). n_fit_delays Lags in the margin-padded fit window (len(blk["fit_delays"])). n_columns Columns of a design or penalty: n_subfeatures * n_delays, summed over blocks. n_real_columns The same, after the fit margin is trimmed off. n_blocks Design blocks — one per selected feature or interaction. n_bands Groups of blocks sharing one λ in a banded ridge. n_folds Cross-validation folds. n_values Regularization strengths tried in a search. One λ is a scalar for an ordinary ridge, a vector with one entry per band for a banded one. n_ratios Distinct band weightings in a banded search. n_resamples Bootstrap resamples. n_subjects Subjects in a cohort. n_permutations Sign-flip permutations of a cluster test. n_segments Segments of a segmented TRFData.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. No abbreviations. n_channels, never n_ch; n_subjects, never n_subj.
  2. No single-letter dimensions. A shape is written (n_samples, n_channels), never (N, C) or (T, C).
  3. A shape in a docstring may only use names that exist as variables.
  4. Single capitals are still used for matrices inside a short numeric function (XTX, XTY, Q, M, Gamma). Those are not counts, and the rules above do not apply to them.
  5. bases.py keeps scikit-learn's fitted-attribute names (n_features_in_, n_basis_); that contract belongs to the external library.

docs.title: The regularization strength
docs.text:
The penalty's weight is called regularization wherever it is an argument or a key (fit(regularization=...), regularization_grid, results(s)["regularization"]), and λ in formulas and prose. It is the same quantity other packages call lambda (the mTRF toolbox) or alpha (scikit-learn). In a banded ridge λ is a vector with one entry per band, and search factors it into a scale, its geometric mean, and a ratio.

Axis order is deliberately not fixed. Different operations want different layouts, and forcing one would cost transposes; the names say what each axis is, whatever position it sits in.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
Features are standardized per column with each fold's train statistics before lagging; targets are standardized with the fold's train statistics. This keeps the CV estimate honest — the test fold is transformed with statistics it did not see.

Choose the scheme independently for features and targets:

Value Transform "Standardize" (default) z-score (subtract mean, divide by std). "Normalize" min–max to [0, 1]; does not centre (see below). None no normalization (identity). 
model = TRFModel(
    TRFDataset=data,
    features=["envelope"],
    feature_preprocess="Standardize",
    target_preprocess=None,
)

Under standardization the kernel maps a feature-sigma to a target-sigma, so the plots label the vertical / colorbar axis σ_EEG/σ_x (or σ_MEG/σ_x, σ_target/σ_x, ... after the channel types in the info); with Normalize or None an appropriate label is used instead.

Normalize does not centre

TRFlearn fits no intercept, and centring is what stands in for one. On the target, Normalize leaves a mean the kernels must reproduce, which breaks the fit, so target_preprocess="Normalize" is deprecated and warns. On the features it adds a penalty on each kernel's sum. Prefer Standardize; see Recommendations.

The normalizer classes (Standardize, Normalize, Identity) live in trflearn.utils.tensor_prep and share a fit_train / fit_test / inverse_transform interface.

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
Every regularized solver builds a penalty matrix M and solves

\[ (X^\top X + \lambda M)\, \mathrm{TRF} = X^\top y \]

without modifying XᵀX in place. Choose it with the solver argument.

Solver Penalty M Use ridge Identity (Tikhonov) Uniform shrinkage. ridge-laplacian Temporal Laplacian Smooth kernels — penalizes differences between neighbouring lags, not size. cross_corr — Unregularized cross-correlation baseline (returns Xᵀy). 
model = TRFModel(TRFDataset=data, features=[...], solver="ridge-laplacian")

ridge-laplacian does not shrink

A constant kernel costs it nothing, so a predictor that carries little signal is not pulled towards zero, and slow noise -- 1/f noise such as EEG's -- can enter it as a large, smooth kernel. See Recommendations.

The penalty matrices and the penalized solve live in trflearn.solvers; new penalties can be added with the @register(name, is_diagonal=...) decorator.

solve_penalized picks among three strategies — one eigendecomposition reused across a run of scales, one batched LU over the whole grid, or one factorization per λ — and which wins is partly a hardware question. The measurements that set those thresholds are not part of this documentation; they live with the source, in development/measured-constants.md.

docs.title: The TRFData container
docs.text: TRFData holds every candidate feature and the neural response. It is window-agnostic and fully lazy — the delay window lives on the model, not the data.

docs.title: Named features
docs.text:
Pass every candidate feature as features={name: array}. Each value is a 2D array (n_samples, n_subfeatures), or a list of per-segment 2D arrays for a segmented recording. Segments are concatenated with a NaN buffer so that no lagged window ever crosses a boundary.

data = TRFData(
    features={
        "envelope": envelope,          # (n_samples, 1)  or a list of segments
        "spectrogram": spectrogram,    # (n_samples, 21) or a list of segments
    },
    y=eeg,                             # (n_samples, n_channels), a list of
                                       # segments, or an mne.Raw
    sample_rate=128,
)

docs.title: Window-agnostic and lazy
docs.text:
TRFData does not take tmin/tmax. It stores only the raw streams, the cheap segment layout and the partition config. The delay window lives on the model (default_window / feature_windows).

Building a model computes its crop window — the union of all its feature windows — and triggers TRFData.materialize(...), which:

  1. concatenates segments with the NaN buffer,
  2. derives the buffer-safe set of usable samples (no lagged window crosses a NaN),
  3. builds the fold indices from the recorded partition config.

Re-materializing for a different crop window recomputes this and invalidates the lagged-feature cache, so several models with different windows can safely share one container.

docs.title: Targets from MNE
docs.text:
y may be an mne.Raw (or a list of Raw, one per segment). The sampling rate must match sample_rate and the length must match the features. Samples spanned by a "bad"/"BAD" annotation are excluded from the folds automatically (reject_by_annotation). The Raw's channel info (montage, channel types) is kept in TRFData.info, so kernels can be exported as Evoked and the topomap/Evoked-based plots become available.

Arrays work too

With plain-array targets the numeric pipeline is identical, and every figure that draws one trace per channel (plot, plot_image, plot_psd, plot_average, validation_plot) works regardless — only the topomap figures require channel positions.

docs.title: Attaching a montage to array targets
docs.text:
No Raw at hand? Attach the channel info yourself — you only need the electrode labels:

data = TRFData(features=feats, y=eeg_array, sample_rate=128,
               target_names=["Fz", "Cz", "Pz", "Oz"])
data.set_montage("standard_1020")          # or set_info(my_mne_info)

Equivalently, pass it at construction with TRFData(..., info=my_mne_info). The info's channel names become target_names. It is pure metadata — it takes no part in materialization, so it can be attached before or after create_partitions / materialize without recomputing anything.

This unlocks to_evoked, every topomap figure (plot_joint, plot_features, plot_metric_topomap, …) and — the one worth watching — the spatial adjacency of TRFGroup.tfce.

TFCE degrades quietly without a montage

With no channel positions, tfce treats the channels as independent (it warns, then carries on). The test still runs and returns plausible numbers, but an effect spread over neighbouring electrodes no longer reinforces itself, so the result is far more conservative than it should be. TRFGroup copies the info from the first subject it fits, so attach it before fit_subject.

See the full API: TRFData.

docs.title: Verbosity
docs.text:
Everything TRFlearn prints is tagged with a level, and only messages at or below the current setting are shown. The default is "info", which is what the library has always printed.

Level Shows "silent" / False / 0 Nothing. "warning" / 1 A computation degraded: a singular system fell back to lstsq, a batched solve ran out of memory, an argument was coerced. Nothing failed, but the result was not obtained the intended way. "info" / True / 2 (default) The above, plus what the library decided on your behalf — creating default partitions, for instance. "debug" / 3 The above, plus package-development diagnostics such as the per-stage GPU/CPU memory report, MNE's progress bar on the permutation tests, and the bootstrap's progress bar over its resamples.

docs.title: Setting it
docs.text:
Process-wide:

import trflearn

trflearn.set_verbosity("warning")

Or for one object only, with the verbose argument that TRFData, every model and TRFGroup accept. It overrides the global setting for that object alone:

data = trflearn.TRFData(features=features, y=y, sample_rate=128, verbose="silent")

Left at its default of None, an object follows the global setting at call time, so a later set_verbosity still reaches objects built before it.

docs.title: Cohort loops
docs.text:
This is the case the levels exist for. One status line per subject buries whatever you are actually reading, so turn the chatter down while keeping the numeric warnings:

with trflearn.verbosity_scope("warning"):
    for subject_id, data in cohort.items():
        group.fit_subject(data, subject_id)

The context manager restores the previous level on exit, including when the block raises. TRFGroup(..., verbose="warning") does the same thing for the cohort's models without touching the global setting at all.

docs.title: Progress on the permutation tests
docs.text:
The cluster / TFCE tests hand their permutation loop to MNE, which can draw a progress bar over it — the one wait in the package long enough to be worth watching. It is off by default and appears at "debug", or on demand for a single call:

t_obs, pvals = group.tfce("envelope", n_permutations=4096, progress=True)

progress=True / progress=False decides for that call alone, so a cohort run kept at "warning" can still watch the one test that takes minutes. MNE gates the bar on its own log level, so showing it also prints MNE's four setup lines — the two cannot be separated from here.

docs.title: Python warnings are separate
docs.text:
This governs TRFlearn's own messages, not warnings.warn. The UserWarning sites — a dropped-sample fraction, a missing montage, an ill-conditioned design — keep Python's machinery, including stacklevel, per-site deduplication and pytest.warns, which a print cannot reproduce. "silent" therefore does not silence them:

import warnings

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    ...

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Complete analyses on real recordings. Unlike the tutorials, these need data that is not in this repository — they are reference material showing what a finished analysis looks like, and each notebook is committed with its outputs so it can be read without being run.

data required 1 01_opm_sensor_trf.ipynb OPM-MEG, 7 participants of a driving-simulator experiment. Three simultaneous predictors, each with its own delay window, jointly fitted 2 02_natural_speech_trf.ipynb EEG, 18 participants listening to an audiobook. Two parts: the envelope TRF with group statistics and TFCE, then joint estimation with a second correlated predictor 3 03_opm_source_trf.ipynb the same OPM-MEG cohort as 1, with parcel timecourses as targets instead of sensors: region centroids in place of a montage, anatomical adjacency for TFCE, and the kernels handed to MNE's 3D brains

docs.title: Getting the data
docs.text:
Neither dataset ships here. 02_natural_speech_trf.ipynb documents its own provenance in full — the two public releases it is built from, how they were cross-referenced, and the preprocessing applied — in its first section.

Note that every notebook resolves its data root at the top and fail with an explanatory message if it is missing, so opening one without the data is harmless.

docs.title: New to the library?
docs.text: Start with the tutorials instead. They run with no downloads and build up the same workflow on data whose ground truth is known.

docs.title: What each one exercises
docs.text:
Generated from the notebooks themselves on every docs build, so it cannot go stale.

documented API used 1 · OPM sensor TRF TRFData, TRFGroup, Standardize 2 · Natural speech TRF TRFData, TRFGroup, io, TRFModel, PooledTRF, Standardize, verbosity 3 · OPM source TRF TRFData, TRFGroup, Standardize, statistics

# Helper functions to make the input features for the TRF model
def impulse_series(onsets_s: np.ndarray, sfreq: float, n_samples: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Unit impulses at the given onset times (seconds from recording start)."""
    idx = np.round(np.asarray(onsets_s, dtype=float) * sfreq).astype(int)
    idx = idx[(idx >= 0) & (idx < n_samples)]
    series = np.zeros(n_samples, dtype=np.float64)
    series[idx] = 1.0
    return series
# Helper functions to make the input features for the TRF model def impulse_series(onsets_s: np.ndarray, sfreq: float, n_samples: int) -> np.ndarray: """Unit impulses at the given onset times (seconds from recording start).""" idx = np.round(np.asarray(onsets_s, dtype=float) * sfreq).astype(int) idx = idx[(idx >= 0) & (idx < n_samples)] series = np.zeros(n_samples, dtype=np.float64) series[idx] = 1.0 return series In [4]: Copied! 
def load_subject(subject_id: str) -> TRFData:
    """Radial magnetometers and the three predictors of one participant."""
    subject_dir = DATA_ROOT / subject_id
    raw = mne.io.read_raw_fif(subject_dir / f"DA2_{subject_id}_meg.fif",
                              preload=False, verbose="ERROR")
    sfreq = raw.info["sfreq"]

    steering = raw.get_data(picks="Steering")[0]
    gas = raw.get_data(picks="Gas")[0]

    # Radial (Z) magnetometers only
    picks = [ch for ch, kind in zip(raw.ch_names, raw.get_channel_types())
             if kind == "mag" and ch.endswith(" Z")]
    meg = raw.copy().pick(picks).load_data(verbose="ERROR")
    n_samples = meg.n_times

    # Onsets in the CSVs are already relative to the file start.
    saccades = pd.read_csv(subject_dir / "saccades.csv")

    features = {
        "saccades": impulse_series(saccades["onset"].to_numpy(), sfreq, n_samples),
        "steering_wheel": np.gradient(steering),
        "gas_pedal": np.gradient(gas),
    }

    # Reshape to the (n_samples, n_subfeatures) layout TRFData expects.
    features = {name: series.reshape(-1, 1) for name, series in features.items()}

docs.title: Group-level sensor-space TRF on real OPM-MEG data¶
docs.text:
End-to-end walkthrough of TRFlearn on a real cohort: seven participants of a driving-simulator OPM-MEG experiment (task DA2).

A single jointly fitted encoding model deconvolves three simultaneous predictors, each with its own delay window:

Feature Source Window (s) saccades saccade onsets (CSV) (-0.2, 0.5) steering_wheel d/dt of the steering wheel (-2.0, 2.0) gas_pedal d/dt of the accelerator pedal (-2.0, 2.0)

docs.title: Steps¶
docs.text:
1. Build a TRFData container per participant.
  2. Fit the cohort with TRFGroup, one model spec for everyone.
  3. Test each feature's kernel against zero with TFCE over subjects.
  4. Plot the grand average with its significance shading.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text:
One folder per participant under examples/data/OPM/ (git-ignored):

<subject>/DA2_<subject>_meg.fif   preprocessed continuous OPM recording
<subject>/saccades.csv            saccade events (onset in seconds, file-relative)

Needs pip install -e ".[mne]".

docs.title: 2. Per-subject loading¶
docs.text:
Everything the cohort loop needs for one participant, in one function: read the recording, build the three predictor columns on its own time grid, and wrap them in a TRFData.

The stimulus/behavioural channels are read before the sensors are picked, so they stay available once the recording is narrowed to the magnetometers.

Passing the MNE Raw as the target carries the sensor montage into the container (so kernels export as Evoked and draw as topomaps) and lets TRFlearn drop the "bad"-annotated samples from every fold. No manual masking.

Folds are contiguous, non-shuffled blocks — deliberate for autocorrelated time series, where a random split would leak neighbouring samples across the train/test boundary and inflate the score.

docs.title: 3. Fit the cohort¶
docs.text:
TRFGroup holds the model spec once and applies it to every participant, so the kernels stay comparable across subjects. Each subject is fitted, reduced to its fold-averaged kernels and channel-wise metric, and the model discarded — only the summary is kept.

fit_method="fit" fits directly at REGULARIZATION; "gridsearch" would search regularization_grid per subject instead.

docs.title: 4. TFCE over subjects¶
docs.text:
One threshold-free cluster test per feature, asking where its kernel differs from zero across participants. The test runs over the full delays × channels map, with the delay lattice and the sensor neighbourhood graph as adjacency, so a real effect can pool evidence over both.

Threshold-free means no cluster-forming t to choose, and a genuine p-value at every point — which is what the figure below shades.

This is the expensive cell: the two ±2 s features carry ~86k test points each.

docs.title: 5. Figures¶
docs.text: One column per feature over the grand average: the kernel butterfly, the channels × delay image and a topomap. The TFCE result is picked up automatically — significant delay intervals are shaded green (positive) or red (negative), the image is greyed out where nothing survives, and the topomap is drawn at the most significant delay with its significant sensors marked. Baselines are applied on the way to each figure; the stored kernels stay untouched.

docs.title: 2 · Natural speech TRF
docs.text:
Recovering the correspondence. Correlating subjects directly does not work: everyone heard the same audiobook, so every pair shares the same stimulus-driven response and correlates at r ≈ 0.6 whether matched or not. The mapping was instead established by resampling OpenNeuro to 128 Hz, searching the lag between the two recordings of each run (OpenNeuro keeps a variable pre-roll of up to ~12 s; Dryad is trimmed to the audio), and requiring the same partner to win in every one of the 20 runs. At the correct lag a true pair reaches r ≈ 0.92–1.00 and wins consistently, while a subject with no counterpart changes partner run to run and never exceeds ~0.82. 18 of 19 subjects map one-to-one; OpenNeuro sub-003 and Dryad Subject5 have no partner and are dropped. A third, sub11, was excluded on inspection of its recordings. That is why this cohort has 17 members and no sub03 or sub11, and why subject numbering follows OpenNeuro's.

Preprocessing already applied to the files read below.

  1. Re-referenced to the average of the two mastoids, and cropped to the length of the corresponding stimulus envelope.
  2. Montage biosemi128; channels flagged bad in OpenNeuro's channels.tsv are interpolated with spherical splines, so info['bads'] is empty in the saved files.
  3. ICA: extended Infomax, 20 components, fitted on the concatenated runs band-passed 1–40 Hz for the fit only. Artefact components were selected by hand from topography and spectrum.
  4. Applied per run. ica.apply is a fixed spatial projection, so the saved .fif files remain broadband — no temporal filter has touched them.

The band-pass is therefore left to the analysis, and this notebook applies it explicitly: a linear-phase FIR, applied with its delay compensated so it is zero-phase. It is MNE's windowed design (firwin, Hamming window, 845 taps, 6.6 s) with a passband of 1.5–14 Hz and transitions of 0.5 and 1 Hz: −6 dB at 1.25 and 14.5 Hz, and more than 50 dB down from 1 Hz and from 15 Hz on. Those are the edges of the original study's filter, a Chebyshev type II IIR (order 4, 20 dB stopband) run forward and backward, whose nominal "1–15 Hz" are where its stopband begins: a FIR asked for 1–15 Hz would instead pass both edges whole, and with them the slow drifts below 1.5 Hz. A causal filter would shift every peak and corrupt exactly the latencies of interest; the FIR's phase is linear by construction rather than cancelled by a second pass, and its stopband is deeper. Like any zero-phase filter it is non-causal: it spreads every deflection to both sides in time, so a response can leak into the negative delays of a kernel.

The predictor. The acoustic envelope is the magnitude of the Hilbert analytic signal of the waveform, resampled to the EEG's 128 Hz — a single continuous channel tracking how the speech's amplitude rises and falls. Part II adds its half-wave-rectified derivative as a second predictor, marking the sharp acoustic edges the envelope itself smooths over.

Getting the data. The preprocessed set is ~4 GB and lives outside this repository; the two source releases are ~22 GB together. Download them from the links above and apply the four steps described in the previous section, or point DATA_ROOT below at an existing copy.

Those four steps are stated there in full — the mastoid reference, the biosemi128 montage with spherical-spline interpolation of the channels OpenNeuro flags as bad, the 20-component extended-infomax ICA fitted on the concatenated runs, and its per-run application that leaves the saved files broadband. Everything the analysis below depends on is in that description; nothing is deferred to a script you would have to read.

One step is not automatable, and that is the point: the ICA components to remove were chosen by visual inspection of topography and spectrum. No threshold reproduces that judgement, so anyone repeating this is adopting a set of hand-made decisions rather than re-running a pipeline. That is exactly what separates an example from a tutorial, and why this notebook lives in examples/ — see tutorials/ for material that runs end to end with no downloads and no human in the loop.

def load_aligned_segment(subject: int, segment: int):
    """One run: band-passed EEG as `mne.Raw`, plus the two stimulus predictors."""
    raw = mne.io.read_raw_fif(
        DATA_ROOT / "eeg_ica" / f"sub{subject:02d}" / f"eeg_segment{segment:02d}.fif",
        preload=True, verbose="error"
    )

    # Zero-phase FIR: no peak is shifted. A causal filter would delay every peak
    # and corrupt the latencies we care about.
    raw.filter(l_freq=BAND[0], h_freq=BAND[1], **FIR, verbose="error")

    env = np.load(DATA_ROOT / "stimuli" / "envelope" /
                  f"envelope_segment{segment:02d}.npy").astype(np.float64)

    # The envelope runs 7-11 samples longer than the EEG; trim both to the common
    # length so every design-matrix row means the same instant on both sides.
    n = min(len(env), raw.n_times)
    raw.crop(tmax=(n - 1) / FS, verbose="error")
    env = env[:n]

    # Acoustic onsets: half-wave-rectified derivative of the envelope. It keeps
    # the sharp rises the envelope smooths over. Used in Part II.
    onset = np.maximum(np.diff(env, prepend=env[0]), 0.0)

    return raw, env.reshape(-1, 1), onset.reshape(-1, 1)


def build_subject(subject: int, segments=SEGMENTS) -> TRFData:
    """A partitioned `TRFData` for one subject: 20 segments, both predictors."""
    raws, envelopes, onsets = [], [], []
    for seg in segments:
        r, e, o = load_aligned_segment(subject, seg)
        raws.append(r); envelopes.append(e); onsets.append(o)

    data = TRFData(
        features={"Envelope": envelopes, "Onset": onsets},
        y=raws,                      # montage + channel names ride along
        sample_rate=FS,
        use_gpu=USE_GPU
    )
    # Folds are a property of the data, not of the model.
    # Block-stratified so each fold draws from every segment instead of being one
    # contiguous chunk.
    return data.create_partitions(n_folds=N_FOLDS, stratify_by_segment=True)

for name, metric, limit in [("Pearson",       "Pearson", None),

        metric=metric,
        metric_aggregation_function="mean",   # how folds are pooled; the default
        metric_limit_percentage=limit,        # None = simply take the best λ
        inner_train_cutoff=0.8,               # the default inner split
        validation_plot=False,
    )
    fits[name] = (model, regularization)

Pearson                0.1585         0.0650         0.0901
R²                     0.1585         0.0046         0.0081
RMSE                   0.1585         0.9982         0.9962
Pearson, 5 %             6.31         0.0615         0.0857

Those four rows are worth reading slowly, because they explain a convention.

Why Pearson is the standard: the main reason is that this metric is scale-invariant, so a response can be real, correctly timed, and still amount to a few percent of correlation without being penalised for its small amplitude. That is precisely why the TRF literature reports correlation, and why this notebook does too.

The rest is bookkeeping worth knowing: RMSE is the only registered metric where lower is better, so the search flips its sign internally to keep "best" meaning one thing; and held-out R² can be negative, which is information rather than failure.

Here the three metrics agree, and the reason is in the curve below: the score is flat from the bottom of the grid up to λ ≈ 0.1 and only then turns. With one predictor, 90 design columns and nearly half a million samples, the normal equations are well conditioned and the penalty has almost nothing to do until it grows large enough to start smoothing the kernel. Whatever the metric, it peaks where that plateau ends.

And then there is the fourth row, which is not a curiosity. Compare it against the first: metric_limit_percentage=0.05 asks a different question — not "which λ scores highest?" but "which is the largest λ still within 5 % of the best?" — and it lands some forty times further along the grid (6.31 against 0.16) for a held-out r a few thousandths lower. That is the plateau's shoulder: the most regularisation the data tolerate before it costs anything that matters.

On a plateau a plain argmax is choosing between near-ties, and for a subject whose curve never turns it settles on the bottom of the grid. That is worth knowing — it says the penalty is not what is limiting that fit — but it is not by itself a problem, and it is why section 9 checks the two grid endpoints separately rather than treating both as warnings.

The cohort below keeps the plain Pearson rule. The 5 % variant is a real option and sometimes the right one, particularly with fewer data per subject or a visibly noisy kernel; here the two score nearly the same (0.0650 against 0.0615), so the notebook stays with the convention and shows the alternative rather than quietly imposing it.

validation_plot — the λ search made visible, and the reason to look at all four. The left panel is the held-out metric against λ with the selection marked; the panel beside it stacks the kernel at every λ on the grid. Read together, the curve says which λ won and the stack says what regularisation was doing to the shape on the way there.

This is where the paragraph above becomes something you can see rather than take on trust: all three curves have the same shape — flat over the bottom of the grid, a barely visible optimum where the plateau ends, and a fall beyond it (a rise, for RMSE) as the penalty starts to shrink the kernel. The stack shows what that fall costs: the peaks lower and widen as λ grows. A metric curve that never turned around, climbing toward the largest λ on offer, would be the signature of a selection rule that wants no model at all; none of these does.

plot_metric_topomap — the same four models, scored on the scalp. The three metrics chose the same λ, so the first three maps score one model three ways. Pearson and R² should show structure, and structure in the right place: fronto-central, where an auditory response belongs. Held-out correlations of a few hundredths per channel are normal for single-trial continuous speech.

RMSE is the control, and it should look empty: in standardised units it sits a hair below 1 on every channel, a flat field on a scale that includes zero. A model that explains a few thousandths of the variance barely moves an error measured against the signal's whole spread — so the same fit that Pearson reads as a clear topography is invisible to RMSE. That is the clearest possible statement that the selection metric is a modelling decision, not a formatting one.

Two of the three say something here, and the third says nothing by construction.

The effective rank is far below the column count. About seven effective directions out of 90 design columns is not a defect — it is what a lagged low-frequency predictor is. Neighbouring delays of a slowly varying signal are nearly the same regressor, so the design's variance concentrates into a handful of directions. This is precisely why ridge is not optional: the unregularised problem is close to singular, and the penalty is what makes it solvable.

The condition number is of the regularised matrix — the one actually inverted. It reflects the problem after λ has done its work, which is why the diagnostic needs a fitted λ and refuses to run before one exists.

The GVIF is empty, and has to be. It measures how much a feature block duplicates the other blocks, and a single-block design has no other blocks. This is not a limitation to work around; it is the diagnostic correctly reporting that the question does not apply yet. In Part II it will.

Now the GVIF says something. A value of 1.0 would mean a block shares nothing with the other; the envelope and its own rectified derivative are related by construction, so a value meaningfully above 1 is expected here. It quantifies a known overlap rather than warning about an unknown one — and read together with vif_aliased, which is empty, it says the blocks are correlated but not redundant. An exact dependency would be the serious case, because then the split between the two blocks would be arbitrary rather than merely uncertain.

docs.title: Natural-speech TRF on a real cohort¶
docs.text:
An end-to-end walkthrough of TRFlearn on 17 participants listening to an audiobook, from the preprocessed recordings to threshold-free cluster-corrected group inference.

This is the repository's one example built on a public, real EEG dataset rather than a simulation, and it is organised in two parts:

  • Part I — the envelope TRF. A single predictor, fitted the way the library is meant to be used, producing the classic auditory response. Everything the library offers around a fit — metric choice, design diagnostics, the whole plotting API, cohort statistics, bootstrap, TFCE — is exercised here.
  • Part II — adding acoustic onsets. A second, correlated predictor enters the same model. This is where joint estimation, between-block collinearity and formal model comparison become meaningful — and where the tidy envelope kernel stops being tidy, for reasons worth understanding.
Data Natural Speech (Di Liberto et al. 2015; Broderick et al. 2018), 17 subjects × 20 runs Recording BioSemi 128-channel ActiveTwo, 128 Hz, mastoid-referenced, ICA-cleaned Predictors acoustic envelope, plus onsets in Part II Window −150 to 450 ms, fitted with a 50 ms margin that is trimmed afterwards Fit cv="pooled", 5 block-stratified folds, ridge, λ searched per subject Inference TFCE, 1024 permutations, full channel × delay adjacency

docs.title: 1 · The data¶
docs.text:
The task. Healthy adult participants listened to a professionally recorded audiobook of Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea, presented as 20 continuous runs of roughly three minutes each — about an hour of speech per person. There is no trial structure and nothing to respond to: subjects simply listened to uninterrupted natural narration while 128-channel EEG was recorded with a BioSemi ActiveTwo system at 512 Hz. That continuity is the point. Because the stimulus never stops, responses to successive acoustic events overlap continuously, and averaging cannot separate them — which is precisely the situation a temporal response function exists to handle.

The recordings come from Di Liberto, O'Sullivan & Lalor (2015) and were extended by Broderick et al. (2018).

Two public releases, and why both are needed. The same experiment was published twice, and neither release is self-sufficient:

Field OpenNeuro (ds004408) Dryad (10.5061/dryad.070jc) State raw, unfiltered, unreferenced, 512 Hz the same signal at 128 Hz, still unreferenced Format BIDS / BrainVision, 128 scalp channels MATLAB .mat: eegData, mastoids, fs Mastoid channels absent present — the only way to re-reference Bad-channel flags present (*_channels.tsv) absent Stimuli .wav + forced-aligned .TextGrid precomputed 128 Hz envelopes

OpenNeuro records which electrodes were bad; only Dryad carries the mastoids the original analysis referenced to. Reproducing the published pipeline needs both — which first requires knowing which OpenNeuro subject is which Dryad subject, since the two releases number their participants differently and neither provides a key.

docs.title: References¶
docs.text:
Data

  • Di Liberto, G. M., O'Sullivan, J. A., & Lalor, E. C. (2015). Low-frequency cortical entrainment to speech reflects phoneme-level processing. Current Biology, 25(19), 2457–2465.
  • Broderick, M. P., Anderson, A. J., Di Liberto, G. M., Crosse, M. J., & Lalor, E. C. (2018). Electrophysiological correlates of semantic dissimilarity reflect the comprehension of natural, narrative speech. Current Biology, 28(5), 803–809.
  • OpenNeuro dataset ds004408, version 1.0.8 — doi:10.18112/openneuro.ds004408.v1.0.8
  • Dryad dataset — doi:10.5061/dryad.070jc

Methods referenced above

  • Crosse, M. J., Di Liberto, G. M., Bednar, A., & Lalor, E. C. (2016). The Multivariate Temporal Response Function (mTRF) Toolbox: a MATLAB toolbox for relating neural signals to continuous stimuli. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 10, 604. — the reference implementation this library is measured against.
  • Gorman, K., Howell, J., & Wagner, M. (2011). Prosodylab-Aligner: a tool for forced alignment of laboratory speech. Canadian Acoustics, 39(3), 192–193. — produced the .TextGrid phoneme alignments shipped with the OpenNeuro release.
  • Fox, J., & Monette, G. (1992). Generalized collinearity diagnostics. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 87(417), 178–183. — the GVIF reported in section 12.
  • Smith, S. M., & Nichols, T. E. (2009). Threshold-free cluster enhancement. NeuroImage, 44(1), 83–98. — the correction used in section 11.

docs.title: 2 · Setup¶
docs.text: The only hard requirement beyond TRFlearn is MNE, which does the file I/O, the filtering and the sensor geometry.

docs.title: 3 · Loading — and why the targets are mne.Raw objects¶
docs.text:
TRFData accepts its targets as plain arrays or as mne.Raw, one per segment. The Raw route is preferable here and not merely for convenience: channel names, channel types and the montage travel with the data into TRFData.info.

That matters more than it looks. Without a montage, TRFGroup.tfce has no channel adjacency to build and falls back to treating the 128 electrodes as independent — which would quietly invalidate the group statistics later on. Since these .fif files already carry biosemi128 embedded, passing Raw gets it right with no montage bookkeeping at all, and every Evoked-based plot works immediately.

Note that both predictors are built here, including the one Part I will not use.

docs.title: 4 · The container holds candidates; the model chooses¶
docs.text:
TRFData is a container of named candidate features, not a fixed design. It holds everything that might be modelled, and each model then names the subset it wants. That separation is what the next two parts are built on: the container below carries Envelope and Onset, Part I fits models that ask only for Envelope, and Part II reuses the very same container to ask for both.

It is also deliberately lazy. Building it validates shapes and records the partition configuration, but nothing is concatenated, no design matrix is assembled and no fold is drawn. All of that depends on the delay window, which lives on the model — so the container cannot know it yet. The first model to be constructed supplies it and triggers materialize.

docs.title: Part I — The envelope TRF¶
docs.text: One predictor, Envelope, selected out of a container that holds two. Everything from here to section 11 uses that single-feature model.

docs.title: 5 · One subject, and what the choices actually do¶
docs.text:
cv="pooled" is TRFlearn's default and the recommended one: for each held-out fold a model is fitted on the pooled complement, so nothing in the reported score was seen while fitting. gridsearchCV searches λ on an inner split of the training data and then refits at the winner — the refit is not optional at the cohort level, so a reported kernel is always one that was actually fitted.

Two settings deserve to be spelled out rather than left at their defaults.

delay_margin=0.05. Ridge regression rings at the edges of the delay window: the first and last lags have no neighbours on one side, and the penalty pulls them toward zero in a way that bends the kernel where it should simply end. Fitting 50 ms wider on each side and then trimming the margin off before predicting moves that artefact outside the window you actually look at. The kernel comes back at the requested −150–450 ms; the fit that produced it was wider.

The metric. Pearson correlation is the convention in the TRF literature, but it is a convention. Below, the same data and the same λ grid are searched under three different metrics, plus one variant that deliberately prefers a smoother model. The parameters are written out in full so the choices are legible, even where they match the defaults.

docs.title: 6 · Diagnosing the design¶
docs.text:
Before trusting a kernel, ask whether the design that produced it was well posed. model.diagnostics() answers that. It is computed on demand rather than during fitting — it costs a full extra pass over the design — and it needs the fitted λ, because the condition number it reports is that of the regularised normal matrix, which is the matrix actually inverted.

quantity what it says condition_number how close the regularised system is to singular; > 1e6 warns effective_rank participation ratio of the unregularised design — how many directions genuinely carry variance vif generalised VIF per feature block (Fox & Monette), so collinearity within the lag axis is not counted as a problem vif_columns / vif_aliased per design column; inf marks exact linear dependence

docs.title: 7 · The plotting API on a single subject¶
docs.text:
Every figure below is a method on the fitted object, returns its Figure, and accepts save_path. Models, cohorts and individual subjects share one API, so nothing here has to be relearned at the group level.

Kernel amplitudes are in coefficient units (σ_EEG / σ_x under standardisation), never µV — the model was fitted on standardised data, and labelling the axis in volts would be a fiction.

docs.title: 8 · Fitting the cohort¶
docs.text:
TRFGroup declares the model spec once, without data, fits it per subject, keeps only the minimal per-subject record — kernels, held-out metric, selected λ, diagnostics — and discards each full model. That is what makes 17 subjects × 60 minutes tractable in a notebook.

Two flags must be set before fitting and cannot be recovered afterwards, precisely because each subject's model is discarded:

  • criteria=True — records AIC/BIC, without which Part II's compare_to cannot run;
  • diagnostics=True — records the design report from section 6 for every subject.

Note also what is absent from the loop: there is no run_fit argument. fit_subject forces run_fit=True and rejects run_fit=False outright — a cohort whose members were never refitted at their selected λ would have no kernels to average, so the API refuses to build one.

docs.title: 9 · Cohort descriptive statistics¶
docs.text: summary() gives cohort size and the spread of the per-subject numbers; grand_average() returns mean / SD / SEM of the kernels across subjects.

docs.title: Two per-subject views, and the cohort's landmarks¶
docs.text:
The figure below is descriptive housekeeping — how well the model predicts for each person, and how much regularisation each one needed. What to look for: prediction accuracy varying by a factor of a few across subjects is normal; λ spanning many orders of magnitude is also normal, because it absorbs per-subject differences in noise level.

The two grid endpoints are checked separately, because they mean opposite things. Landing on the ceiling is a genuine warning: the search wants more regularisation than the grid offers, which is a model being shrunk toward nothing, and the resulting kernel would be flat. Landing on the floor is the flat-curve situation from section 5 — the one subject that does so here has a design well enough conditioned that ridge has little left to do, which is a fact about an hour of single-predictor data rather than a fault in the search.

The final block reads the classic auditory landmarks — P1, N1, P2 — off the channel-averaged group kernel. This is the notebook's real validation step: if those latencies land near the values reported for this paradigm, then the whole chain — filtering, alignment, folds, the λ search, the margin trimming — is behaving.

docs.title: Design diagnostics across the cohort¶
docs.text: Section 6 diagnosed one subject, which cannot say much on its own. The question a cohort asks is whether this subject's design is the odd one out, so summary()["diagnostics"] reports the spread across subjects and names anyone carrying an exact dependency. aliased_subjects should be empty; if it is not, those subjects have redundant design columns and their kernels are not identified in those directions.

docs.title: 10 · Bootstrap distributions per subject¶
docs.text:
bootstrap=True resamples folds with replacement at fit time, giving each subject a distribution for its held-out metric rather than a single number. plot_bootstrap draws one violin per subject with the observed value, a percentile interval and the cohort mean.

This is the figure that separates "the cohort average is positive" from "the cohort average is positive and most individuals are individually credible" — a distinction a bar chart of means cannot make.

docs.title: 11 · Group inference with TFCE¶
docs.text:
The question is whether the cohort's kernel departs from zero, controlling the family-wise error over the whole delay × channel grid — 128 channels times the delay axis is a lot of opportunities to find something.

group.tfce(spec) wraps mne.stats.spatio_temporal_cluster_1samp_test and builds the full adjacency lattice (delays × channel neighbourhood) from the montage carried in TRFData.info. This is where section 3's choice to pass mne.Raw pays off: without that montage the channel adjacency degrades to the identity, every electrode becomes an island, and the correction goes wrong without raising anything. The cell therefore captures warnings and reports whether the adjacency fallback fired — an empty list is the check that the correction used real sensor neighbourhoods.

Why TFCE rather than cluster mass. Under cluster mass the p-value belongs to the cluster, not to any delay or channel inside it, so "this cluster is significant" is the only honest statement and reading a latency off its edges is unsupported. TFCE returns a genuine per-point p-value, which is what makes the shaded figures below interpretable.

What to expect: a fraction of the grid significant, concentrated around the N1 and the P2 over fronto-central sensors. Nothing significant, or everything significant, would both be signs that something upstream is wrong.

docs.title: Significance-aware figures¶
docs.text: Once the test has run its result is cached on the cohort, and the plotting API picks it up automatically — the same calls from section 7 now shade what survived correction.

docs.title: Part II — Adding acoustic onsets¶
docs.text:
The container has carried an Onset predictor since section 3 without any model asking for it. Now one does.

The point of this part is not that two predictors are better than one. It is that adding a correlated predictor changes what the first one means, and that TRFlearn gives you the tools to see that happening rather than discover it later: a between-block collinearity diagnostic that was empty in Part I, and a formal comparison that prices the extra complexity instead of rewarding it automatically.

docs.title: 12 · Two blocks, and a diagnostic that now has something to say¶
docs.text: The same container, the same window, the same margin — only the feature list changes.

docs.title: 13 · What the second predictor does to the first¶
docs.text:
Here is the part worth being careful about. The Envelope kernel is not the same object in the two models. Fitted alone it absorbs everything the envelope correlates with, acoustic edges included. Fitted alongside an onset block it keeps only what the onsets do not already explain, and the shared variance — the GVIF above says there is plenty — gets divided between them.

So the tidy P1–N1–P2 shape from Part I is not expected to survive, and its not surviving is not instability. It is deconvolution doing exactly what it is for. The practical consequence is blunt: a TRF latency quoted without naming the model that produced it means nothing.

docs.title: 14 · The joint cohort¶
docs.text: The same 17 subjects, the same loading path, a different spec.

docs.title: 15 · Does the onset predictor earn its place?¶
docs.text:
TFCE asks whether a kernel differs from zero. A different question is which model spec describes the cohort better — and no held-out metric can answer it, because adding a feature block almost never makes the fit worse.

compare_to ranks the two cohorts by AIC and BIC, which price the extra complexity, and reports the comparison two ways rather than choosing one quietly:

  • random effects (median, n_favouring_self, wilcoxon) — each subject is one observation, so an unusual subject shows up in the vector instead of dominating;
  • fixed effects (total) — the cohort as one large model, dominated by whoever contributed the most data.

When the two disagree, that is the finding, not something to resolve by picking the convenient one.

Two sign conventions to keep straight: the difference is self − other and lower is better for both criteria, so a positive delta favours other. That is the opposite of permutation_test_contrast, where a positive t_obs favours self.

docs.title: 16 · Persisting a fitted cohort¶
docs.text: A fitted cohort is a result, and results should outlive the session that produced them. save writes the whole object — kernels, metrics, λ, diagnostics, cached statistics — and trflearn.load restores one with the same API, so every figure above can be redrawn without touching the 4 GB of source data again.

docs.title: 17 · Summary¶
docs.text:
.fif (broadband, ICA-cleaned, mastoid-referenced)
   -> linear-phase FIR 1.5-14 Hz, zero-phase
   -> mne.Raw + Envelope / Onset predictors
   -> TRFData(y=[Raw, ...])  ->  create_partitions(5 folds, block-stratified)
        |
        |-- Part I   TRFGroup(["Envelope"])            -> the classic P1/N1/P2 kernel
        |-- Part II  TRFGroup(["Envelope", "Onset"])   -> joint estimation + GVIF
        |
   -> grand average -> TFCE over delays x channels -> AIC/BIC comparison

What was demonstrated. A container of named candidate features from which each model selects its own subset; mne.Raw ingestion carrying the montage all the way through to the group statistics; delay_margin fitting wide and trimming the edge artefact away; four λ selection rules compared on one subject, including a smoothness-preferring one; design diagnostics before and after a second block exists to compare against; the complete plotting API at model, cohort and single-subject level; bootstrap distributions per subject; TFCE with a real sensor adjacency; AIC/BIC model comparison under both random- and fixed-effects readings; and a save/load round trip.

What was not established. Held-out correlations of a few hundredths are normal for single-trial continuous speech, but they are small. Nothing here says the envelope is the right representation of speech — only that it predicts above chance. Section 15 ranks two specifications against each other; it does not suggest the winner is correct. And every result inherits the upstream choices described in section 1, including a band-pass that shapes the width of every kernel plotted above.

def impulse_series(onsets_s: np.ndarray, sfreq: float, n_samples: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Unit impulses at the given onset times (seconds from recording start)."""
    idx = np.round(np.asarray(onsets_s, dtype=float) * sfreq).astype(int)
    idx = idx[(idx >= 0) & (idx < n_samples)]
    series = np.zeros(n_samples, dtype=np.float64)
    series[idx] = 1.0
    return series


def beamform_to_parcels(meg: mne.io.BaseRaw, subject_id: str):
    """Project sensors onto parcel centroids -> (Raw of regions, centroids)."""
    src_dir = SOURCE_ROOT / subject_id

    filters = read_beamformer(src_dir / LCMV_TEMPLATE.format(sid=subject_id))
    stc = apply_lcmv_raw(meg, filters)

    # The forward is read only for src["rr"] -- the centroid coordinates.
    fwd = mne.read_forward_solution(
        src_dir / FWD_TEMPLATE.format(sid=subject_id), verbose="ERROR")
    src = fwd["src"]
    labels = mne.read_labels_from_annot(
        subject_id, parc=PARC, subjects_dir=SUBJECTS_DIR, verbose="ERROR")

    names, centroids, timecourses = [], [], []
    seen = set()
    for hemi_idx, hemi in enumerate(("lh", "rh")):
        hemi_labels = [lab for lab in labels if lab.hemi == hemi]
        offset = 0 if hemi_idx == 0 else len(stc.vertices[0])
        for row, vertex in enumerate(stc.vertices[hemi_idx]):
            owner = next((lab.name for lab in hemi_labels if vertex in lab.vertices),
                         f"{hemi}_vert{vertex}")
            # One row per label. A few labels catch two source-space vertices, and
            # which ones differs between subjects; keeping both would make
            # mne.create_info append '-0'/'-1' and those names would no longer
            # match the same region in the next subject, so the cohort
            # intersection would drop the region entirely.
            if owner in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(owner)
            names.append(owner)
            centroids.append(src[hemi_idx]["rr"][vertex])
            timecourses.append(stc.data[offset + row])

    info = mne.create_info(names, meg.info["sfreq"], ch_types="misc", verbose="ERROR")
    raw_src = mne.io.RawArray(np.asarray(timecourses), info, verbose="ERROR")
    # Re-referenced to the recording start, which a RawArray has no meas_date for.
    raw_src.set_annotations(mne.Annotations(
        onset=meg.annotations.onset - meg.first_time,
        duration=meg.annotations.duration,
        description=meg.annotations.description))
    return raw_src, np.asarray(centroids)

def load_subject(subject_id: str) -> TRFData:
    """Parcel timecourses and the three predictors of one participant."""
    subject_dir = DATA_ROOT / subject_id
    raw = mne.io.read_raw_fif(subject_dir / f"DA2_{subject_id}_meg.fif",
                              preload=False, verbose="ERROR")
    sfreq = raw.info["sfreq"]

    # Read before picking the sensors, so they survive the pick.
    steering = raw.get_data(picks="Steering")[0]
    gas = raw.get_data(picks="Gas")[0]

    # Radial (Z) magnetometers only -- the set the beamformer was built for.
    picks = [ch for ch, kind in zip(raw.ch_names, raw.get_channel_types())
             if kind == "mag" and ch.endswith(" Z")]
    meg = raw.copy().pick(picks).load_data(verbose="ERROR")
    meg.info.normalize_proj()
    n_samples = meg.n_times

    raw_src, centroids = beamform_to_parcels(meg, subject_id)

    # Onsets in the CSVs are already relative to the file start.
    saccades = pd.read_csv(subject_dir / "saccades.csv")
    features = {
        "saccades": impulse_series(saccades["onset"].to_numpy(), sfreq, n_samples),
        "steering_wheel": np.gradient(steering),
        "gas_pedal": np.gradient(gas),
    }
    features = {name: series.reshape(-1, 1) for name, series in features.items()}

    data = TRFData(features=features, y=raw_src, sample_rate=int(sfreq))
    data.set_source_positions(centroids)      # the one source-space-specific call
    data.create_partitions(n_folds=N_FOLDS)
    return data
